Grignard addition to an ester: methylmagnesium bromide reacts with methyl octanoate to give the tertiary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑nonanol and methanol as the leaving‑group alcohol. Two equivalents of the Grignard reagent add sequentially to the carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide that is hydrolyzed on work‑up. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using an in‑situ generated peroxyacid (etic acid + hydrogen peroxide). This peracid oxidation converts the pyrrole‑2‑carbaldehyde functional group into pyrrole‑2‑carboxylic acid, with water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions are dilute acetic acid as solvent, 0–25 °C, and gentle stirring; no metal catalyst is required.

Catalytic reductive amination of 2‑formylpyridine with ammonia. Hydrogen gas in the presence of Raney nickel reduces the imine intermediate formed from the aldehyde and ammonia, yielding 2‑pyridyl‑methanamine (a primary amine). Reactions are carried out under 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol; Raney Ni acts as both hydrogenation and dehydrogenation catalyst.

Eschweiler‑Clarke methylation of benzylamine with formaldehyde and formic acid; the primary amine is converted to the N‑methyl secondary amine with loss of CO₂ and H₂O. Reaction is performed by heating benzylamine with excess aqueous formaldehyde (37 % w/w) and formic acid (≈ 10 % v/v) under reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; the process is acid‑catalyzed and proceeds in a sealed tube or round‑bottom flask.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol to the corresponding alkene. Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates the hydroxyl group, facilitating loss of water and formation of 2‑methyl‑1‑butene via an E1 mechanism. The reaction is performed at 140–180 °C, often in the acid itself as solvent or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., toluene) under reflux.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis reaction lead(II) chromate and sodium hydroxide. Hydroxide ions replace the chromate anion, giving soluble sodium chromate and insoluble lead(II) hydroxide precipitate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete exchange.

Acid–base neutralization; calcium oxide (basic oxide) reacts with sulfuric acid to form the salt calcium sulfate and water. Purpose is to generate gypsum or remove acid. Key transformation: O^2– + 2H^+ → H2O and Ca^2+ + SO4^2– → CaSO4. Typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or gentle heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde using sodium bromate as the oxidant in the presence of CuCl₂/HCl. The bromate acts as the terminal oxidant while Cu(II) mediates electron transfer under acidic conditions, converting the primary alcohol to the aldehyde with formation of NaCl, NaBr, and water. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–2 M), CuCl₂ catalytic amount (0.1 eq), NaBrO₃ (1 eq), temperature 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation.

Acid‑base formation of a double salt (chromic potassium sulfate) from chromium(III) oxide, potassium sulfate, and sulfuric acid. The oxide dissolves in hot concentrated H₂SO₄ to give chromic sulfate, which then combines with K₂SO₄ to precipitate K₂Cr₂(SO₄)₃ (chromic potassium sulfate) while water is liberated. Reaction is performed by heating the mixture of solid reagents in excess H₂SO₄ (≈95 %) until a clear solution forms, then cooling to crystallize the double salt.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (acyl substitution); 3‑methylthiophene‑2‑carbonyl chloride reacts with methanol to give methyl 3‑methylthiophene‑2‑carboxylate and HCl; nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl carbon, chloride leaves; carried out in excess methanol as solvent, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; temperature ambient to reflux.

Acid‑catalyzed trans‑orthoester exchange (formation of an alkyl orthoester). Trimethyl orthoformate reacts with ethanol in the presence of catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid to replace one methoxy group with an ethoxy group, producing ethyl orthoformate and liberating methanol. Conditions: catalytic amount of p‑TsOH (≈5 mol %), anhydrous solvent such as toluene or benzene, reflux temperature; methanol is removed by distillation to drive the equilibrium to the products.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated reduction) of a tertiary alkyl chloride. Zinc dust serves as a reducing metal, abstracting the chloride from tert‑butyl chloride and delivering a proton (from trace water or solvent) to afford 2‑methylpropane (isobutane) while forming zinc chloride. Typical conditions: excess zinc dust in dry ether or THF, gentle reflux or room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Gas‑phase oxidation (combustion‑type redox) of disulfur monoxide by molecular oxygen. O₂ oxidizes S₂O to yield sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and sulfur monoxide (SO); the reaction proceeds at elevated temperature (often >300 °C) in the gas phase, sometimes in a flow reactor. No solvent; the process is catalytic in the sense that radical chain propagation, but no added catalyst is needed.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde. Phenylmagnesium bromide adds to acetaldehyde, forming a new C–C bond; after aqueous work‑up the alkoxide is protonated to give 1‑phenylethanol, while magnesium bromide remains as a salt. Conditions: anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), low temperature (0 °C) during addition followed by gradual warming to room temperature; quench with dilute ammonium chloride or aqueous acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) N‑alkylation of glycine; purpose: synthesis of N‑methylglycine (sarcosine); key transformation: methyl iodide reacts with the deprotonated amine of glycine (generated by NaOH) to form an N‑CH3 bond, releasing I⁻ and producing NaI; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH, excess base, ambient to moderate heating; solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: preparation of aluminum oxalate; key transformation: exchange of Na⁺ and Al³⁺ ions forming insoluble aluminum oxalate (Al(C₂O₄)₃) and NaCl in solution; typical conditions: aqueous solutions stirred at room temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Direct chlorination (halogenation); purpose is to prepare thulium chloride; key transformation: Tm2O3 + 3 Cl2 → 2 TmCl3 + 3/2 O2 (or O2); carried out at high temperature (300–600 °C) under a chlorine gas flow, using equipment resistant to chlorine; no solvent, no catalyst.

Metallothermic reduction (single‑replacement redox) of VCl₄ by sodium metal to give elemental vanadium and sodium chloride. Usually carried out in an anhydrous inert atmosphere, often in a sealed tube or melt at 300‑500 °C; sometimes performed in dry ether or THF at lower temperature, no additional solvent.

Chlorination/halogenolysis of silicon sulfide; purpose: conversion of SiS₂ to SiCl₄ and SCl₂; key transformation: replacement of Si–S bonds by Si–Cl and S–Cl bonds, yielding silicon tetrachloride and sulfur dichloride gases; typical conditions: dry Cl₂ gas passed over solid SiS₂ at 0–200 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent (gas‑phase); no catalyst.

Solid‑gas reduction; purpose: lower the oxidation state of mixed‑valent terbium oxide (Tb₄O₇) to terbium(III) oxide (Tb₂O₃); key transformation: reduction of Tb₄O₇ by H₂, with oxygen transferred to hydrogen to give water (Tb₄O₇ + H₂ → 2 Tb₂O₃ + H₂O); typical conditions: flow of H₂ gas over powdered Tb₄O₇ at 500–900 °C, quartz or alumina reactor, no solvent, inert carrier gas optional.

Halide exchange/oxidation state shift; purpose: generation of antimony(V) chloride from SbCl₃; key transformation: PCl₅ transfers two chloride ions to SbCl₃, producing SbCl₅ and reducing to PCl₃; typical conditions anhydrous, inert atmosphere, dry non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, 0–25 °C; no catalyst.

Acid‑base proton transfer (salt metathesis); purpose: liberation of formic acid and formation of tetramethylammonium hydrogen sulfate; key transformation: H⁺ from H₂SO₄ protonates the formate anion to give HCOOH, while the sulfate anion pairs with tetramethylammonium; typical conditions: aqueous or aqueous‑organic medium at ambient temperature; solvent: water or water‑methanol; no catalyst.

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction; purpose is cation exchange to obtain potassium malate. Disodium malate reacts with potassium carbonate in aqueous solution, swapping Na⁺ and K⁺ ions to form potassium malate and sodium carbonate. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Phosgenation (isocyanate formation); purpose: synthesis of 1,3‑diisocyanatobenzene from m‑phenylenediamine; key transformation: each –NH₂ group reacts with diphosgene to give an N‑COCl intermediate that eliminates HCl to form an isocyanate, overall producing 4 HCl; typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or toluene), base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge HCl, 0 °C to room temperature then gentle reflux; catalyst: optional DMAP; inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution/cyclization. Ethylenediamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of carbonyl diimidazole, displacing imidazole and forming a five‑membered cyclic urea (2‑imidazolidinone). Imidazole is released as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous organic solvent (THF, DMF, CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to rt, no additional catalyst required.

Acid–baseization (salt formation). Two equivalents of heptanoic acid are deprotonated by sodium carbonate, yielding two equivalents of sodium heptanoate and carbonic acid, which rapidly decomposes to CO2 and H2O. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acyl chloride formation using oxalyl chloride. Fluoroacetic acid reacts with oxalyl chloride, producingoroacetyl chloride while releasing gaseous by‑products CO, CO2 and HCl. Performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement metathesis/precipitation. Potassium sulfate exchanges anions with mercury(I) acetate, giving insoluble mercurous sulfate (Hg2SO4) as a precipitate and soluble potassium acetate in solution. Conducted in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide. Morpholine attacks the less‑substituted carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to afford N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)morpholine. Reaction proceeds in polar aprotic solvents (THF, acetonitrile) at 0–50 °C; no catalyst is required, though a base can be added to suppress polymerization.

Grignard substitution on phosphorus (nucleophilic substitution of P‑Cl by phenyl groups); employed to install diphenylphosphino substituents on a benzene scaffold, yielding 1,2‑bis(diphenylphosphino)benzene. Two equivalents of phenylmagnesium bromide attack the PCl bonds of 1,2‑bis(dichlorophosphino)benzene, producing MgClBr as by‑product. is carried out in dry THF (or Et₂O) at –78 °C to 0 °C under argon, with excess Grignard reagent (2–3 equiv) and slow addition to control exotherm.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Diphenylcarbazone is reduced by molecular hydrogen in the presence of palladium on carbon, converting the =N–N= functionality to the corresponding diphenylcarbazide (hydrazide). Typical conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature ambient to reflux.

Metal‑metallothermic reduction; sodium reduces osmium tetrachloride to elemental osmium while being oxidized to sodium chloride. Key transformation: OsCl4 + 4 Na → Os + 4 NaCl. Typically carried out under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (argon) in dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature; sodium is used as a solid piece or dispersion. No catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert nicotinic (pyridine‑3‑carboxylic) acid into its methyl ester (methyl nicotinate). Key transformation: replacement of the carboxylic‑OH by –OCH₃ with formation of water. Typical conditions: reflux of nicotinic acid in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of hydrochloric acid (often 2–5 % v/v); water removed by azeotropic distillation or Dean–Stark trap. No special solvent beyond methanol; acid acts as catalyst.

Epoxide ring‑opening fluorination of ethylene oxide with hydrogen fluoride to afford 2‑fluoroethanol; HF adds across the strained three‑membered ring, yielding HO‑CH₂‑CH₂F; typically performed at 0‑50 °C in anhydrous HF or HF‑pyridine (HF‑Py) medium, sometimes with a Lewis‑acid catalyst (e.g., BF₃·OEt₂) and a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile; inert atmosphere is used to avoid side reactions.

Redox (oxidative decomposition) of hydroxylamine by manganese(IV) oxide in strongly acidic medium. Purpose is to destroy hydroxylamine, generating nitrogen gas. Key transformation: hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) is oxidized to N₂, MnO₂ is reduced to Mn²⁺, which complexes as manganese(II) sulfate; water is formed from the acid‑base steps. Typical conditions: aqueous solution containing sulfuric acid (conc. or 1–2 M), solid MnO₂ added, then hydroxylamine sulfate; mixture is heated gently (0–50 °C) until gas evolution ceases. No organic solvent needed.

Nitrile reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; a strong, non‑catalytic reduction that converts the –CN group of phenylacetonitrile into a primary amine, yielding phenethylamine. Typically carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, refluxing or at reflux temperature, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere. No additional catalyst is required; work‑up involves careful quenching with water or dilute acid.

Halide exchange (metathesis) between gallium(III) chloride and hydrofluoric acid; chloride is displaced by fluoride producing gallium(III) fluoride and hydrogen chloride; generally conducted in aqueous or gaseous HF, often under reflux; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of acetic acid with isoamyl (3‑methyl‑1‑butanol) alcohol. Purpose is to produce isoamyl acetate, a banana‑flavor ester. Key transformation: acetic acid loses –OH, isoamyl alcohol loses –H, forming isoamyl acetate and water. Typical conditions: reflux in excess isoamyl alcohol (or use of a Dean–Stark trap) with catalytic sulfuric acid (≈5 % v/v) or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; reaction time 2–6 h. No additional solvent needed; the alcohol acts as both reactant and solvent.

This is a catalytic hydrogenation reaction, specifically hydrogenolysis, used to remove carbamate protecting groups and produce amines. The key transformation is the reduction of the carbamate functional group in benzyl carbamate to yield benzylamine and carbon dioxide. Typical conditions include hydrogen gas under moderate pressure, palladium on carbon as a catalyst, and solvents such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature.

Oxidative disulfide formation with hypochlorite; sodium hypochlorite (bleach) oxidizes butyl mercaptan to dibutyl disulfide. The thiol is converted to the disulfide while the oxidant is reduced to chloride, producing NaCl and water. Typically performed in aqueous alkaline solution (pH ≈ 8–9) at 0–25 °C; the reaction is rapid and may be quenched with a reducing agent if over‑oxidation is a concern.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl acetate with phenol to give phenyl acetate and ethanol. Purpose is synthesis of phenyl acetate, an aromatic ester. Key transformation: exchange of the alkoxy group: EtO‑C(=O)CH₃ + PhOH → PhO‑C(=O)CH₃ + EtOH. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous ethanol or toluene with a catalytic amount of sodium ethoxide or potassium carbonate; reaction proceeds 3–12 h. Removal of ethanol (by distillation) drives the equilibrium toward product.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl acetoacetate with methanol, yielding methyl acetoacetate and ethanol. Purpose is to prepare the methyl ester for further condensation reactions. Key transformation: EtO‑C(=O)CH₂‑C(=O)CH₃ + CH₃OH ⇌ Me‑C(=O)CH₂‑C(=O)CH₃ + EtOH. Typical conditions: reflux methanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (≈1 % v/v) or catalytic amount of sodium methoxide; reaction time 1–4 h. Excess methanol or azeotropic removal of ethanol shifts equilibrium to the methyl ester.

This is an acid-base neutralization reaction. Calcium methoxide (a strong base) reacts with phosphoric acid (a triprotic acid) to form calcium phosphate (an inorganic salt) and methanol. The reaction occurs via stepwise protonation of the methoxide ions by phosphoric acid. The final product may depend on the stoichiometry and pH, but calcium phosphate precipitates as a solid. Conditions typically involve aqueous or alcoholic solvents, and the reaction is exothermic. No catalysts are required.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; used to prepare N‑nitrosamines for study or synthesis. Sodium nitrite provides nitrosonium (NO⁺) which attacks the piperidine nitrogen, forming N‑nitrosopiperidine and water; the acetate anion pairs with Na⁺ to give sodium acetate. Performed in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute acetic acid or HCl) at 0–5 °C to limit side reactions; common solvent is water or a water/acetone mixture; no metal catalyst required.

Reaction type: hydrolysis of an acid chloride. Purpose: convert the reactive N,N‑dimethylcarbamoyl chloride into the corresponding carbamic acid and generate HCl as by‑product. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon, displacement of chloride ion. Typical conditions: aqueous work‑up at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is often performed in a biphasic system (e.g., CH2Cl2/H2O) with a base such as pyridine or NaHCO3 to trap the liberated HCl. Common solvents/catalysts: dichloromethane or THF as organic phase, water as nucleophile, pyridine (or other tertiary amine) as HCl scavenger.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; converts the strained double bond of 1‑methylcyclopropene to the saturated 1‑methylcyclopropane. Hydrogen gas adds across the C=C bond in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) under 1–5 atm H₂, typically at room temperature to 50 °C. Solvent is usually a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol; reaction proceeds to completion with complete consumption of the alkene.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); hydrogen selenide (a weak diprotic acid) reacts with NaOH, deprotonating to give the hydrogen selenide anion (HS⁻) as sodium hydrogen selenide and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring ensures complete neutralization. No catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) of metal salts; Ag⁺ ions exchange with Cs⁺ ions to form insoluble silver phosphate (Ag₃PO₄) and soluble cesium nitrate (CsNO₃). Performed in water at room temperature; the silver phosphate precipitates and is filtered off. No catalyst; the reaction is driven by the low solubility product of Ag₃PO₄.

Metathesis (ion‑exchange) of nitrate and tetrafluoroborate salts; potassium nitrate and ammonium tetrafluoroborate exchange cations to afford ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) and potassium tetrafluoroborate (KBF₄). Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; both products remain soluble, and separation may be achieved by crystallization or selective precipitation. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (neutralization with gas evolution); acetic acid reacts with magnesium carbonate, protonating the carbonate to release CO₂ gas and forming magnesium acetate. Conducted in water or aqueous acetic acid at room temperature with stirring; the CO₂ bubbles out, driving the reaction forward. No catalyst required.

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation of 1‑chloro‑4‑methylbenzene with aqueous potassium permanganate under alkaline conditions (NaOH/KMnO₄) and heat (reflux). Converts the benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid, giving 4‑chlorobenzoic acid; water is formed as a by‑product. Reaction is typically carried out in water or aqueous acetone.

Redox precipitation; elemental selenium is produced by reducing selenious acid (Se^IV) while nitrite is oxidized to nitrate (N^V). Typically carried out in aqueous solution under acidic conditions, often at room temperature or mild heating; no external catalyst required. Water is the solvent and the reaction yields solid selenium precipitate.

SN1 hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl chloride; water attacks the carbocation formed from 2‑chloro‑2,4‑dimethylpentane, yielding 2,4‑dimethylpentan‑2‑ol and releasing HCl. Conducted by heating the chloride in aqueous media (often water or aqueous ethanol) at reflux; acid or neutral conditions may be used to promote ionization, no catalyst required.

Gattermann–Koch formylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); ethylbenzene is formylated by CO and HCl in the presence of AlCl₃ (Lewis acid) and CuCl (co‑catalyst) to give 4‑ethylbenzaldehyde. The reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, typically in a dry, inert solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂, at 0–50 °C and under a CO atmosphere (1–5 atm). No additional reagents beyond the listed Lewis acids are needed.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; purpose is to convert the basic silver oxide into a soluble silver salt; key transformation: silver oxide reacts with tetrafluoroboric acid to form silver tetrafluoroborate and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; solvent is water; no catalyst required.

Sulfonylation to form a mesylate ester; cyclohexanol reacts with methanesulfonyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the generated HCl, yielding cyclohexyl methanesulfonate. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF under inert atmosphere; the base (triethylamine) is essential to neutralize HCl.

General type: acyl chloride esterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: synthesize propyl benzoate. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of n‑propyl alcohol attacks benzoyl chloride, forming the ester and HCl, which is trapped by pyridine to give pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: pyridine used as both solvent and base, reaction carried out at 0 °C to room temperature under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; dry conditions are required.

General type: Fischer esterification of a carylic acid with ethanol. Purpose: prepare the ethyl ester of 2‑(4‑chlorophenoxy)‑2‑methylpropionic acid. Key transformation: the carbonyl of the acid is protonated, ethanol attacks, and water is eliminated, giving the ester. Typical conditions: reflux in excess ethanol with catalytic strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid), often with a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water; ethanol serves as solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed rearrangement/dehydration of α‑terpineol to 1,8‑cineole; involves protonation of the allylic alcohol, intramolecular cyclization and loss of water to give the bicyclic ether; performed with dilute to conc. H₂SO₄ at 0–30 °C to avoid polymerization; solvent may be dichloromethane or the substrate itself; reaction is typically quenched with ice‑water.

E2 elimination of tert‑butyl chloride with aqueous potassium hydroxide to give 2‑methylpropene; purpose is formation of an alkene from a tertiary halide. Key transformation: removal of H and Cl to form C=C. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH, heating (often 60‑100 °C); water serves as solvent; reaction proceeds under basic conditions without added catalyst.

General type: reduction of a sulfone to a sulfide. Purpose: convert methyl phenyl sulfone into thioanisole. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ reduces both S=O bonds, replacing them with hydrogen to afford the thioether. Typical conditions: dry ethereal solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C followed by reflux; reaction performed under nitrogen or argon; work‑up involves careful quench with water or dilute acid.

General type: N‑alkylation (quaternization) of acridine nitrogen by methyl bromide followed by halide exchange. Purpose: generate the methylacridinium salt with chloride as counter‑ion. Key transformation: the lone pair on the nitrogen of 3,6‑diaminacridine attacks methyl bromide in an SN2 step, giving the acridinium bromide; anion exchange with NaCl replaces bromide with chloride, producing sodium bromide. Typical conditions: reflux in polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, excess methyl bromide, and NaCl present; reaction run under sealed tube or inert atmosphere to contain volatile methyl bromide.

Hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate; purpose: conversion to the corresponding acid; key transformation: cleavage of the methyl ester to give 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoic acid and methanol; typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (NaOH) at reflux, water or water/methanol solvent mixture.

General type: acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (Markovnikov hydration) of an alkene. Purpose: convert cyclohexene to cyclohexanol. Key transformation: protonation of the double bond to form a carbocation at the more substituted carbon, followed by nucleophilic attack of water and deprotonation to give the alcohol. Typical conditions: dilute aqueous sulfuric acid (≈1–5 %), temperature 0–50 °C; water acts as solvent; reaction may be performed in a biphasic system with vigorous stirring.

Thermal decomposition of mercury(II) nitrate; type: decomposition reaction. Upon strong heating (≈200–300 °C) solid Hg(NO₃)₂ breaks down to mercury(II) oxide (HgO) solid, nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) gas, and oxygen (O₂) gas. Reaction is carried out in a dry furnace or heating mantle; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (hydroiodic cleavage). HI protonates the ether oxygen, then iodide attacks the secondary carbon, breaking the C–O bond to give a secondary alkyl iodide and methanol. Typically performed with excess HI, reflux heating, often neat or in a polar solvent such as ethanol; no additional catalyst required.

Direct halogenation (synthesis): elemental rhenium is combined with bromine gas to form rhenium tribromide. The metal is oxidized while bromine is reduced, yielding the covalent metal halide. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often by heating Re metal in a sealed tube or quartz ampoule with Br₂ at 200–300 °C; inert atmosphere, no solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of an α‑bromo ketone. 4‑Bromobutan‑2‑one reacts with water, typically under reflux in aqueous ethanol or water, to replace the bromide with a hydroxyl group, yielding 4‑hydroxybutan‑2‑one and HBr (which is neutralized by the solvent). The reaction proceeds via SN1/SN2 depending on conditions; no additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement/precipitation metathesis; aqueous mixture of NaOH and zinc chromate; NaOH converts the chromate anion to soluble sodium chromate while Zn²⁺ precipitates as zinc hydroxide; performed at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst needed.

Dehydrative chlorination (acyl chloride formation) using triphosgene; each molecule of hexanoic acid is converted to hexanoyl chloride with evolution of CO₂ and HCl; typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, with a base such as triethylamine to capture HCl; inert atmosphere, no added catalyst.

Redox oxidation of sodium hypophosphite by nitric acid; hypophosphite (P + 1) is oxidized to phosphate (P + 5) while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide; typically performed in aqueous solution with dilute HNO₃ at 0–70 °C, no additional catalyst, water as solvent.

Lewis‑acid mediated ether cleavage (dealkylation) with boron tribromide; the para‑methoxy group of 4‑methoxy‑3‑ethoxybenzaldehyde is demethylated to a phenol, releasing methyl bromide and giving ethylvanillin; performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen; BBr₃ acts as the reagent, no additional catalyst.

Grignard formation (organomagnesium synthesis); purpose is to prepare isopropylmagnesium iodide as a nucleophilic carbon reagent. Anhydrous Mg turnings insert into one C–I bond of 2,2‑diiodopropane in dry diethyl ether or THF under nitrogen or argon, producing the Grignard reagent (i‑PrMgI) and magnesium iodide as a by‑product. The mixture is usually refluxed or heated gently; catalyst may be a small iodine crystal to activate Mg.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification): the butyl ester of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid is cleaved by aqueous NaOH, producing sodium p‑hydroxybenzoate and n‑butanol; typically performed in water or aqueous ethanol with reflux heating.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to a chloride (nucleophilic substitution) using thionyl chloride; the –OH of 4‑chloro‑1butanol is replaced by Cl, producing 1,4‑dichlorobutane with gaseous by‑products HCl and SO₂; usually carried out in anhydrous pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine can act as HCl scavenger.

Electrophilic addition of halogen across a carbon–carbon double bond; Cl₂ adds to 1‑butene to give the vicinal 1,2‑dichlorobutane via a bromonium‑like chloronium intermediate; reaction proceeds at room temperature in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or CHCl₃; no catalyst required.

Acid‑salt reaction with gas evolution; sulfuric acid protonates the sulfite ion of calcium sulfite, releasing SO₂ gas and forming water; the remaining calcium ion with sulfate to precipitate calcium sulfate; typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off SO₂; no catalyst needed.

Amide‑formation (condensation) between propionic acid and dimethylamine to give N,N‑dimethylpropionamide. Because direct dehydration of a carboxylic acid with an amine is inefficient, the acid is usually activated first (e.g., conversion to the acid chloride with SOCl₂ or formation of an activated ester using DCC/DMAP). The activated acid is then reacted with dimethylamine in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, with a tertiary amine base (e.g., triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HCl. Water is formed after aqueous work‑up.

Metallurgical comproportionation/reduction: elemental zirconium reduces zirconium tetrabromide (ZrBr4) to the lower bromide zirconium tribromide (ZrBr3). Conducted in a sealed tube or high‑temperature furnace under an inert atmosphere (argon) at temperatures of 400–800 °C; no solvent is used, and the product is isolated as a solid halide.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis): ammonium oxalate reacts with iron(III) sulfate in aqueous solution to precipitate insoluble iron(III) oxalate while forming soluble ammonium sulfate in the filtrate. Performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the medium, and the solid iron(III) oxalate is collected by filtration and washing.

Dehydration/condensation of sulfuric acid: upon heating concentrated H2SO4, two molecules condense with loss of one water molecule to give disulfuric acid (pyrosulfuric acid, H2S2O7). The reaction occurs at temperatures above ~140 °C under reflux; excess sulfuric acid acts both as reactant and solvent, and water is removed azeotropically or by distillation.

Ether cleavage (dealkylation) with boron tribromide: BBr3 attacks furfuryl methyl ether, cleaving the C–O bond and generating methyl bromide (CH3Br) and furfuryl alcohol. Reaction is performed in anhydrous dichloromethane (or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; stoichiometric BBr3 is added dropwise, and the mixture is quenched with ice/water after completion.

Acid–base neutralization with bicarbonate: perrhenic acid (HReO4) reacts with potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) in aqueous solution, producing potassium perrhenate (KReO4) and carbonic acid, which instantly decomposes to CO2 gas and water. The reaction proceeds at room temperature with effervescence; the inorganic salt precipitates (or remains dissolved) depending on concentration, and CO2 evolution drives the equilibrium forward.

Grignard addition followed by oxidation; magnesium turnings generate 3‑thiophenylmagnesium bromide from 3‑bromothiophene, which attacks ethylene oxide to give 3‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)thiophene; the primary alcohol is then oxidized with sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid to the corresponding carboxylic acid (3‑thiophenacetic acid). Typical conditions: anhydrous ether, inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux for Grignard step; then acidic dichromate oxidation at 80‑100 °C. No additional solvent needed beyond ether and aqueous acid.

This is an acid-base neutralization reaction. It converts salicylic acid into its water-soluble sodium salt (sodium salicylate) using sodium hydroxide. The reaction occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, producing water as a byproduct.

Substitution (chlorination) of both the phenolic and benzylic alcohol groups; thionyl chloride converts the 2‑hydroxy group of salicyl alcohol to a chloride and simultaneously replaces the benzylic –CH2OH with –CH2Cl, yielding 2‑chlorobenzyl chloride. Conditions usually involve refluxing the substrate in excess SOCl₂ (often 50‑80 °C) under anhydrous conditions; pyridine or triethylamine may be added as an HCl scavenger. The reaction produces gaseous SO₂ and HCl as by‑products.

Protonolysis (hydrolysis) of a strong non‑nucleophilic base; one equivalent of water protonates sodium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (NaHMDS) to give hexamethyldisilazane (HN(SiMe₃)₂) and sodium hydroxide. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in an aprotic solvent such as THF or directly as a neat mixture; no catalyst is required.

Partial (incomplete) combustion of carbon (charcoal) in limited oxygen; elemental carbon reacts with O₂ to produce a mixture of carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. The process is a redox oxidation of carbon; it occurs at high temperature (≥700 °C) in a flame or heated furnace where O₂ supply is restricted, resulting in CO as a major product alongside CO₂.

Acylation (amide formation) of the α‑amino group of DL‑aspartic acid; acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the amino nitrogen, catalyzed by 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP), giving N‑acetyl‑DL‑aspartic acid and liberating acetic acid. Typical conditions: room temperature to 40 °C, solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, catalytic DMAP (5‑10 mol %). Reaction is generally fast and proceeds to completion in 1‑2h.

E2 elimination using potassium tert‑butoxide; converts 2‑bromo‑1‑chloropropane to the alkene 1‑chloroprop‑1‑ene by abstracting a β‑hydrogen and expelling bromide; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or THF at 0–100 °C.

General type: combustion (complete oxidation) of an alkane. Purpose: convert chemical energy to heat, producing CO₂ and H₂O. Key transformation: C–H and C–C bonds of methylcyclobutane are broken and oxygen is reduced, yielding carbon dioxide and water. Typical conditions: excess O₂, ignition temperature (~500 °C) in open air or flame, atmospheric pressure. No solvent; reaction occurs in the gas phase, sometimes aided by a spark or flame.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Methoxide ion abstracts a proton from L‑ascorbic acid, yielding methanol and the sodium salt of ascorbic acid (sodium ascorbate). Typically carried out in aqueous or methanolic solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Exchange of anions produces soluble zinc chloride and poorly soluble calcium sulfate, which precipitates out. Conducted in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement) reaction. Samarium metal reduces hydrofluoric acid, generating hydrogen gas and samarium(III) fluoride. Usually performed by adding samarium to excess HF at room temperature under controlled, corrosion‑resistant equipment; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification with an acyl chloride); menthol’s hydroxyl attacks benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give menthyl benzoate and HCl; conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Reaction type: acylation of an aromatic amine (amide formation). Purpose: introduce an acetyl protecting group on 3‑methoxyaniline. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the aniline nitrogen on acetic anhydride, producing N‑(3‑methoxyphenyl)acetamide and acetic acid. Typical conditions: reaction in pyridine or anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with pyridine acting as both solvent and acid scavenger; reaction time 1–2 h. No metal catalyst is required.

Palladium‑catalyzed amination (Buchwald‑Hartwig C–N coupling) of 1‑iodo‑2‑methylbenzene with ammonia; Pd(OAc)₂ with triethylamine as base converts the aryl iodide to 2‑methylaniline, forming triethylammonium iodide as by‑product; typical solvent DMF or toluene, temperature 80–120 °C, under an NH₃ atmosphere or in NH₃‑sat. solution.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) using an acyl fluoride. Methanol attacks trifluoroacetyl fluoride, forming methyl trifluoroacetate and releasing HF. Reaction is typically run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) added to scavenge the HF.

Selective oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide. Thioanisole is oxidized by sodium hypochlorite in the presence of the nitroxyl radical TEMPO, producing methyl phenyl sulfoxide, water and sodium chloride. Common conditions: aqueous buffered medium (pH 8–10), 0 °C to rt, often with a biphasic organic/aqueous solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂/H₂O); TEMPO acts as the catalytic oxidant.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an azo bond. Azobenzene is hydrogenated over platinum on carbon under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) to give hydrazobenzene. Typical setup uses a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to moderate temperature; Pt/C serves as the heterogeneous catalyst.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) using an anhydride. Purpose: convert the primary amine of 2‑amino‑1‑propanol into the corresponding methacrylamide while generating methacrylic acid as a stoichiometric by‑product. Key transformation: the lone pair on nitrogen attacks one carbonyl of methacrylic anhydride, forming N‑(2‑hydroxypropyl)methacrylamide and releasing methacrylic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; a base (triethylamine or pyridine) is added to neutralize the liberated acid. Reaction is generally short (1–2 h) and monitored by TLC.

Acid‑base decomposition of sulfite; hydrochloric acid protonates ammonium sulfite, giving ammonium chloride, water, and sulfur dioxide gas; conducted in water at low temperature (0–25 °C) with vigorous stirring to vent SO₂; no catalyst.

Type: metal‑mediated reductive dehalogenation. Purpose: remove the two bromine atoms from 1,4‑dibromo‑2,3‑butanediol to afford the diol 2,3‑butanediol. Key transformation: zinc dust donates electrons to the C–Br bonds, forming ZnBr₂ and generating carbon‑hydrogen bonds in place of the C‑Br bonds. Typical conditions: excess zinc dust in a polar protic solvent (e.g., aqueous ethanol or acetic acid) under reflux, often with stirring for several hours. The reaction may be performed under nitrogen to avoid oxidation.

Type: condensative cyclocondensation (heterocycle formation) leading to a pyrazine. Purpose: synthesize tetramethylpyrazine, a flavor compound, from diketone precursors. Key transformation: three molecules of 2,3‑butanedione condense with two equivalents of ammonium acetate; ammonia from the acetate reacts with carbonyl groups to form dihydropyrazine intermediates which aromatize, releasing four molecules of acetic acid and two molecules of water. Typical conditions: heating at 150–200 °C in a sealed tube or oil bath, often neat or in a high‑boiling polar solvent such as acetic acid; no external catalyst is required, though the acidic environment of acetic acid assists the condensation.
Halogenation of an organolithium with iodine; hexyl Li attacks I₂ in dry THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, giving 1‑iodohexane and LiI; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Full reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert the ester into the two corresponding primary alcohols. Key transformation: 2‑methylpropyl benzoate + 4 eq LiAlH₄ → benzyl alcohol + 2‑methylpropanol (plus Al‑containing by‑products). Typical conditions: dry ether (THF or Et₂O), 0 °C to reflux under N₂, 2–4 h. Quench with aqueous NaOH or water at low temperature.

Hydrolysis of methyl 3‑(methylthio)propionate to 3‑(methylthio)propionic acid and methanol; carried out under basic conditions (NaOH or KOH aqueous solution, reflux) followed by acid work‑up, or under acidic aqueous conditions at elevated temperature.

Thermal or solution‑phase decomposition (reverse of polyiodide formation); CsI₃ dissociates into caesium iodide (CsI) and elemental iodine (I₂). The reaction proceeds upon heating or by dilution in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., acetone, ether). No catalyst is needed. Employed to regenerate CsI or to release I₂ in situ.

Ester hydrogenolysis; purpose is to cleave the ester bond of 2‑octyl acetate into the corresponding alcohols. Key transformation: 2‑octyl acetate + H2 → 2‑octanol (from the alkyl side) + ethanol (from the acyl side). Typically performed under high‑pressure hydrogen (50–100 atm) with a nickel catalyst at 150–200 °C. Common solvents are alcohols such as ethanol or isopropanol, sometimes run neat.

Base‑induced hydrolysis of an isothiouronium salt; purpose is to decompose S‑(2‑aminoethyl)isothiouronium bromide to free thiol and urea. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the C=N bond of the isothiouronium, yielding 2‑aminoethanethiol, urea, water and NaBr. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 60–80 °C, often with vigorous stirring. No special catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis; deprotonation of 2‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑ol with NaH to form the alkoxide followed by SN2 attack on methyl iodide to give 1‑methoxy‑2‑methylcyclohexane. Conducted under anhydrous, inert atmosphere in aprotic solvents such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature; sodium iodide is formed as by‑product.

Double‑displacement precipitation analogous to reaction 4 but using potassium carbonate; aqueous copper(II) nitrate and potassium carbonate produce copper(II) carbonate precipitate and potassium nitrate in solution; typical conditions are room temperature, aqueous medium, stirring, and filtration; no catalyst necessary.

Nitrile reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert the nitrile group of indole‑3‑acetonitrile to a primary amine, producing tryptamine. Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the C≡N carbon, sequentially forming an imine then a primary amine. Reaction is carried out in dry ether or THF under anhydrous conditions, typically at 0 °C to reflux (25–70 °C) for several hours, followed by cautious aqueous work‑up.

Esterification (Fisher esterification) of tert‑butanol with acrylic acid to give tert‑butyl acrylate; purpose is to synthesize a protected acrylate monomer; key transformation is condensation of the alcohol OH with the carboxylic acid COOH, forming an ester bond and releasing water; typical conditions are reflux (60‑80 °C) in an inert organic solvent such as toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap, using a catalytic amount of a strong Brønsted acid (e.g., 1‑5 mol % H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH); the reaction is moisture‑sensitive and often performed under nitrogen.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (silyl ester formation); sodium trimethylsilanolate attacks acetyl chloride to give trimethylsilyl acetate and NaCl; carried out in dry aprotic solvents such as THF or CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ether synthesis (addition of an alcohol to an alkene); isobutylene adds to methanol under strong acid catalysis (e.g., H₂SO₄, solid acid resin) to give methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE); typically performed at 30–80 °C under pressure, with excess methanol as both reactant and solvent.

Salt metathesis/precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange the anions of silver nitrate and the hydrochloride salt, generating insoluble silver chloride and free nitric acid. Key transformation: AgNO3 + HCl (from urea·HCl) → AgCl (s) + HNO3, with urea remaining unchanged. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the appearance of a white AgCl precipitate indicates completion. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of rubidium carbonate with hydrochloric acid; Rb2CO3 + 2 HCl → 2 RbCl + CO2 ↑ + H2O. Produces a soluble rubidium chloride solution and evolves carbon dioxide gas. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring may be used; no catalyst required.

Halogenation/substitution reaction; chlorine gas reacts with hydrogen disulfide to produce hydrogen chloride gas and disulfur dichloride (S₂Cl₂). Performed in a dry, non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control exotherm; no catalyst required.

Reductive dehalogenation; rhenium(V) chloride (ReCl5) is reduced by hydrogen gas at high temperature (300‑500 °C) in an inert atmosphere, yielding metallic rhenium solid and hydrogen chloride gas; no solvent, carried out in a sealed tube or flow reactor.

Oxidation of fluoroacetaldehyde to fluoroacetic acid using hydrogen peroxide; H₂O₂ acts as the oxidant, converting the aldehyde functional group to a carboxylic acid and producing water; commonly performed in aqueous solution, sometimes with a trace metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺) or under mildly basic conditions; yields fluoroacetic acid as the product.

Strong reduction of an acetate ester to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; a typical ester‑to‑alcohol conversion. LiAlH4 serves as both reductant and catalyst; the reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), usually at 0 °C to reflux temperature, and quenched with water or dilute acid to yield 2-(pyridin‑2‑yl)ethanol.

Reductive cleavage of an imine (reductive amination); purpose is to reduce the N‑[(E)‑benzylideneamino]aniline imine to the secondary amine N‑benzylan. Key transformation: NaBH4 delivers hydride to the C=N bond, converting the imine to a single C–N bond. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, typically 1–2 h, with the reaction mixture quenched with water after completion. No additional catalyst is required.

O‑acylation of phenol with bromoacetyl chloride to give phenyl 2‑bromoacetate (ester formation); generates HCl as by‑product; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of phenoxide on the acyl chloride carbonyl; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl; inert atmosphere is advisable.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration (heterocycle formation); converts a 1,3‑diol and ammonia into the morpholine ring of phenmetrazine with loss of water; typically performed by heating the diol with excess aqueous or gaseous ammonia at 150‑200 °C, often in a sealed tube or high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or xylene; no metal catalyst required, acid (e.g., HCl) may be added to promote protonation of the hydroxyl groups.

Hydrolytic cleavage of a hydroxamic‑acid prodrug; water attacks the N‑hydroxy‑amide bond of ibuproxam to afford ibuprofen (carboxylic acid) and hydroxylamine; carried out in aqueous buffer at pH 4‑7, often at 25‑37 °C; can be accelerated with weak acid (e.g., acetic acid) or base (e.g., NaOH) depending on desired rate; no special catalyst needed.

Reductive cleavage of a tert‑butoxycarbonyl (Boc) carbamate using sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminum hydride (Red‑Al); the carbamate is reduced to the free amine while the tert‑butyl group is reduced to tert‑butanol; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon; stoichiometric Red‑Al is used, and the reaction is quenched with aqueous work‑up.

General type: acid–base metathesis (salt formation) producing hydrazoic acid. Purpose: generate volatile and reactive HN₃ from a stable azide salt. Key transformation: proton transfer from hydrochloric acid to the azide anion (N₃⁻), yielding hydrazoic acid (HN₃) and cesium chloride (CsCl). Typical conditions: aqueous solution kept cold (0–5 °C) to minimize decomposition of HN₃; reactions are performed in a sealed or well‑ventilated apparatus under an inert atmosphere. Common solvent: water; safety precautions are essential because HN₃ is explosive and toxic.

Double‑replacement precipitation forming tin(II) sulfide; sulfide anion displaces chloride from SnCl₂, producing insoluble SnS solid and soluble NaCl; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the mixture is stirred until precipitation is complete, then the solid SnS is filtered and washed; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base exchange producing ferrous tartrate and hydrochloric acid; tartaric acid protonates chloride ligands of FeCl₂, yielding Fe(II) tartrate complex in solution and releasing HCl; typically performed in aqueous medium at room temperature, often with slight heating to ensure dissolution; the reaction may be conducted under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of Fe²⁺; no additional catalysts are required.

Thermal decomposition (redox) of lead(IV) fluoride that generates lead(II) fluoride and elemental fluorine gas; requires high temperature (≈300‑500 °C) under inert or vacuum atmosphere, no solvent or catalyst employed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous potassium hydroxide reacts with chromium(III) sulfate to precipitate chromium(III) hydroxide and form soluble potassium sulfate; purpose is to isolate Cr(OH)3 or remove chromium from solution; performed at room temperature in water with stirring, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of ethyl acetonedicarboxylate back to acetonedicarboxylic acid and ethanol. Usually performed with aqueous HCl or dilute H₂SO₄ under reflux; alternatively base‑catalysed saponification (NaOH, reflux) followed by acid work‑up. Solvent mixture of water/ethanol or water/THF.

Fischer esterification of salicylic acid with methanol to produce methyl salicylate. The carboxylic acid is protonated by a catalytic acid (commonly concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and reacts with methanol, forming the methyl ester and water. Reflux in methanol with catalytic acid, often with removal of water (Dean–Stark or azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium. Used to prepare wintergreen oil.

Strong oxidative oxidation (acidic oxidative cleavage) of hexamethylbenzene using chromic acid; methyl groups are oxidized to carboxyl groups producing mellitic acid while Cr(VI) is reduced to chromium(III) oxide; used to prepare the polycarboxylic acid; typically carried out in refluxing aqueous sulfuric acid with excess chromic acid at 80‑100 °C, water as solvent.

Organolithium mediated lithium‑halogen exchange and formylation; n‑butyllithium exchanges lithium for bromine on 2‑bromopyridine to give pyridyl‑Li, which attacks DMF to afford 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde after aqueous work‑up, while n‑butyl bromide is formed as a side product; used to synthesize heteroaryl aldehydes; carried out in anhydrous THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen or argon, no additional catalyst.

Copper‑catalyzed reduction of carbon tetrachloride by hydrogen; H₂ reduces CCl₄ over heated copper metal producing chloroform (CHCl₃) and hydrogen chloride; method for preparing chloroform; performed by passing a mixture of H₂ and CCl₄ over copper at 200‑300 °C in a gas‑phase reactor, no solvent.

Acid‑base protonolysis of methyllithium; water protonates the carbon‑lithium bond, yielding lithium hydroxide and methane gas; used to quench organolithium reagents; typically done by adding water dropwise to a solution of MeLi in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst.

Combination (synthesis) reaction; direct formation of hydrogen chloride gas from elemental hydrogen and chlorine. Initiated by ultraviolet light or a spark to generate radicals; proceeds exothermically in the gas phase. Typical conditions: dilute gases, ambient or slightly elevated temperature, illumination with UV or ignition source. No solvent required.

Benzylic oxidation using selenium dioxide; oxidizes the ethyl side chain of 1‑ethyl‑2‑nitrobenzene to the corresponding aldehyde, preserving the nitro substituent, affording 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde; SeO₂ is employed (≈ 1.2 equiv) in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent such as 1,4‑dioxane or pyridine, heated under reflux (80–120 °C); water is liberated during the oxidation.

Thermal decomposition of a hypervalent oxide. Iodine pentoxide decomposes on strong heating (often above 200 °C) to afford elemental iodine and oxygen gas. The reaction is performed in a sealed tube or under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Appel reaction; converts primary alcohol to alkyl iodide using triphenylphosphine and iodine. Proceeds via formation of a phosphonium intermediate followed by SN2 displacement of iodide. Typically run in dichloromethane (or carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; reagents are used in stoichiometric amounts, no additional catalyst required.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of phenol: phenol is acylated with acetyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminum chloride, typically in a dry non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction proceeds via electrophilic aromatic substitution to give mainly the para product, 4‑hydroxyacetophenone, with HCl released; AlCl₃ is the Lewis‑acid catalyst and the medium must be moisture‑free.

Redox (gas‑phase reduction‑oxidation); carbon monoxide reduces nitrous oxide to nitrogen while being oxidized to carbon dioxide. Conducted at high temperature (600–900 °C) in a flow reactor over a metal catalyst (e.g., Pt, Rh, Cu) in an inert carrier gas. No solvent; reaction pressure near atmospheric.

Metathesis/precipitation; barium sulfide exchanges anions with sodium carbonate to produce sparingly soluble barium carbonate as a white solid and soluble sodium sulfide in solution; typically carried out in water at room temperature with filtration of the BaCO3 precipitate.

Oxidation (chromic acid oxidation) of a benzylic methyl group; converts 4‑chlorotoluene to 4‑chlorobenzoic acid using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid. Key transformation: oxidation of –CH₃ to –CO₂H, reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III). Purpose: preparation of aromatic carboxylic acids from alkylbenzenes. Typical conditions: reflux in concentrated H₂SO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇ added portion‑wise, temperature 80–100 °C, aqueous acidic medium. No additional solvent beyond the acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an N‑nitrosoguanidine to aminoguanidine. Hydrogen gas is added in the presence of palladium on carbon (Pd/C) to reduce the nitroso group to an amine. Purpose: de‑nitrosation and formation of the free guanidine functionality. Typical conditions: ethanol or methanol as solvent, 1–5 atm H₂, room temperature to 50 °C, catalytic amount of Pd/C (5–10 % Pd). Reaction monitored until gas uptake ceases.

Acid‑base neutralization; ammonium hydroxide neutralizes acetic acid to give ammonium acetate and water; typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, enabling buffer preparation; no catalyst required.

Esterification (perester formation) of tert‑butyl alcohol with perbenzoic acid to give tert‑butyl peroxybenzoate and water. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the peracid yielding a peroxide ester. Purpose: synthesis of organic peroxide for initiator or oxidant use. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent, 0 °C to rt, catalytic amount of acid may be added to speed acyl transfer, reaction kept away from strong heat to prevent decomposition.

Combustion (complete oxidation) of an alkane; purpose is to convert hydrocarbon fuel to CO2 and H2O releasing heat; key transformation is oxidation of all C–H and C–C bonds to carbon dioxide and water; typical conditions require a supply of excess oxygen and ignition at high temperature (flame); no solvent or catalyst is used, though a spark or flame initiates the reaction.

Metathesis (acid‑base double displacement) between hydrochloric acid and sodium iodide. Generates sodium chloride and hydroiodic acid in aqueous solution. Purpose: in‑situ preparation of HI or removal of chloride ions. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, stoichiometric amounts, ambient temperature; often performed in a sealed tube if HI is to be collected.

Hofmann isocyanide synthesis (carbylamine reaction) converting 1,5‑diaminonaphthalene to 1,5‑naphthalenediyldiisocyanide using chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide. Key transformation: each primary amine reacts with chloroform/NaOH to form an isocyanide (–NC) group, with evolution of water and chloride ions. Purpose: preparation of diisocyanide ligands. Typical conditions: reflux in a mixture of chloroform and aqueous 10–20 % NaOH, vigorous stirring, temperature around 60–80 °C, reaction time 2–4 h. No organic solvent beyond chloroform; the aqueous phase provides the base.

Combustion reaction of a hydrocarbon; oxidative degradation of 5‑methylnonane by molecular oxygen producing carbon dioxide and water. Highly exothermic, requires excess O₂ and elevated temperature (flame or furnace). No catalyst needed; typically out in open air or under controlled combustion conditions.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; ethanol nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl of isopropyl acetate, exchanging alkoxy groups to give isopropanol and ethyl acetate. Commonly performed with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOEt) under reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene or using excess ethanol as both reagent and solvent. Removal of the formed alcohol drives the equilibrium.

Single‑displacement acid‑metal reaction; zinc metal dissolves in acetic acid, producing zinc acetate and hydrogen gas. Carried out in dilute acetic acid, often with gentle heating to accelerate the reaction; no catalyst, aqueous medium.

Acid‑base double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; strong nitric acid protonates samarium(III) phosphate, converting the insoluble phosphate into soluble samarium(III) nitrate while releasing phosphoric acid. Typically carried out at room temperature or with gentle heating in water; no special catalyst required.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; sodium nitrite reacts with sulfuric acid to generate nitrous acid, which nitrosates morpholine forming N‑nitrosomorpholine. The reaction also yields water and sodium hydrogen sulfate as by‑products. Conducted in cold aqueous acidic medium (0–5 °C) to control the rate and minimize side reactions; often performed in water or a water‑acetone mixture without additional catalyst.

Hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of fluorogermane; dihydrogen cleaves the Ge–F bond in GeH₃F, producing germanium tetrahydride (GeH₄) and hydrogen fluoride (HF). Requires elevated temperature (typically 150–300 °C) and a metal catalyst such as palladium, platinum, or nickel on an inert support. Performed in the gas phase or in a high‑pressure reactor; inert carrier gas may be used.

Oxidative hydrolysis (deboronation) of 2‑aminopropylboronic acid; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the B‑C bond, yielding 2‑amino‑1‑propanol and boric acid. Usually performed in aqueous medium, often mildly basic (e.g., NaOH) to facilitate peroxide decomposition, at ambient to slightly elevated temperature (0–25 °C). No transition‑ catalyst is strictly necessary, though catalytic amounts of Cu(II) or Ti(IV) can accelerate the reaction.

Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; cation exchange between ammonium nitrate and potassium metavanadate to form soluble potassium nitrate and ammonium metavanadate (often precipitated); typically performed by mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature and allowing crystallization; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution of bromine cyanide by sulfide ion; cyanogen bromide reacts with sodium sulfide to give sodium bromide and sodium thiocyanate; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of sodium borohydride in methanol (metal‑hydride decomposition); NaBH₄ reacts with methanol to generate hydrogen gas and sodium metaborate; phenolphthalein is only an indicator and does not participate; performed at room temperature in methanol, inert atmosphere optional; no catalyst.

Thermal decomposition of praseodymium(III) sulfate; upon strong heating the salt breaks down to praseodymium(III) oxide and sulfur trioxide gas; usually conducted in a furnace at >800 °C in air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst.

Double displacement (anion exchange) in aqueous medium; silver nitrate reacts with ammonium tetrafluoroborate to give ammonium nitrate and silver tetrafluoroborate, the latter isolated by crystallization (often from acetone or acetonitrile); performed at low temperature, water as solvent; no catalyst.

Oxidation of a thiol to a disulfide using iodine; iodine oxidizes 2‑aminoethanethiol dihydrochloride (cysteamine·2HCl) to cystamine dihydrochloride while producing hydroiodic acid; typically carried out in water or dilute ethanol at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation of a secondary amine). Acetic anhydride reacts with the ethylamino group of 2‑(ethylamino)ethanol, converting it to an N‑ethyl‑2‑hydroxyacetamide while one equivalent of acetic acid is generated. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to absorb the released acid.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransferase (COMT) of a phenolic acid. 3,4‑Dihydroxyphenylacetic acid is methylated by catechol‑O‑methyltransferase using S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine, giving homovanillic acid and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7.0–7.5) with Mg²⁺ at physiological temperature; the reaction is enzyme‑catalyzed and does not require additional solvents or reagents.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride. Difluoroacetic acid reacts with SOCl₂, releasing HCl and SO₂ gases and forming difluoroacetyl chloride. Usually carried out under reflux in an inert, non‑protic solvent (dry CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) with a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP to trap HCl. Anhydrous conditions are essential.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (full acetal); purpose to produce dimethoxymethane (methylal) used as solvent or protecting group; formaldehyde reacts with excess methanol in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., H2SO4, p‑TsOH) under reflux; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or using a drying agent; methanol serves as both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization to form a pharmaceutical sodium salt. Phenobarbital (a weak acid) reacts with sodium bicarbonate, yielding phenobarbital sodium, water and carbon dioxide. Performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol media at ambient temperature with gentle stirring; mild heating may be applied to drive off CO₂. No special catalyst is required.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation (reduction of a nitro arene). Nitrobenzene is reduced by formic acid in the presence of palladium on carbon and HCl, producing benzenamine as its hydrochloride salt. Reaction is typically run under reflux in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 60‑80 °C. Pd/C serves as the catalyst; excess formic acid supplies hydrogen and HCl protonates the formed aniline.

Redox (reducing‑oxidizing) reaction between iodine and ascorbate. Sodium ascorbate reduces I₂ to I⁻, being oxidized itself to dehydroascorbic acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature, often in mildly acidic or neutral pH. No catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds rapidly with stoichiometric amounts of reagents

Oxidative benzylic C–H oxidation; converts the benzylic methylene of 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene to a carbonyl to give the corresponding ketone. Typically performed with catalytic RuCl₃ and stoichiometric NaIO₄ as the terminal oxidant, in a mixed organic/aqueous solvent (e.g., AcCN/H₂O or acetone/H₂O) at ambient temperature to reflux, providing a mild, selective oxidation.

Acylation of a primary amine (amide formation) using acetic anhydride. Propylamine attacks the anhydride carbonyl, yielding N‑propylacetamide and one equivalent of acetic acid as by‑product. Reaction is usually done neat or in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, with optional removal of the generated acetic acid by azeotropic distillation or by using a base to scavenge it.

Acid-base reaction involving aluminum oxide and nitric acid. Al₂O₃ neutralizes HNO₃ to generate aluminum nitrate and water. Reaction occurs in aqueous nitric acid solution, often requiring mild heating. Water is the solvent; no additional catalysts are used.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; the alcohol (n‑butanol) exchanges with the alkoxy group of ethyl butyrate, producing butyl butyrate and ethanol. Common conditions involve catalytic sulfuric acid or sodium methoxide, an excess of the alcohol as solvent, and gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to shift equilibrium toward the desired ester.

Catalytic hydrogenation; 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline is hydrogenated over Pd/C under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) at 25–50 °C to fully saturate the aromatic ring, producing decahydroisoquinoline. Zinc oxide is not involved. Purpose: convert a partially saturated heterocycle to its fully saturated analogue.

Acyl transfer (nucleophilic acyl substitution) using an activated acyl donor; acetyl imidazole donates its acetyl group to the amino group of 3‑aminophenol, forming 3‑hydroxyacetanilide (an acetanilide derivative) and releasing imidazole. The reaction proceeds in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt, usually without additional catalyst, sometimes in the presence of a base like pyridine to scavenge the liberated acid.

Esterification with diazomethane (Diazomethyl ester formation); diazomethane reacts with 2‑phenylbutanoic acid to give methyl 2‑phenylbutanoate while evolving nitrogen gas. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in dry ether or diethyl ether, the diazomethane solution is added dropwise to the acid solution under an inert atmosphere; excess diazomethane is quenched with acetic acid after completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a dihalide with hydroxide to afford a diol; purpose is conversion of 1,9‑dibromononane to 1,9‑nonanediol; key transformation is two Br atoms displaced by OH groups forming C‑OH bonds; typical conditions are reflux in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol solution with excess base; water or ethanol used as solvent, no catalyst required.

Reaction type: thermal decarboxylation of an α‑keto acid; purpose: generate phenylacetaldehyde from phenylpyruvic acid; key transformation: loss of CO₂ from the carboxyl group yielding the aldehyde; typical conditions: heating 120‑180 °C, often in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., xylene) or neat; no catalyst required, sometimes a mild base (pyridine) is added to trap CO₂.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) between sulfur dioxide (reducing agent) and iodic acid (oxidizing agent); purpose is reduction of iodic acid to elemental iodine while oxidizing SO₂ to sulfuric acid; key transformation involves SO₂ being oxidized to H₂SO₄ and HIO₃ being reduced to I₂; performed in aqueous acidic medium, often with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Solid‑state redox reduction (metallothermic reduction) of niobium(V) oxide by calcium; purpose is preparation of niobium(IV) oxide and calcium oxide; key transformation is Ca metal reducing Nb₂O₅ to NbO₂ while forming CaO; carried out at high temperature (≈800‑1000 °C) in a furnace under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst, reaction occurs between solids.

Halide exchange (metathesis) precipitation in acidic medium. Hydroiodic acid reacts with aqueous lead(II) bromide, yielding insoluble lead(II) iodide precipitate and hydrogen bromide (in solution or as gas). Carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst.

Ether cleavage with hydrobromic acid: 3‑ethoxypentane treated with concentrated HBr gives 3‑bromopentane and ethanol. Protonated ether undergoes nucleophilic substitution by Br⁻. Conducted under reflux (≈80‑100 °C) in 48 % HBr aqueous solution; no separate catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation; purpose is formation of insoluble lead(II) oxalate from lead(II) oxide and oxalic acid; key transformation is PbO + H₂C₂O₄ → PbC₂O₄ (solid) + H₂O; typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or with slight heating; water is the medium, no catalyst required.

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction; analogous to reaction 0 but uses potassium hydroxide to generate soluble potassium silicate and magnesium hydroxide precipitate. Performed in aqueous KOH solution, often heated to reflux (≈80‑100 °C); water serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of a secondary alcohol to an alkene; purpose is synthesis of 3‑ethyl‑2‑pentene from 3‑ethylpentan‑2‑ol; key transformation involves protonation of the OH, loss of water, and β‑hydrogen removal to form the C=C bond; carried out with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 140‑170 °C; conc. H₂SO₄ acts as both catalyst and solvent.

Hydrolysis of an amide in water; cleavage of the N‑ethyl amide bond of L‑theanine to give L‑glutamic acid and ethylamine. Usually performed by heating the aqueous mixture (80‑100 °C) for several hours; the reaction may be accelerated with a small amount of acid or base catalyst. Solvent is water, no additional reagents required for simple hydrolysis.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) halide exchange (Finkelstein reaction); purpose is replacement of bromide by iodide on the allyl substrate; key transformation is I⁻ attack on allyl carbon displacing Br⁻ to give allyl iodide; typically performed by refluxing potassium iodide with allyl bromide in dry acetone, where KBr precipitates; acetone (polar aprotic) is the solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Reductive amination; converts indole‑3‑carboxaldehyde to the secondary amine Gramine by in‑situ formation of an imine with dimethylamine followed by reduction with sodium cyanoborohydride. Usually performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to maintain mildly acidic conditions; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation to azoxy compound; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the azo group of azobenzene to the N‑O‑N azoxy functionality, producing azoxybenzene and water; typically carried out in a mixed solvent such as methanol/water or acetic acid at 0–25 °C; acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄, pH ≈ 2–3) may be added to promote the reaction.

Dehydrative chlorination (SOCl₂ mediated alcohol‑to‑chloride conversion); replaces the 6‑hydroxyl of 6‑hydroxypurine with chlorine to give 6‑chloropurine, generating HCl and SO₂ gases. Conducted in anhydrous solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, reflux or gentle heating (≈40–80 °C); pyridine acts as base and HCl scavenger.

O‑Methylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of 2,5‑dichlorophenol using dimethyl sulfate; the phenoxide attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate to afford 2,5‑dichloroanisole and methyl hydrogen sulfate. Typically carried out in acetone or DMF with a mild base (K₂CO₃ or NaOH) at 0 °C to 25 °C; reaction is quenched with aqueous work‑up.

Aerobic benzylic oxidation (partial oxidation); ethylbenzene reacts with oxygen to afford phenylacetaldehyde and water; commonly performed with catalytic amounts of copper or manganese salts, sometimes under solvent‑free conditions or in acetonitrile, at temperatures of 80–120 °C, often with a radical initiator or peroxide to promote selective aldehyde formation.

Transesterification (alkoxy exchange) between ethyl acetate and sodium 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanolate; the trifluoroethoxide attacks the carbonyl of ethyl acetate, swapping the alkoxy groups to give 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl acetate and sodium ethoxide. Performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) or solvent‑free, often at 80–120 °C; the reaction proceeds to equilibrium and may be driven by removal of the more volatile ethanol byproduct.

Thermal pyrolysis (high‑temperature decomposition) of hexafluoroethane; C₂F₆ cleaves to generate tetrafluoroethylene (C₂F₄) and elemental fluorine (F₂). Requires very high temperatures (≈1000 °C) or plasma/electric discharge in a fluorine‑resistant reactor; no solvent or catalyst is used, and fluorine is typically trapped or reacted in situ.

Gas‑phase radical oxidation; hydroperoxyl radical reacts with nitrogen monoxide producing nitrogen dioxide and regenerating a hydroxyl radical; key step in atmospheric NOx and radical cycles; proceeds at ambient temperature and pressure without solvent or catalyst.

Thermal/photolytic decomposition and CO redistribution of iron pentacarbonyl; Fe(CO)₅ fragments to give carbon monoxide and the dinuclear complex diiron nonacarbonyl, Fe₂(CO)₉. Conducted under inert atmosphere by heating (150–200 °C) or UV irradiation, often in anhydrous hydrocarbon solvent such as toluene; the liberated CO is removed or collected, and Fe₂(CO)₉ is isolated as the product.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; 3‑methyl phenyl acetate reacts with excess ethanol to exchange the acetate group, forming ethyl acetate and 3‑methyl phenol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the carbonyl followed by departure of the phenoxy group; usually carried out in refluxing ethanol (10–20 % excess) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (H₂SO₄, p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or solid acid resin; reaction time 2–6 h, followed by removal of excess ethanol and purification.

Oxidation of a tertiary phosphine to its selenide; forms triphenylphosphine selenide (P=Se). Typically performed by stirring triphenylphosphine with elemental selenium under reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene, THF, or dichloromethane. No external catalyst is required; heat drives the chalcogenide formation. The reaction serves to generate a P–Se reagent useful for selenation or as a protecting group.

Acylation (acetylation) of a diamine; both amino groups of p‑phenylenediamine are converted to N‑acetyl groups yielding N,N‑diacetyl‑p‑phenylenediamine with liberation of two equivalents of acetic acid. Conducted by heating the diamine with excess acetic anhydride, often in pyridine or neat acetic anhydride as solvent, sometimes with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer. Used to protect the amines or to prepare diacetylated aromatic diamine derivatives.

Electrophilic aromatic acylation of indole (Friedel‑Crafts acylation) at the C‑3 position, giving 3‑acetylindole and acetic acid as by‑product. Typically carried out by treating indole with acetic anhydride in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as ZnCl₂, AlCl₃, or FeCl₃, often in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform under reflux or gentle heating. Provides a carbonyl‑functionalized indole useful for further synthetic elaboration.

Acid‑ or metal‑catalyzed allyl‑to‑propenyl isomerization: the allyl side chain of 1‑allyl‑4‑methoxybenzene migrates the double bond to give trans‑anethole (4‑methoxy‑β‑methyl‑styrene). Common conditions involve heating the substrate with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., HCl, H₂SO₄) or a metal halide (ZnCl₂, FeCl₃) in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane, toluene, or nitrobenzene. The reaction serves to produce the more stable conjugated olefin anethole.

Redox oxidation of iron(II) to iron(III) by persulfate. In aqueous solution, two equivalents of FeSO₄ are oxidized by sodium persulfate (Na₂S₂O₈) to give Fe₂(SO₄)₃ and sodium sulfate as the counter‑ion. Performed at ambient temperature, typically in acidic or neutral pH, under stirring. This reaction is used as a chemical oxidant in analytical chemistry and in oxidative polymerization or Fenton‑type processes.

Selective reduction of the aldehyde function of citral to the allylic alcohol citronellol using sodium borohydride. NaBH₄ (1–1.5 eq) is added to a solution of citral in methanol, ethanol, or THF at 0 °C–room temperature; the conjugated C=C remains untouched, yielding citronellol after work‑up.

Borane‑mediated reduction of a ketone: morpholine‑borane (Morph‑BH₃) donates hydride to cyclohexanone, producing cyclohexanol while the borane is hydrolyzed to boric acid and the morpholine ligand is released unchanged. Conducted in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). Provides a mild, chemoselective reduction of carbonyl groups without over‑reduction or metal residues.

This is an acid‑base neutralization (acidification) of a carboxylate salt. Adding aqueous HCl protonates the 2‑methylpentanoate anion, liberating 2‑methylpentanoic acid and forming NaCl in solution. The reaction is usually performed in water or a water‑acetone mixture at 0 °C to 25 °C with vigorous stirring; the organic acid can be extracted with an immiscible organic solvent (e.g., diethyl ether).

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction in water; exchange of nitrate and carbonate ions leads to formation of insoluble zinc carbonate and soluble sodium nitrate; purpose is to isolate ZnCO₃ as a precipitate; performed by mixing aqueous solutions of zinc nitrate hexahydrate and sodium carbonate at ambient temperature with stirring; the product ZnCO₃ is filtered and washed; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Single‑displacement redox reaction (metal displacement); purpose is to generate copper metal and zinc bromide; key transformation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2 e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu(s) (bromide counter‑ions remain associated); typical conditions: aqueous CuBr₂ solution, ambient temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to exchange cations between two soluble salts to prepare barium acetate. Conducted in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature; the products remain in solution and can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization. No catalyst required; common solvent is water.

Selective reduction of a ketone (valerophenone) to a secondary alcohol (1‑phenylpentan‑1‑ol) using sodium borohydride. Performed in protic solvents such as methanol, ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is quenched with water or dilute acid. No additional catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑bromopropane with silver nitrite to give 1‑nitropropane and precipitated silver bromide. Reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone) under reflux; the insoluble AgBr drives the equilibrium forward. No catalyst beyond the silver nitrite reagent.
