Williamson ether synthesis forming phenyl glycidyl ether from phenol and epichlorohydrin; purpose is preparation of a glycidyl ether monomer; key: deprotonation of phenol by potassium carbonate to give phenoxide, nucleophilic attack on the less‑ hindered carbon of epichlorohydrin, displacement of chloride and formation of the epoxy‑functional ether; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF, K₂CO₃ (1.5–2 equiv), temperature 60–80 °C under nitrogen; water and KCl are by‑products and are removed by filtration and aqueous work‑up.

Thermal decomposition (explosive). Silicon tetraazide decomposes on rapid heating (often 150‑200 °C) without solvent, releasing nitrogen gas and forming solid silicon nitride (Si₃N₄). The process is highly exothermic and is conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) with careful temperature control; no catalyst is involved.

Acet transfer (acylation) – acetyl imidazole serves as an activated acetyl donor, transferring the acetyl group to the amino group of guanabenz to give guanabenz acetate while releasing imidazole as the leaving group. Typically performed at room temperature or mild heating in an aprotic polar solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative rearrangement (Pd(II)-catalyzed oxidation). Molecular oxygen serves as the terminal oxidant while catalytic PdCl₂ (≈5 mol %) promotes dehydrogenation and skeletal rearrangement of α‑humulene to the azulene framework, producing guaiazulene. Typically run in acetonitrile or chlorobenzene at reflux (80‑120 °C) under an O₂ atmosphere (1‑5 atm); no additional ligands are required.

Salt formation (acid‑base neutralization) – pilocarpine, a basic alkaloid, reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to give the pilocarpine hydrochloride salt. Reaction is performed at ambient temperature in water or a water‑ethanol mixture; the product typically precipitates on cooling and can be isolated by filtration.

Halogen displacement/redox reaction; purpose is to convert chloride ion to elemental chlorine while forming sodium fluoride; F2 oxidizes Cl‑ to Cl2 and is reduced to F‑; carried out in the gas phase with dry, inert apparatus, typically at room temperature or slightly below; no solvent, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis (acid‑base exchange) – piperidinium acetate reacts with hydrochloric acid, exchanging the acetate anion for chloride to afford piperidinium chloride and free acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at temperature; the mixture can be separated by extraction (acetate moves into the organic layer) or by evaporation of the aqueous phase to isolate the chloride salt.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation): 2‑chlorofuran is reduced with hydrogen gas over palladium on carbon to give furan. The C–Cl bond is replaced by hydrogen. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature 25‑50 °C under stirring.

Double displacement (alkaline neutralization) – sodium hydroxide neutralizes ammonium persulfate, swapping the cations to generate ammonium hydroxide and sodium persulfate in solution. Performed in water at ambient temperature; the products remain in the aqueous phase and may be isolated by evaporation or crystallization of sodium persulfate.

Reaction type: synthesis of an aryl chloroformate from a phenol using triphosgene (phosgene equivalent). Purpose: generate p‑nitrophenyl chloroformate as an activated carbonyl reagent for further coupling reactions. Key transformation: the phenolic OH attacks a carbonyl carbon of triphosgene, displacing a chloride and forming the chloroformate; one equivalent of CO2 and HCl are released. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to ambient temperature, under nitrogen atmosphere; a stoichiometric base such as pyridine or triethylamine is added to neutralize generated HCl.

Acid–base metathesis (acid displacement). Concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with caesium nitrate to liberate volatile nitric acid and form caesium bisulfate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with heating (reflux) to drive off HNO₃, using water as solvent; no external catalyst required.

Redox halogenation of a metal sulfide. Bromine oxidizes silver sulfide, reducing to silver bromide precipitate while sulfur is liberated as elemental sulfur. Usually performed in aqueous media at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution/hydrolysis (haloform degradation); hydroxide attacks chloroform, leading to successive replacement of chlorides and ultimately formation of formate ion. Key transformation: CHCl₃ → HCOO⁻ with formation of NaCl and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (strong, often >1 M), heated (60–100 °C) for several hours. No catalyst required.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone. Ozone oxidizes dimethyl sulfide to dimethyl sulfone. The reaction is conducted by bubbling O₃ through a solution of D in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or methanol) at low temperature (0 °C to –20 °C) to control over‑oxidation; no additional catalyst is required.

Halogen‑oxygen exchange (oxidative halogenation) of a metal oxide. Bromine oxidizes tantalum(V) oxide, releasing oxygen gas and forming tantalum(V) bromide. Carried out in the solid‑state or gas phase at high temperature (typically 400–600 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent or catalyst is.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction). Pertrifluoroacetic acid (peroxytrifluoroacetic acid) transfers an oxygen atom to 2‑butene, yielding 2‑butene oxide and regenerating trifluoroacetic acid. Reaction is performed in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to 25 °C, often under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (acetate alkylation). Acetate ion displaces iodide in benzyl iodide to give benzyl acetate while forming potassium iodide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or DMF) at reflux or mild heating; reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); purpose is to convert metaphosphoric acid into its lithium salt. The hydroxide deprotonates the phosphoric acid, producing water and lithium metaphosphate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water serves as solvent.

N‑alkylation via SN2 nucleophilic substitution; purpose is to methylate the nitrogen of 2‑hydroxyacetamide. The amide nitrogen attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide and forming N‑methyl‑2‑hydroxyacetamide while generating hydrogen iodide. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone, often at 0 °C to reflux, with a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to scavenge HI.

Metal displacement (single‑replacement) with hydrogen evolution; method for preparing sodium selenide. Metallic sodium reacts with H2Se, reducing the acid and releasing H2 gas while Na+ combines with Se2‑ to give Na2Se. Typically performed in dry, aprotic solvents such as liquid ammonia or THF under nitrogen or argon at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) to control vigorous H2 evolution; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: dehydration of an amide to a nitrile (dehydrative chlorination). Purpose: convert pentanamide into the corresponding nitrile. Key transformation: the carbonyl oxygen of the amide is replaced by a nitrogen, forming pentanenitrile while thionyl chloride supplies chloride and generates SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: add thionyl chloride to the amide under anhydrous conditions, usually at 0 °C then reflux (40–60 °C) for 1–3 h. A base such as pyridine or triethylamine is often used to scavenge the generated HCl. Common solvent: dry dichloromethane or chloroform; the reaction can also be performed neat with excess SOCl₂.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; purpose is to esterify nipecotic acid (piperidine‑2‑carboxylic acid) to its methyl ester. Sulfuric acid protonates the carboxyl group, facilitating nucleophilic attack by methanol; water is eliminated to give methyl piperidine‑2‑carboxylate. Conducted by refluxing neat methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Selective carbonyl reduction with sodium borohydride; purpose is to convert the ketone of 1‑penten‑3‑one to the corresponding secondary alcohol NaBH₄ delivers a hydride to the C=O, affording 1‑penten‑3‑ol after aqueous work‑up. Typically performed in ethanol, methanol, or THF at 0 °C to room temperature.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde; purpose is to obtain 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde; key transformation: conversion of –CH₂OH to –CHO; typical conditions: aqueous acetic acid with added H₂O₂ (30 %); reaction proceeds via in‑situ formation of peracetic acid, generally at 0 °C to 25 °C, then mild warming; product isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Lewis‑acid mediated demethylation of an aryl methyl ether; purpose is to convert the 4‑methoxy group of 4‑methoxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine to a phenolic OH, yielding psilocin. Boron tribromide coordinates to the ether oxygen and cleaves the C‑O bond, producing methyl bromide and the phenol. Reaction is run in anhydrous dichloromethane at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere, followed by quench with methanol or water.

Acid dissolution of dysprosium oxide to give dysprosium iodide; acid–base (salt‑formation) reaction. Dysprosium oxide is treated with aqueous hydroiodic acid (typically 5–10 M) and heated gently (50–80 °C) until complete conversion, producing DyI3 in solution and water as by‑product. No catalyst required.

Selective reduction of a cyclic ketone with sodium borohydride; purpose is to reduce the carbonyl at C‑4 of 1‑acetylpiperidin‑4‑one to a secondary alcohol while leaving the N‑acetyl group intact. NaBH₄ adds hydride to the ketone, giving 1‑acetyl‑4‑hydroxypiperidine after work‑up. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Nucleophilic addition (cyanohydrin formation); converts the carbonyl of acetone into a cyanohydrin by attack of cyanide; typically performed at 0–5 °C using aqueous HCN or KCN/HCl in water/acetone mixture; pyridine or a weak acid may be added as catalyst; isolated by careful neutralization and extraction.

Reductive transformation; reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an amine using sodium dithionite in aqueous medium. The nitro group of 3‑nitroanisole is converted to a primary amine yielding 3‑methoxyaniline, while sodium dithionite is oxidized to sodium sulfite. Typical conditions are aqueous solution (often slightly alkaline), room temperature to 50 °C, no organic solvent required; Na2S2O4 is used in excess to ensure complete reduction.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis); zirconium metal reacts with elemental sulfur to zirconium sulfide (commonly ZrS₂). The reaction is carried out by intimately mixing the powders and heating to high temperature (800–1000 °C) under an inert atmosphere (argon or vacuum) to prevent oxidation. No solvent or catalyst is used; the product is obtained as a solid sulfide after cooling.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) reaction; converts chloroform to chlorodifluoromethane (HCFC‑22) by replacing a chlorine atom with fluorine using hydrogen fluoride. Typically carried out at 150‑250 °C under excess HF, often with a Lewis‑acid catalyst such as SbCl₅ or a pyridinium‑HF complex; no additional solvent is required as HF acts as both reagent and medium.

Hydride reduction; sodium borohydride reduces trifluoroacetaldehyde (CF₃CHO) to 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol (CF₃CH₂OH). The aldehyde is dissolved in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or THF, and NaBH₄ is added at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction proceeds rapidly, giving the primary alcohol after aqueous work‑up; the by‑product is sodium borate.

Electrophilic ether cleavage (demethylation); boron tribromide cleaves the methyl ether of papaverine to generate the phenolic 6‑hydroxypapaverine and methyl bromide as the volatile by‑product. The reaction is usually conducted in dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under nitrogen; BBr₃ is added dropwise to the solution of papaverine. After gradual warming, the mixture is quenched with methanol or water to hydrolyze any borate complexes, yielding the hydroxylated product.

Acid dissolution/solvolysis; gadolinium oxalate reacts with excess nitric acid to form soluble gadolinium nitrate and liberates oxalic acid. The solid oxalate is suspended in concentrated aqueous HNO₃ and heated gently (50–80 °C) until complete dissolution. The resulting solution contains Gd(NO₃)₃; upon cooling, oxalic acid remains in solution or can be isolated by evaporation. No additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis reaction; water breaks the cyclic trimer metaldehyde into three molecules of acetaldehyde. Typically carried out by heating metaldehyde in aqueous solution, often with a dilute mineral acid (e.g., HCl) as catalyst. Reaction is performed at reflux temperature; no special solvent beyond water is required.

Acid–base neutralization (metal oxide dissolution) forming holmium acetate. Six equivalents of acetic acid react with one equivalent of Ho₂O₃ to give two equivalents of holmium(III) acetate and three equivalents of water. Conducted by heating a suspension of Ho₂O₃ in excess glacial acetic acid, usually under reflux until gas evolution ceases and a clear solution is obtained. No additional catalyst needed; water is removed by distillation or evaporation.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid–base reaction producing magnesium selenate and acetic acid. One mole of H₂SeO₄ reacts with one mole of magnesium acetate in aqueous solution, exchanging the cations and anions to give MgSeO₄ (as the hydrated salt) and two equivalents of acetic acid. The mixture is heated gently (≈50 °C) to promote completion; the product salts can be isolated by crystallisation. No catalyst required; water serves as the reaction medium.

Reaction type: Acid‑base neutralization (hydrolysis of an amine salt). Purpose: Liberate free 3‑methoxyphenethylamine from its hydrochloride salt. Key transformation: NaOH deprotonates the ammonium ion, forming the free amine, NaCl, and water. Typical conditions: Aqueous NaOH solution (1 M), ambient temperature or mild heating (≤40 °C), stirring for 15–30 min; the free amine can be extracted into an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) or isolated by acid‑base extraction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 2‑fluoroethyl bromide by aqueous ammonia to afford 2‑fluoroethylamine and hydrobromic acid. The reaction is performed in concentrated aqueous NH₃, often under reflux (≈80‑100 °C) to increase the rate. Excess ammonia is used to drive the reaction to completion and to neutralise the generated HBr. No additional catalyst is needed; the solvent is water/ammonia mixture.

Condensation/cyclodehydration to form N‑ethylmaleimide (imide synthesis). Ethylamine first adds to maleic anhydride forming an N‑ethylsuccinamic acid intermediate; acetic anhydride (with sodium acetate as base catalyst) then promotes dehydration and cyclisation to the imide, releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. The reaction is carried out neat or in excess acetic anhydride, heated to 80‑120 °C under nitrogen. Sodium acetate acts as a mild base catalyst; the by‑product acetic acid is removed vacuum or azeotropic distillation.

Hydrolytic cleavage of di‑tert‑butyl peroxide yielding tert‑butanol and tert‑butyl hydroperoxide. Water attacks the peroxide bond under mild acidic or neutral conditions, typically at 25‑60 °C. The reaction may be catalysed by a small amount of mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH) to accelerate peroxide cleavage. No organic solvent is essential; the mixture is aqueous and the products separate into organic (tert‑butanol) and peroxide phases.

Acid–base neutralization of a metal carbonate: zinc carbonate reacts with nitric acid in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, releasing CO₂ gas and water while forming soluble zinc nitrate; no catalyst required.

LiAlH₄‑mediated reduction of a thioester: lithium aluminium hydride in dry THF (0 °C to reflux) cleaves S‑ethyl thioacetate, yielding ethanol from the acyl portion and ethanethiol from the thio‑alkyl fragment; the reaction is a reductive cleavage with no additional catalyst.

Enzymatic methyl transfer: S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine serves as a methyl donor to daidzein in an aqueous buffered medium (pH 7–8) using a SAM‑dependent O‑methyltransferase, producing S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine and the methylated isoflavone biochanin A; typical cofactors include Mg²⁺.

Double‑replacement/precipitation (acid‑base neutralization); employed to isolate aluminum as the insoluble hydroxide while producing a soluble nitrate salt of sodium. An aqueous solution of Al(NO₃)₃ is mixed with NaOH, producing a gelatinous Al(OH)₃ precipitate and NaNO₃ in the filtrate; the reaction proceeds at ambient temperature, often with excess NaOH to ensure complete precipitation.

Oxidative coupling to a phenoxazinone: o‑aminophenol is oxidized by ferric chloride (FeCl₃) in an acidic organic solvent (e.g., ethanol/H₂O under reflux, forming 2‑aminophenoxazin‑3‑one while FeCl₃ is reduced to FeCl₂ and generates HCl; the reaction is an Fe(III)‑mediated oxidative cyclization.

Acidic redox reaction of thiosulfate with chromate: in concentrated HCl solution, sodium thiosulfate is oxidized by potassium chromate; thiosulfate yields sulfate and elemental sulfur, while chromate is reduced to Cr³⁺ (forming CrCl₃); the process proceeds at room temperature in aqueous medium, no external catalyst needed.

Salt hydrolysis / acid‑base equilibrium (reverse of 4); tert‑butylammonium iodide dissociates in water, regenerating tert‑butylamine and hydroiodic acid, especially upon gentle heating. Carried out in aqueous solution, sometimes with slight heating to shift equilibrium; no catalyst required.
Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dealkylation) of, on alumina). Reactions are usually performed in the gas phase or in high‑boiling solvents such as decalin.

Oxidation; selective oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide using Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate); diphenyl sulfide loses two electrons to form diphenyl sulfoxide while Oxone is reduced to potassium bisulfate and water is generated; generally carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile with a small amount of water, at 0 °C to ambient temperature, without additional catalyst.

Condensation (C‑N bond formation) of cyanoguanidine with guanidine to give biguanide. The nucleophilic guanidine attacks the electrophilic carbon of the nitrile group, followed by proton transfers. Commonly carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., methanol) at elevated temperature (≈80 °C) without added catalyst.

Acidic oxidation of iodide by potassium periodate. Purpose: to generate elemental iodine from iodide. Key transformation: IO₄⁻ + I⁻ + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + SO₄²⁻ + H₂O (overall produces K₂SO₄). Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid solution, often at room temperature or with mild heating. Water is the solvent; no extra catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (dehydro‑hydrolysis); 3‑hydroxypropionic acid loses water to give acrylic acid. Typically heated (150‑250 °C) over solid acid catalysts (H₂SO₄, zeolites, or alumina) or in the presence of a strong mineral acid in the liquid phase. The key transformation is elimination of the β‑hydroxyl group to form the C=C bond, producing acrylic acid and water.

Electrophilic addition; bromine adds across the carbon–carbon triple bond of acetylene in two successive steps, giving the fully brominated alkane 1,1,2,2‑tetrromoethane; no catalyst is required; the reaction is usually performed in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature to control exotherm.

Catalytic dehydration/oxidation of glycerol to hydroxyacetone (1‑hydroxy‑2‑propanone) with release of water. Involves intramolecular rearrangement where the secondary alcohol is oxidized to a carbonyl while one primary hydroxyl is eliminated as water. Typical conditions: 180‑200 °C, solid base or metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., Ca(OH)₂, Cu‑CeO₂), sometimes in a solvent‑free or low‑boiling‑solvent (water or glycerol itself) system.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification (alkoxide exchange); sodium ethoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of isopropyl acetate, displacing isopropoxide and forming ethyl acetate while generating sodium isopropoxide; usually conducted in refluxing ethanol (which also serves as solvent and source of ethoxide) under inert atmosphere; equilibrium can be driven to products by using excess ethanol or by removing the formed isopropanol.

Type: Electrophilic methylation using dimethyl sulfate; purpose: N‑methylation of aniline; key transformation: nitrogen attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, producing N‑methyl aniline and methyl hydrogen sulfate; typical conditions: pyridine or DMF as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, with excess base (pyridine, NaH) to scavenge the acidic by‑product.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis (saponification) of an acid chloride; benzoyl chloride reacts with two equivalents of potassium hydroxide; the acyl chloride is converted to the potassium benzoate salt, water is formed from the hydroxide, and potassium chloride is liberated as a by‑product; performed in aqueous KOH solution, often at 0 °C initially then warmed to reflux to ensure complete conversion.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; sodium selenide exchanges anions with silver tetrafluoroborate, producing insoluble silver selenide (Ag₂Se) as a precipitate and soluble sodium tetrafluoroborate; typically carried out in a dry, aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF under inert atmosphere at room temperature; no additional catalyst is required.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of furan; electrophilic aromatic substitution of furan with acetyl chloride in the presence of AlCl₃ giving 2‑acetylfuran and HCl; carried out under anhydrous conditions, usually in dichloromethane or nitrobenzene at 0 °C to reflux; AlCl₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous magnesium chloride hexahydrate reacts with ammonium carbonate to give magnesium carbonate precipitate, ammonium chloride in solution, and water. Carried out in water at room temperature or with gentle heating to improve solubility; stirring ensures complete mixing. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation. Purpose: Convert lactic acid into its amide (lactamide) using ammonia as the nucleophile. Key transformation: Carboxyl group of lactic acid is activated by DCC to form an O‑NHS ester; ammonia attacks the activated ester to give the amide, releasing dicyclohexylurea. Typical conditions: Anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; DCC (1.2 eq) and NHS (1.2 eq) are added to a solution of lactic acid, followed by aqueous ammonia or ammonium carbonate. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Acid‑base salt formation (neutralization). Purpose: Isolate the amine as a crystalline hydrochloride salt for improved stability and handling. Key transformation: Protonation of the amine nitrogen by H to give the ammonium chloride salt. Typical conditions: Dissolve 2-(3‑methylphenyl)ethan‑1‑amine in a suitable solvent (ether, ethanol, or methanol) and add aqueous or gaseous HCl at 0 °C to rt; the precipitated hydrochloride is filtered and dried. No catalyst needed.

Type: Hydrolysis of a silicon halide. Purpose: Convert silicon tetrabromide into metasilicic acid while liberating hydrogen bromide. Key transformation: Water attacks SiBr₄, replacing each bromide with hydroxyl groups; the resulting silicic species condenses to H₂SiO₃ (metasilicic acid) and HBr is released. Typical conditions: Slow addition of SiBr₄ to ice‑cold water or aqueous acid under stirring; reaction is exothermic and generates gaseous HBr, so it is performed in a fume hood. No catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis). Nitrogen gas reacts with fluorine to form dinitrogen tetrafluoride (N₂F₄), the dimer of NF₂ radicals. Carried out at low temperature (typically –196 °C to –78 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible reactor (e.g., nickel or Monel vessel); no solvent; reaction is highly exothermic and pressure‑controlled.

Halogenation with phosphorus tribromide; an SN2 displacement of the hydroxyl group yielding heptyl bromide and phosphorous acid; performed in dry ether or dichloromethane under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C to reflux; a base such as pyridine may be added to neutralize generated H₃PO₃.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to cleave the ester bond of 2‑ethylhexyl formate, yielding potassium formate and 2‑ethylhexanol. Hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give the formate anion and releases the alcohol. Conditions: aqueous KOH (1–2 equiv), reflux at 80–100 °C, often in a mixed solvent (water/ethanol) to improve solubility; after reaction the mixture is cooled and acidified if free acid is required.

Type: Oxidative chlorination (redox). Purpose: Generate chlorine gas from chloride ions using hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant, with copper(II) acting as a catalyst. Key transformation: H₂O₂ oxidizes Cu(II) to Cu(III) transiently, which then oxidizes Cl⁻ to Cl₂; Cu(II) is regenerated as CuSO₄. Typical conditions: Dilute H₂SO₄ (1–2 M) to maintain acidity, aqueous H₂O₂ (30 % w/w) added dropwise at 0–25 °C, catalytic amount of CuCl₂ (≈5 mol %). The evolution of Cl₂ is collected or vented. No additional solvent beyond water is needed.

Selective oxidation of the thio‑ether in Disulfoton to the sulfoxide using hydrogen peroxide. Provides the metabolite O,O‑diethyl O‑(4‑(methylsulfinyl)phenyl) phosphorothioate. Reaction is performed at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or methanol, often with a small amount of a catalyst (e.g., tungstate, molybdate, or a phase‑transfer agent) to control over‑oxidation.

Type: Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann hydroxylation (aryl halide to phenol). Purpose: Convert bromobenzene to phenol via nucleophilic substitution with hydroxide. Key transformation: Cu(I) bromide mediates the formation of an aryl‑copper intermediate which reacts with hydroxide to give phenol, releasing NaBr and water. Typical conditions: A mixture of bromobenzene, aqueous NaOH (2–5 M), and CuBr (5–10 mol %) is heated to 120–150 °C in a high‑boiling polar solvent such as DMSO or N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone; after completion, the mixture is cooled, acidified, and phenol is extracted. No additional ligands are strictly required, though diamine ligands can improve yield.

Conversion of benzyl amine to benzyl isothiocyanate using thiophosgene; the amine attacks the thiophosgene carbon, displacing a chloride and forming the isothiocyanate functional group while liberating an equivalent of hydrogen chloride; carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt; a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) is added to neutralize the generated HCl.

Combustion reaction. The reaction involves the complete oxidation of 2,3,4-Trimethylpentane (a branched hydrocarbon) in the presence of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water. It is an exothermic reaction typical of alkane combustion. Reaction occurs under high-temperature conditions such as those found in internal combustion engines or flame. No solvent or catalyst is required beyond the presence of oxygen.

Acid-base metathesis reaction. Sulfuric acid reacts with potassium fluoride to produce hydrogen fluoride and potassium hydrogen sulfate. This reaction is used to generate hydrogen fluoride (a weak acid) from sulfuric acid and potassium fluoride. The reaction occurs under ambient conditions upon mixing aqueous or solid reactants. No catalyst is required; concentrated sulfuric acid is typically used.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a benzyl‑amino group. 1‑Benzyl‑4‑methyl‑piperazine undergoes cleavage of the N‑CH₂Ph bond under H₂, producing 1‑methyl‑piperazine and toluene. Conditions: H₂ (1–5 atm), 10 % Pd/C (or Pd‑BaSO₄), solvent ethanol or methanol, ambient to 50 °C, with stirring under inert atmosphere.

Quaternization of pyridine by methyl iodide to afford N‑methylpyridinium iodide; SN2 methyl transfer to the nitrogen atom; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as MeCN or CH2Cl2 at room temperature; often performed without added catalyst, sometimes with a weak base to absorb liberated HI.

Base-catalyzed isomerization reaction. Isoxanthohumol (a chalcone derivative) is converted to xanthohumol via a structural rearrangement using potassium hydroxide. The reaction involves deprotonation and electrophilic reorganization of the aromatic rings. It typically occurs under mild heating in a protic solvent such as ethanol or water.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 2‑aminopropanenitrile hydrochloride (alanine nitrile HCl) to 2‑aminopropanoic acid (alanine) with formation of ammonium chloride. Conducted by refluxing the hydrochloride salt in excess water (or aqueous HCl) at 100 °C for several hours. No external catalyst is required beyond the acidic medium; the reaction proceeds via protonation of the nitrile followed by stepwise addition of water.

Peracid oxidation of 4‑ethoxybenzonitrile to 4‑ethoxybenzoic acid using in‑situ generated peracetic acid (from acetic acid and H₂O₂). The nitrile is first oxidized to the corresponding amide and then further to the carboxylic acid, releasing water. Typical conditions: 50‑70 °C, aqueous acetic acid/H₂O₂ mixture (30 % H₂O₂), sometimes with a catalytic amount of sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid to accelerate peracid formation.

Synthesis reaction. Sulfuric acid reacts with sulfur trioxide to form oleum (fuming sulfuric acid, H2S2O7), a disulfuric acid. The reaction is used industrially to produce sulfonating agents. Conditions involve mixing SO3 gas with concentrated sulfuric acid at moderate temperatures. No solvent or catalyst is required beyond the reactants themselves.

Single‑displacement (acid‑metal) reaction; holmium metal reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce holmium(III) chloride and hydrogen gas; metal is oxidized, protons reduced; typically performed at room temperature or with gentle heating in dilute HCl solution; no catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state oxide synthesis; lithium oxide combines with aluminum oxide to form lithium aluminate (LiAlO₂); used for preparing ceramic materials; carried out by thoroughly grinding the oxides and calcining them at about 1000–1500 °C in a furnace, usually in air; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

General type: methyl ester synthesis via diazomethane (O‑methylation). Purpose: convert isobutyric acid to its methyl ester. Key transformation: the carboxylate attacks diazomethane, nitrogen gas is expelled and the methyl group is transferred, yielding methyl isobutyrate. Typical conditions: performed in dry ether (e.g., diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere and protected from light; no catalyst required.

General type: nucleophilic aromatic ether cleavage (dealkylation) using hydroiodic acid. Purpose: convert pentachloroanisole to pentachlorophenol while generating methyl iodide. Key transformation: iodide performs an SN2 attack on the methyl group of the aryl ether, displacing it as CH₃I and leaving the phenolic oxygen. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HI (≈57 % aqueous) heated to reflux (100‑150 °C), often neat or as the reaction medium; no additional catalyst.

Dehydrofluorination (E2 elimination) of 1,1,1,3,3‑pentafluoropropane to form 1,1,3,3,3‑pentafluoroprop‑1‑ene and hydrogen fluoride; typically requires a strong base such as potassium tert‑butoxide or a Lewis‑acid catalyst and elevated temperature (≈200‑300 °C); solvent may be anhydrous aprotic medium (e.g., THF or DMSO); purpose is to introduce a C=C double bond.

General type: lithium‑halogen exchange (metalation). Purpose: generate phenyl‑lithium for subsequent organolithium chemistry; n‑butyl iodide is formed as a by‑product. Key transformation: n‑butyllithium swaps lithium for iodine on iodobenzene, producing phenyl‑lithium and n‑butyl iodide. Typical conditions: dry THF or diethyl ether, –78 °C, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); reagent added dropwise; no catalyst.

General type: double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Purpose: isolate insoluble cadmium oxalate and form soluble sodium nitrate. Key transformation: Na₂C₂O₄ + Cd(NO₃)₂ → CdC₂O₄↓ + 2 NaNO₃ in aqueous solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed; no catalyst.

General type: alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an aryl acetate. Purpose: deprotect the 2,4,6‑trichlorophenyl acetate to give 2,4,6‑trichlorophenol. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon of the acetate, cleaving the ester to produce the phenol and acetate ion, which pairs with Na⁺ as sodium acetate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heated 50‑80 °C, water or water/ethanol solvent; no catalyst.

General type: oxidation of iodobenzene to a hypervalent iodine(III) species (iodosylbenzene). Purpose: prepare PhIO as an oxidizing reagent or synthetic intermediate. Key transformation: iodobenzene reacts with H₂O₂ in ac acid, inserting an oxygen atom onto iodine to form iodosylbenzene and water. Typical conditions: glacial acetic acid as solvent, 30 % H₂O₂ added at 0‑25 °C under stirring; often a catalytic amount of acid is present; no additional catalyst.

Oxidative conversion (potassium permanganate oxidation) of 1,2,4‑trihydroxybenzene under alkaline aqueous conditions; the aromatic ring is cleaved to give trimellitic acid while KMnO4 is reduced MnO2. Typical conditions: reflux in water with excess KOH and KMnO4, solid precipitation of MnO2; no organic solvent required.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling between 4‑pyridineboronic acid and 2‑bromo‑1‑benzofuran to form a C–C bond yielding 4‑(2‑benzofuranyl)pyridine. Usually performed with a palladium catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or PdCl2(dppf)), a base such as K2CO3 or Na2CO3, in a mixed solvent (toluene/water, dioxane/water, or DMF), heated to 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of 3,3‑dimethylbutyl acetate with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford 3,3‑dimethyl‑1‑butanol and sodium acetate. Conducted in water or water/ethanol mixture, refluxed until complete hydrolysis; no additional catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of dysprosium carbonate to dysprosium oxide with release of carbon dioxide gas. Performed by heating the carbonate in air at 600–800 °C; the reaction is a simple solid‑state decomposition, no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization to generate the hydrochloride salt of 1‑cyclohexylpropan‑2‑amine. The amine is dissolved in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., ether, THF, or MeCN) and treated with aqueous or gaseous HCl at 0–25 °C, producing the crystalline amine·HCl salt; no catalyst needed.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed cyclization (Friedel‑Crafts type) of diphenyl sulfide with diphenylacetylene to form the tricyclic thioxanthene skeleton; typical conditions employ AlCl3 or FeCl3 in an inert non‑protic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or nitrobenzene) at reflux.

Nucleophilic substitution/epoxide formation between bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin in the presence of triethylamine, yielding bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and triethylammonium chloride. Reaction carried out at 50–80 °C in an aprotic solvent such as chlorobenzene or diphenyl ether; excess epichlorohydrin drives the reaction, and the base scavenges the released HCl.

Esterification (condensation) of acetic acid with 2‑butoxyethanol to give 2‑butoxyethyl acetate and water; used to prepare the acetate ester as a solvent. Typically performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or a Lewis acid, often using the alcohol as solvent and removing water azeotropically (toluene or benzene) to drive the equilibrium.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2). Sodium ethoxide acts as a strong base to abstract a β‑hydrogen from 2‑iodo‑2‑methylheptane, eliminating HI and forming the internal alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑heptene. Typical conditions are NaOEt in absolute ethanol, reflux under inert atmosphere; NaI precipitates as a by‑product.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) with cyanide; produces 4‑cyanopyridine; key transformation: CN⁻ attacks the 4‑position of the pyridine and eliminates Cl⁻; commonly performed with NaCN (1.5‑2 equiv) in polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 80‑120 °C; safety precautions due to cyanide toxicity; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (proton transfer) between acetic acid and potassium tert‑butoxide, yielding tert‑butanol and potassium acetate. The strong, non‑nucleophilic base abstracts the acidic proton of acetic acid. Usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) methylation of 2‑mercaptobenzimidazole with methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (methyl triflate), forming thiabendazole (a thio‑methyl benzimidazole) and trifluoromethanesulfonic acid as by‑product. Reaction is performed at low temperature (0 °C to rt) in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., triethylamine) is often added to neutralize the liberated TfOH.

Oxidative chlorination of indium arsenide with chlorine gas, producing arsenic trichloride and indium trichloride. This halogenation is used to convert the semiconductor into volatile metal chlorides for further processing. Conducted in a sealed quartz tube or flow reactor at elevated temperatures (150–300 °C) under anhydrous conditions; no solvent or catalyst is required, but excess Cl₂ ensures complete conversion.

Acid‑base/halide formation; converts insoluble palladium(II) hydroxide to soluble palladium(II) chloride; Pd(OH)2 + 2 HCl → PdCl2 + 2 H2O; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of dimethylacetoxysilane (a silyl acetate) with water, yielding dimethylsilanol and acetic acid. This is a silyl‑ester cleavage reaction commonly employed to generate silanols. Can be carried out at room temperature or with gentle heating in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (e.g., THF/water); mild acid (p‑TsOH) or base (NaHCO₃) may be used to accelerate the reaction.

Acid–base neutralization; hydrogen iodide reacts with lithium hydroxide, yielding lithium iodide and water; performed in aqueous medium, sometimes at low temperature to control HI vapor; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Aqueous double‑displacement (precipitation) reaction between sodium sulfide and holmium bromide forming holmium sulfide (Ho₂S₃) and sodium bromide. The insoluble Ho₂S₃ precipitates out of solution. Reaction is performed in water, often with gentle heating and stirring to promote complete precipitation; no catalyst is needed, and the solid product is isolated by filtration and washing.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation aqueous solution; sodium carbonate reacts with calcium perchlorate, exchanging cations and anions; insoluble calcium carbonate precipitates, soluble sodium perchlorate remains in solution; typically performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst; water is solvent.

Base-induced E2 elimination (dehydrohalogenation); aqueous or alcoholic KOH deprotonates β‑hydrogen of 2‑bromo‑2,5‑dimethylhexane, bromide leaves forming 2,5‑dimethylhex‑2‑ene; water and potassium bromide are by‑products; reaction usually heated under reflux (e.g., KOH in ethanol); no catalyst needed.

Reductive dechlorination of pentachlorophenol with sodium dithionite. Na₂S₂O₄ serves as a mild reducing agent, removing one chlorine atom from the aromatic ring to give 2,3,4,5‑tetrachlorophenol, while generating sulfite/bisulfite and HCl. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution (pH ≈ 7–9) at ambient temperature, often with vigorous stirring. Sodium dithionite is added portionwise to a suspension of pentachlorophenol; after completion, the mixture is acidified to precipitate the tetrachlorophenol product.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis; 1‑bromoheptane undergoes Pd/C‑catalyzed hydrogenation in the presence of H2 to give heptane, removing the bromide. Typically run in ethanol or ethyl acetate under 1–5 bar H2 at room temperature.

Salt hydrolysis / acid‑base dissociation; aqueous dissolution of cyanamide hydrochloride liberates free cyanamide (H₂N‑C≡N) and generates hydrochloric acid. Usually carried out in water at ambient temperature; gentle heating may be applied to accelerate dissolution.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of acetic anhydride by dimethylamine; dimethylamine attacks carbonyl, forming dimethylacetamide and releasing acetic acid; typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine (which also scavenges acid); no metal required.

Double displacement precipitation; silver nitrate reacts with ammonium sulfide in aqueous solution; silver sulfide, an insoluble black precipitate, forms; ammonium nitrate stays dissolved; performed at room temperature with stirring; water is solvent; no catalyst.

LiAlH₄ reduction of nitrile; converts 2‑methylbutanenitrile to 2‑methylbutan‑1‑amine; key transformation is nucleophilic hydride delivery to the nitrile carbon, forming an imine intermediate that is further reduced to the amine; performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; LiAlH₄ is the reductant and the solvent is dry ether.

N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS)‑mediated benzylic chlorination of 4‑nitrotoluene to give 1‑(chloromethyl)-4‑nitrobenzene. The reaction proceeds via a radical pathway; NCS serves as a mild chlorine source. Typical conditions: 1.0–1.5 equiv NCS in dry CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄ at 0 °C to room temperature, often initiated by a peroxide (e.g., benzoyl peroxide) or light. Succinimide is formed as the stoichiometric by‑product.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of acetyl fluoride; purpose is to convert the acyl fluoride to the corresponding acetate salt. Fluoride is displaced by hydroxide, yielding acetate anion and HF (which is immediately neutralized to give NaF). Conducted in aqueous sodium hydroxide (or dilute NaOH in water/ethanol) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base reaction with carbonate; gaseous hydrogen selenide (a weak acid) reacts with solid barium carbonate in aqueous suspension; carbon dioxide gas is liberated, water forms, and barium selenide precipitates; usually carried out under an inert atmosphere to control H₂Se gas, at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; water is solvent; no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); aqueous sodium hydroxide attacks phenyl 4‑fluorobenzoate, cleaving the ester bond to give phenoxide ion and 4‑fluorobenzoate ion (as their sodium salts); reaction is conducted at reflux in water or aqueous ethanol; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/complexation reaction; purpose is to generate a soluble cyanide complex of rhodium for further synthesis or analytical work; key transformation is substitution of the three chloride ligands of RhCl3 by six cyanide ligands to give the hexacyanorhodate(III) anion, with formation of KCl as by‑product; typically carried out in aqueous solution with excess KCN at room temperature to mild heating; no special catalyst needed, water is the solvent.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization) – nitric acid protonates acetate anion of praseodymium acetate, displacing nitrate and liberating acetic acid. Used to convert a lanthanide acetate to the corresponding nitrate salt. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; the reaction mixture is often refluxed briefly to ensure complete exchange. No catalyst required; water serves as solvent.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide – peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfur of S‑methyl‑L‑cysteine, giving 2‑amino‑3‑methanesulfinylpropanoic acid and acetic acid. The purpose is selective sulfoxidation without over‑oxidation to the sulfone. Conducted in a buffered aqueous medium (often phosphate buffer) at 0 °C to 25 °C to control rate; a water–methanol mixture is common. Peracetic acid itself is the oxidant, no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis – water attacks the carbon of 1‑naphthonitrile, ultimately yielding 1‑naphthoic acid and releasing ammonia (or ammonium in acidic work‑up). This conversion is used to obtain the carboxylic acid from the nitrile. Typical conditions involve refluxing the nitrile in aqueous hydrochloric acid (2–6 M) for several hours, or using aqueous NaOH followed by acidification. Solvent is water or aqueous ethanol; strong acid or base acts as catalyst.

Dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination). A strong, non‑nucleophilic base (potassium tert‑butoxide) removes a β‑hydrogen and the bromide from 3‑bromo‑3‑ethylpentane, forming the internal alkene 3‑ethyl‑2‑pentene and potassium bromide. Typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMSO at 0 °C to reflux, under anhydrous conditions.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a ketone – hydrogen gas adds across the C=O bond of 2‑methylpentan‑3‑one to give the secondary alcohol 2‑methylpentan‑3‑ol. Employed to reduce carbonyl groups to alcohols. Conducted in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol, or water) under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–80 °C. No additional reagents are required.

Chemical reduction of a platinum(II complex – hydrogen gas reduces ammonium tetrachloroplatinate(II) to elemental platinum, generating ammonium chloride and hydrogen chloride as by‑products. This reaction is used to recover platinum metal from its soluble salt. Typically performed in aqueous solution under H₂ pressure (1–3 atm) with gentle heating (50–80 °C). No external catalyst is needed; the platinum complex itself is the reducible species.
Hydrolysis of boron trichloride with water producing boric acid and hydrogen chloride gas; vigorous reaction in aqueous medium, typically under cooling to control exotherm; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization to form a salt – formic acid protonates cyclohexylamine, yielding cyclohexylammonium formate. The reaction serves to prepare the amine as its formate salt, often to improve solubility or stability. Carried out at room temperature by simply mixing equimolar amounts of the acid and amine in a solvent such as water, ethanol, or methanol. No catalyst is required.

Phenol O‑methylation (SN2 alkylation); phloroglucinol is deprotonated by sodium carbonate and its phenoxide oxygens attack dimethyl sulfate, replacing the methyl groups to give 1,3,5‑trimethoxybenzene. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF or acetonitrile) at ambient temperature; Na2CO3 acts as base and Na2SO4 is the by‑product.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation; iodine monochloride (ICl) delivers electrophilic I⁺ to the activated aromatic ring of phenol, preferentially at the para position, forming 4‑iodophenol and releasing HCl. Reaction is usually at 0 – 25 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often with a mild acid scavenger.

Epoxy ring‑opening nucleophilic substitution; phenoxide (generated from phenol under basic conditions) attacks the less‑hindered carbon of chlorooxirane (epichlorohydrin), opening the epoxide to give phenoxy‑propylene oxide and HCl (or NaCl when NaOH is used Typical conditions: NaOH or K₂CO₃ as base, aqueous/organic biphasic medium (e.g., water/THF), 50‑80 °C.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester; methyl ricinoleate (containing a C=C bond) is reduced with H₂ over palladium on carbon to afford saturated methyl 12‑hydroxy stearate. Standard conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 10 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C.

Swern oxidation; DMSO activated by oxalyl chloride forms a chlorosulfonium intermediate that oxidizes cyclhex‑3‑en‑1‑ol to 3‑cyclohexene‑1‑carbaldehyde. The reaction is performed at –78 °C in dichloromethane, with triethylamine added after the activation step to neutralize HCl and drive the oxidation to the aldehyde.

Oxidation reaction: potassium permanganate oxidizes allyl alcohol to acrylic acid while being reduced to manganese dioxide; water is formed as a by‑product. Typically carried out in aqueous alkaline medium, often at 0 °C to 25 °C, then acidified to precipitate MnO₂. No additional catalyst; water is the solvent.

Sulfide precipitation (gas‑solid double displacement). Hydrogen sulfide gas reacts with solid PtCl2, replacing chloride with sulfide to give solid PtS and gaseous HCl. Typically carried out in a sealed tube or furnace at 200–300 °C under a flow of H2S, inert atmosphere, no solvent or catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; converts soluble neodymium acetate into insoluble neodymium carbonate while forming soluble sodium acetate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization: alendronic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to form the sodium salt (sodium alendronate) and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water acts as solvent, no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro group (reductive amination). Purpose: reduce the nitro functionality of 3‑nitro‑4‑aminopyridine to give the diamine 3,4‑diaminopyridine while leaving the existing amino group intact. Key transformation: –NO2 → –NH2. Typical conditions: hydrogen gas (1–3 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C (5–10 wt % relative to substrate) in ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 2–6 h. The reaction proceeds under mild pressure and does not require additional reagents.

Double displacement precipitation; iodide exchanges with nitrate yielding insoluble lead(II) iodide and soluble barium nitrate; used to isolate PbI2 or for a qualitative iodide test; conducted in water at ambient temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Acid‑base salt formation with gas evolution: phosphoric acid protonates samarium(III) carbonate, yielding samarium(III) phosphate, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Performed in aqueous media, often with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; water is the solvent, no needed.

Acid‑base proton transfer: sulfuric acid protonates lithium cyanide to generate volatile hydrogen cyanide and lithium hydrogen sulfate. Usually done in cold aqueous solution under a fume hood; water is the solvent, no catalyst; careful temperature control is essential due to HCN volatility.

Hydrolysis of N‑oxalylglycine back to glycine and oxalic acid; amide bond cleavage under acidic (e.g., reflux in aqueous HCl) or basic (e.g., reflux in aqueous NaOH) conditions; aqueous solvent; affords the free amino acid and oxalic acid.

Electrophilic α‑chlorination: N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) chlorinates the α‑carbon of mandelic acid, producing 2‑chloromandelic acid and succinimide as by‑product. Commonly performed in dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) of a tertiary alkyl halide by hydrosulfide ion; produces tert‑butyl mercaptan and sodium chloride; carried out in polar protic solvents such as ethanol or water at ambient or gently heated temperatures; sodium hydrosulfide is used as the nucleophile.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction where the deprotonated aniline (from aniline and NaOH) attacks the chloromethyl group of chloromethyl methyl ether. The reaction introduces a methoxymethyl group into aniline, producing N-(methoxymethyl)aniline, with sodium chloride and water as byproducts. It typically occurs in aqueous or alcoholic solvents at elevated temperatures, with NaOH providing basic conditions to deprotonate the amine.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium cyanide; simple dissociation of an unstable salt. Upon gentle heating or even at ambient temperature, NH₄CN breaks down into gaseous ammonia (NH₃) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). Conducted in sealed or open vessels, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (fluoride substitution) using CsF; produces trimethylsilyl fluoride and precipitates CsBr; performed in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or DMF at rt under inert atmosphere; a convenient method to generate TMSF.

Metal reduction (metallothermic reduction) of Ti(IV)ide with lithium; yields lower‑valent Ti(II) iodide and lithium iodide; typically carried out in dry THF or diethyl ether, under nitrogen or argon, often with gentle heating after addition of Li.

Metathesis/precipitation; H₂S gas is bubbled through an aqueous solution of gold(I) chloride, precipitating gold(I) sulfide and generating HCl in solution; typically performed at room temperature to ~50 °C in water; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt precipitation; exchanges acetate and nitrate ions to give sparingly soluble silver acetate and soluble thallium nitrate; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; used for isolation or purification of silver acetate.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of an intermetallic silicide; titanium metal reacts directly with silicon powder to form titanium silicide; performed under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at temperatures typically above 1000 °C; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (protecting‑group installation); ethylene glycol cyclizes with formaldehyde (from paraformaldehyde) to give 1,3‑dioxolane, releasing water; uses catalytic trifluoroacetic acid, reflux in a Dean‑Stark apparatus (toluene or benzene) or solvent‑free condition; provides a cyclic acetal protecting group for diols.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous mixing of hydrogen selenide gas with aqueous mercury(II) nitrate results in formation of insoluble black mercury(II) selenide precipitate and nitric acid as by‑product. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature; no added catalyst required.

Acid–base/salt‑formation reaction; silver(I) oxide reacts with hexafluorophosphoric acid to give silver hexafluorophosphate, a soluble, non‑coordinating salt, and water. Commonly carried out in dry polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere to avoid premature hydrolysis; no additional catalyst needed.

Halogenolysis/redistribution of organotin; purpose is to convert tetrabutyltin into tributyltin chloride and n‑butyl chloride. Key transformation is cleavage of a Sn–C bond with substitution of a butyl group by chlorine, giving SnBu₃Cl and BuCl. Typical conditions involve bubbling chlorine gas through a solution of tetrabutyltin in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0–25 °C, often under UV light to initiate radicals; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic alkyl‑transfer (dealkylation) reaction; a trimethylsulfonium tetrafluoroborate salt is treated with potassium tert‑butoxide, which abstracts a methyl group as dimethyl sulfide while the tert‑butoxide attacks the remaining methyl to form t‑butyl methyl ether. Potassium tetrafluoroborate is generated as the inorganic salt. Typically performed in aprotic solvents like THF or DME at 0 °C to room temperature; strong base serves as the only reagent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile; cyclopropyl cyanide is reduced under H₂ gas in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney nickel, Pd/C, or PtO₂) to afford cyclopropylamine. Reaction is conducted in an alcohol solvent (ethanol, methanol) or ethereal solvent under several atmospheres of hydrogen pressure (1– atm) at 25–80 °C.

Acid–base (protonation) reaction of ammonium carbamate with hydrochloric acid, producing ammonium chloride and carbonic acid, which readily decomposes to CO2 and water. Key transformation: NH2COONH4 + HCl → NH4Cl + H2CO3 (→ CO2 + H2O). Carried out in dilute aqueous HCl at room temperature; water is the solvent and the reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Hydrolysis of phosphorus pentachloride; addition of a stoichiometric amount of water to PCl₅ yields phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and two equivalents of hydrogen chloride gas. The reaction is highly exothermic, normally performed in a dry, inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) with careful, dropwise addition of water at 0–5 °C to control HCl evolution.

Alkene epoxidation with peracetic acid; a peroxyacid transfers an oxygen atom to 2‑pentene to afford 2‑pentyloxirane. Typically carried out at 0 °C to ambient temperature in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, using dilute peracetic acid (often generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide). Acetic acid is formed as the by‑product.

Thermal cyclodehydration (intramolecular condensation) of butanediamide to give succinimide and ammonia; heated to 180–200 °C in a sealed tube or under reduced pressure, often with a small amount of anhydrous acid or catalyst such as phosphorus oxychloride to promote dehydration; solvent‑free or high‑boiling solvent (e.g., xylene).

Oxidative aromatic hydroxylation; 3‑methylphenol reacts with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of a catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, or a peroxidase enzyme) to introduce a second ortho‑hydroxyl group, producing 3‑methyl‑1,2‑dihydroxybenzene (3‑methyl catechol) and water. The reaction is typically carried out in aqueous buffer at mild temperatures (20–40 °C) with controlled H₂O₂ addition to avoid over‑oxidation.

Reaction type: Halogenation. Purpose: Chlorination of chromium silicide to metal halide and nonmetal halide. Key transformations: Chlorine oxidizes chromium and silicon; Cr forms CrCl₃, Si forms SiCl₄. Conditions: High-temperature reaction in chlorine gas. No catalyst required.

Acetylation (esterification) of a secondary alcohol using acetic anhydride; the hydroxyl of lactic acid is acetylated to give acetyl 2‑hydroxypropanoate, with acetic acid formed as a by‑product; typically carried out in dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine to scavenge the generated acid.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to convert cobalt(II) acetate to cobalt(II) nitrate and generate acetic acid. Key transformation: acetate anion exchanges with nitrate anion. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with stirring, often at mild heating (40‑60 °C). No catalyst required; water serves as solvent.

Base‑promoted conversion of dichromate to chromate (acid‑base equilibrium shift); purpose is to generate sodium chromate from sodium dichromate. Key transformation: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2 OH⁻ → 2 CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O. Conducted in aqueous solution with excess NaOH, usually at room temperature or slight heating. No catalyst needed.

Direct aqua regia leaching. Gold metal reacts with aqua regia (the in‑situ mixture of concentrated HNO3 and HCl, usually 1:3 v/v) to form chloroauric acid, nitrogen dioxide, and water. The reaction is the same overall as (2) but the acids are combined immediately before use. Conditions: ambient to gentle reflux temperature, vigorous stirring, and proper ventilation for NO2. No additional reagents or catalysts are needed.

N‑acylation (amide formation) of benzylamine with acetyl chloride, using pyridine as a base/HCl scavenger (Schotten‑Baumann type). Purpose: synthesis of N‑acetylbenzylamine. Key steps: nucleophilic attack of amine on acetyl chloride, formation of amide and pyridinium chloride. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with pyridine (1‑equiv or excess) as base. No external catalyst.

Salt metathesis (ion‑exchange) to prepare tetra‑n‑butylammonium hexafluorophosphate, a common phase‑transfer catalyst or electrolyte salt. Key transformation: exchange of Br⁻ for PF₆⁻ between the two salts. Usually done in a polar aprotic solvent (acetonitrile, acetone, or dichloromethane) where the product precipitates; reactions are performed at rt, without additional catalyst.

N‑Methylation of 3,4‑methylenedioxyamphetamine via SN2 alkylation with methyl iodide. Purpose: synthesis of MDMA. Key transformation: deprotonated amine attacks CH₃I, displacing I⁻. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaH) at 0 °C to reflux. No catalyst required.

Reductive conversion of a quinone to a dihydroxy (hydroquinone) compound; sodium dithionite reduces 2‑methyl‑1,4‑naphthoquinone to 2‑methyl‑1,4‑dihydroxynaphthalene while being oxidized to sulfate; carried out in aqueous alkaline solution (often buffered) at room temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) of potassium hydrogen phosphate with barium nitrate. Insoluble barium hydrogen phosphate precipitates, and potassium nitrate stays in solution. Performed in water at room temperature; the precipitate is isolated by filtration.

Dehydration of an amide to a nitrile using thionyl chloride; purpose is to convert chloroacetamide into chloroacetonitrile. The carbonyl carbon loses the amide nitrogen and gains a nitrile triple bond while HCl and SO₂ are evolved. Typical conditions are reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, with excess SOCl₂, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; pyridine or triethylamine is added to neutralize the generated HCl.

Copper‑mediated nucleophilic substitution (alkynylation) of cyclopropyl chloride with sodium acetylide to give cyclopropylacetylene. Sodium acetylide forms a copper acetylide complex with CuI, which then undergoes SN2 displacement of chloride. Conducted in a dry, polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, under nitrogen, at 0 °C to room temperature; triethylamine serves as base, CuI (≈10 mol %) is the catalyst.

SN2 N‑alkylation (methylation) of ammonia with dimethyl sulfate; ammonia attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate to give methylamine and methyl hydrogen sulfate. Performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution of ammonium hydroxide (5–30 % NH3) at 0–25 °C, typically in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., methanol) to improve nucleophilicity; excess dimethyl sulfate is used to drive the reaction.

Oxymercuration‑demercuration (Markovnikov hydration) of dodec‑1‑ene to afford 2‑dodecanol. Mercuric acetate adds across the terminal double bond to give an organomercury intermediate, which is subsequently reduced (commonly with NaBH₄) to release the secondary alcohol. Reaction performed in an aqueous THF or water mixture at 0 °C to rt; after addition, NaBH₄ in methanol or aqueous solution is used to remove mercury.

Oxidation (hydride combustion) of lanthanum trihydride with oxygen to form lanthanum oxide and water. Solid LaH₃ reacts with O₂ gas, each hydride proton being oxidized to water while lanthanum is oxidized to La₂O₃. Conducted as a controlled gas‑phase reaction, often at low to moderate temperatures (<100 °C) to avoid runaway; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acyl‑chloride esterification of ethylene glycol monoethyl ether with acetyl chloride to give 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate. The alcohol attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride, displacing chloride as HCl and forming the ester. Performed in dry dichloromethane or ethyl ether at 0 °C to rt, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; no additional catalyst is needed.

Reduction of trimethylamine N‑oxide to trimethylamine using sodium borohydride; purpose is removal of the N‑oxide oxygen to regenerate the tertiary amine; key transformation is hydride transfer from NaBH₄ to the N‑oxide, producing NaBO₂ (sodium metaborate) and water; typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in methanol, ethanol, or a THF/water mixture; NaBH₄ is added portionwise under inert gas.

Hydrolysis of iron(II) bromide in water to produce iron(II) hydroxide and hydrobromic acid. FeBr₂ reacts with H₂O, undergoing an acid‑base exchange that precipitates Fe(OH)₂ and releases HBr into solution. Carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; no catalyst or special solvent is required.

Salt metathesis/precipitation in aqueous solution; purpose is to obtain lutetium phosphate by exchanging the sulfate anion for phosphate; key transformation: Lu₂(SO₄)₃ + 2 K₃PO₄ → LuPO₄(s) + 3 K₂SO₄(aq) (or the appropriate stoichiometry yielding insoluble LuPO₄); typical conditions: aqueous medium, gentle heating if needed, pH adjusted to maintain phosphate solubility, stirring and filtration to collect the lutetium phosphate precipitate.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of a metal halide; elemental fluorine oxidatively replaces iodide in terbium(III) iodide to form terbium tetrafluoride and liberates iodine. Conducted gas‑phase, often in a sealed nickel or quartz reactor at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) under dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer‑type) using acetic acid as both reagent and solvent. Cinnamyl alcohol is converted to cinnamyl acetate in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid and excess acetic acid, typically under reflux (≈80 °C) with removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation). The process yields cinnamyl acetate and water; the acid catalyst is recovered after work‑up.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; aims to replace the nitrate anion with sulfate, yielding silver sulfate and calcium nitrate. Key transformation: 2 Ag⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Ag₂SO₄, Ca²⁺ + 2 NO₃⁻ → Ca(NO₃)₂. Performed by mixing aqueous AgNO₃ with CaSO₄ (or CaSO₄ suspension) at ambient temperature; water as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Multicomponent Mannich‑type condensation and cyclization (TACN synthesis); formic acid, formaldehyde and N,N‑dimethylethane‑1,2‑diamine combine to give the macrocyclic ligand 1,4,7‑trimethyl‑1,4,7‑triazacyclononane with loss of CO₂ and H₂O. Usually performed in aqueous or methanolic solution, refluxing for several hours; no external catalyst needed.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage of an alkene); purpose is to fragment the C=C bond of cinnamic acid into aldehyde and acid fragments; key transformation is cleavage of the double bond to give benzaldehyde from the phenyl‑substituted carbon and glyoxylic acid from the carboxyl‑bearing carbon; typically performed by bubbling O₃ through a solution of cinnamic acid in dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by a reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide or Zn/AcOH) to afford the stable products.

Nucleophilic substitution (double SN2) of a dibromoalkane with hydroxide; 1,7‑dibromoheptane is hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH to give 1,7‑heptanediol and NaBr. Typical conditions: excess NaOH in water or MeOH/H₂O (1:1), heated to reflux (≈80 °C) for 2–4 h; no catalyst required.

Dehydrative nitrile formation via amide intermediate; propionic acid reacts with gaseous NH₃ in the presence of phosphorus pentoxide, which acts as a strong dehydrating agent, to afford propanenitrile with water as by‑product. Carried out in a dry, inert environment (often in a sealed tube) at 150–200 °C; P₂O₅ is the sole reagent/catalyst, solvent is usually absent or a high‑boiling aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene) can be used.

Free‑radical halogenation (chlorination) of methane; chlorine gas under UV light or high temperature abstracts a hydrogen atom from methane, forming methyl chloride and hydrogen chloride. Performed in the gas phase with a quartz reactor, illuminated with UV or heated to ≈400 °C; no solvent, catalyst, or additive needed.

Hydrogen reduction of copper(I) sulfide; general type: reduction; purpose: to obtain metallic copper and hydrogen sulfide gas; key transformation: Cu2S + H2 → 2 Cu + H2S; typical conditions: heating Cu2S in a flow of H2 at 400–600 °C; no solvent, no catalyst.

Alkaline degradation (Hofmann-type dequaternization) of a quaternary ammonium salt; tetramethylammonium acetate reacts with aqueous NaOH, cleaving the N–CH₃ bond to produce trimethylamine, methanol and sodium acetate. Usually carried out in water at 80–100 °C for 1–2 h; no additional catalyst required.

Ester formation via acid‑chloride acylation; but‑3‑en‑2‑ol reacts with acetyl chloride in pyridine, giving but‑3‑en‑2‑yl acetate and pyridinium chloride as the by‑product. Pyridine serves both as solvent and as a base to neutralize HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, dry environment, inert gas; sometimes a catalytic amount of DMAP is added to accelerate acyl transfer. Work‑up includes aqueous wash to remove pyridinium salt.

Acid‑base/ion‑exchange; nitric acid protonates azide ion to give hydrazoic acid (HN3) and forms rubidium nitrate; key transformation: RbN3 + HNO3 → RbNO3 + HN3; performed in cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) to minimize volatilization of HN3; inert atmosphere may be used.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of thietane by ammonia; a basic substitution that converts the four‑membered sulfur heterocycle into the primary thiol‑amine cysteamine. Typically performed by heating excess gaseous or aqueous NH3 with thietane (often neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent) at reflux; no catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification of propionic acid with 2‑ethyl‑1‑butanol; produces 2‑ethylbutyl propanoate and water; standard method for preparing fatty acid esters used as flavors or plasticizers; acid catalyst such as H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or solid acid resin; reflux in an inert solvent (toluene or excess alcohol) with azeotropic removal of water; typical temperature 80–120 °C.

Hydrolysis of a selenium(VI) oxofluoride; replaces the fluorine atoms with hydroxyl groups to give selenic acid while liberating HF; performed simply by adding the reagent to water, often at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required; aqueous medium is the solvent.

Acid‑base (fluorination) reaction; purpose: produce calcium fluoride and neutralize HF; key transformation: oxide O²⁻ is protonated to H₂O while Ca²⁺ combines with F⁻ to give CaF₂ precipitate; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water acts as solvent, reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Metallothermic reduction of tantalum(V) bromide with sodium metal; a solid‑state redox that furnishes elemental tantalum and sodium bromide. Conducted in an inert atmosphere (argon or glovebox) at elevated temperatures (≈400–600 °C) in a sealed tube; no solvent or additional catalyst is used.

Aminolysis of ethyl 2‑methylpentanoate with ammonia to give 2‑methylpentanamide and ethanol; an ester‑to‑amide conversion via nucleophilic acyl substitution. Generally carried out by refluxing the ester with excess gaseous or aqueous NH3 (or ammonium hydroxide) in a sealed pressure vessel; the reaction proceeds without catalyst, though a polar aprotic solvent such as THF can be employed.

Selective oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide; used to prepare dimethyl sulfoxide from dimethyl sulfide. Typically carried out with aqueous hydrogen peroxide (30 % H₂O₂) at ambient temperature, often in a polar organic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile to improve miscibility. The reaction proceeds without added catalysts, though mild acids (e.g., acetic acid) may be added to control rate and avoid over‑oxidation to the sulfone.

Single‑displacement redox (metal displacement) reaction. Metallic magnesium reduces copper(II) bromide to elemental copper, itself being oxidized to magnesium bromide. Typically carried out in the solid state at elevated temperature (300–400 °C) under an inert atmosphere (argon) to prevent oxidation of magnesium. No solvent; the reaction is heterogenous and may be assisted by grinding the reactants together.

Oxidative cyclization of 4‑hydroxybutanal with sodium chlorite (NaClO₂); the aldehyde is oxidized to the corresponding carboxylic acid (4‑hydroxybutanoic acid) which spontaneously lactonizes to γ‑butyrolactone. Typical conditions are aqueous buffered media (e.g., NaH₂PO₄/Na₂HPO₄) at 0–25 °C, using NaClO₂ as the oxidant; the reaction may be assisted by a phase‑transfer catalyst but no metal catalyst is required.

General type: Halogen exchange (Finkelstein reaction, SN2). Purpose: Convert a chloroalkane to the corresponding iodoalkane for further synthetic utility. Key transformations: I⁻ from NaI attacks the primary carbon, displacing Cl⁻ to give 1‑iodopropane; NaCl precipitates out. Typical conditions: Anhydrous acetone as solvent, excess NaI, reflux or gentle heating, reaction time several hours to overnight. Common/catalysts: Anhydrous acetone (poor solvent for NaCl, promoting precipitation), sodium iodide as nucleophile.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of pyrene using acetyl nitrate as the nitronium source; generates 1‑nitropyrene with acetic acid as the by‑product. Performed at low temperature (0–5 °C) in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with acetyl nitrate prepared in situ from acetic anhydride and nitric acid; the reaction proceeds via an EAS mechanism without additional catalysts.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 1‑propanol to propene; a classic elimination (E1) reaction where the protonated alcohol loses water to form the terminal alkene. Conducted with a strong Brønsted acid (e.g., 5–10 %₂SO₄) at temperatures of 150–200 °C, either in the liquid phase or over a solid acid catalyst (e.g., zeolite H‑Beta); water is the only by‑product.

Acid–carbonate reaction (gas‑evolving neutralization); purpose is to generate rubidium bromide while releasing carbon dioxide; carbonate ion is protonated to form CO₂ and water; typically performed by adding aqueous hydrobromic acid to rubidium carbonate at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide opening of ethylene oxide with acetic acid, producing 2‑hydroxyethyl acetate (acetoxyethanol). Typically refluxed in excess acetic acid (which acts as both reagent and solvent) or in a mixture of acetic acid and a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., BF₃·OEt₂) at 80‑120 °C.

Halogenation (chlorination) of phosphoric acid by phosphorus pentachloride; converts P‑OH groups to P‑Cl, generating phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) as a useful chlorinating reagent and releasing HCl; typically performed neat or in inert solvent at low to moderate temperature under anhydrous conditions.

Double displacement precipitation (metathesis) between sodium fluoride and cadmium sulfate in aqueous solution; insoluble cadmium fluoride precipitates while sodium sulfate remains dissolved; carried out at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Sulfidation of a metal carbonyl; tungsten hexacarbonyl reacts with hydrogen sulfide at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in the gas phase, replacing CO ligands with sulfide to give tungsten disulfide while liberating carbon monoxide and hydrogen; no solvent, inert carrier gas may be used.

Conversion of 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol to 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); an S_N2 chlorination of an alcohol, producing SO₂ and HCl as gases; usually refluxed in anhydrous solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, with pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) of phenyl salicylate with methanol to give methyl salicylate and phenol; ester exchange reaction catalyzed by acid (H₂SO₄) or base (NaOCH₃); carried out under reflux in excess methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid or base.

Acetylation (esterification) of diethylene glycol by acetic anhydride, forming the monoacetate 2‑(2‑hydroxyethoxy)ethyl acetate and acetic acid as by‑product; typically heated neat or in a solvent like pyridine or dichloromethane, sometimes with a catalytic amount of base to absorb the generated acid.

Acid‑base reaction of tin(II) oxide with hydrogen bromide, yielding tin(II) bromide and water; performed by bubbling HBr gas through a suspension of SnO or by mixing aqueous HBr with SnO at elevated temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); purpose is to convert isopropanol and acrylic acid into the monomeric ester isopropyl acrylate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the protonated carbonyl of acrylic acid followed by loss of water; typically performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and a water‑removing apparatus such as a Dean–Stark trap; common solvents include toluene, benzene or xylene.

Oxidative decomposition (redox) of ammonium tetrathiomolybdate; employed to generate molybdenum(VI) oxide and elemental sulfur while regenerating ammonium hydroxide. In water, H₂O₂ oxidizes the MoS₄²⁻ anion to MoO₃, liberating S⁰; NH₄⁺ combines with OH⁻ formed from water to give NH₄OH. Reaction is usually done at 0–25 °C to control gas evolution, using excess dilute H₂O₂; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt formation; protonation of urea by hydrochloric acid yields urea hydrochloride (urea·HCl); performed by dissolving urea in water and adding aqueous HCl, usually at low temperature (0‑25 °C) to avoid decomposition; water serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

N‑Methylation using a sulfonium salt; purpose is to install a methyl group onto the nitrogen of aniline to give N‑methylaniline; key transformation involves transfer of a methyl cation from trimethylsulfonium tetrafluoroborate to the amine, with dimethyl sulfide generated as the leaving group; typically run in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst; tetrafluoroboric acid is formed as a co‑product.

Acylation of an allylic alcohol with acetic anhydride; purpose is to protect the (E)-hex‑2‑en‑1‑ol as its acetate or to prepare the allylic acetate ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, producing the acetate ester and acetic acid; commonly performed in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (dichloromethane or CH₂Cl₂) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine, often accelerated by a catalytic amount of DMAP; reaction is carried out at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Acid‑base/ionic exchange reaction forming aluminum iodide; purpose is to generate AlI₃ from Al₂O₃ and hydroiodic acid; key transformation is protonation of the oxide lattice by HI, releasing water and producing AlI₃; typically conducted by heating aluminum oxide with excess aqueous or gaseous HI under reflux or elevated temperature (≈100–150 °C) to drive off water; no external catalyst is required; the reaction yields water as the only by‑product.

Partial reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to obtain isobutyraldehyde from methyl isobutyrate while avoiding over‑reduction to the alcohol; key transformation is delivery of one hydride equivalent to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide/aluminum complex that on aqueous work‑up releases methanol and the aldehyde; performed at low temperature (typically –78 °C) in dry, aprotic solvents such as toluene or THF under an inert atmosphere; stoichiometric DIBAL‑H (≈1 equiv) and careful quench with methanol/water are essential.

Thermal decomposition of rubidium hydrogen carbonate; heating the bicarbonate releases carbon dioxide and water while forming rubidium carbonate. Typically performed by gently heating the solid (≈120 °C) in a dry flask; no solvent required.
