Reaction is carried out in an aqueous bath at pH 4‑5, temperature 80‑95 °C, with vigorous stirring; no external catalyst is required.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenolysis of a benzylic ether. Purpose: reductive cleavage of the C–O bond to generate toluene and methanol, often used for deprotection. Key transformation: Pd/C mediates addition of H₂ across the C–O bond, breaking it to give PhCH₃ (toluene) and CH₃OH. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or THF, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 2–6 h. The catalyst is filtered off after completion.

Bimolecular elimination (E2) of a primary alkyl bromide; purpose is synthesis of the terminal alkene 4‑methyl‑1‑pentene. Potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the C–Br bond breaks, giving the alkene and KBr. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or DMSO, temperature 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere; base is used in excess.

Acid–base/ salt formation reaction; cuprous oxide (Cu2O) reacts with acetic acid to dissolve the oxide forming copper(I) acetate and water; typically performed by heating Cu2O in excess glacial acetic acid (reflux) to ensure complete conversion; no special catalyst required, aqueous or neat acetic acid serves as solvent.

Oxidative dissolution of metal by nitric acid (redox reaction); furnishes terbium(III) nitrate while reducing nitric acid to nitrogen dioxide. Terbium metal is treated with dilute nitric acid, generating Tb(NO₃)₃, NO₂ gas, and water. Reaction is performed under reflux or gentle heating (60–80 °C) to drive off NO₂; concentration of HNO₃ is usually 1–3 M. Conducted in aqueous solution; no catalyst is needed.

O‑Acylation (esterification) of a phenol with acetic anhydride; purpose is protection of the phenolic hydroxyl as an acetate. The phenolic oxygen attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming 2‑methoxy‑phenyl acetate and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Conducted by heating the phenol with 1.1‑1.2 equiv of acetic anhydride in pyridine or dichloromethane at 50‑80 °C; pyridine (or a catalytic amount of DMAP) acts as base and solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to generate tetramethylammonium chloride; key transformation: proton transfer from HCl to tetramethylammonium hydroxide yielding the chloride salt and water; typical conditions: aqueous or methanolic solution at room temperature.

Reductive amination (hydrazone reduction) of meta‑hydroxybenzaldehyde with hydrazine; purpose is installation of a hydrazinylmethyl side chain. The aldehyde condenses with hydrazine to give a hydrazone intermediate, which is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to the primary hydrazine product 3‑(hydrazinylmethyl)phenol. Performed in methanol or ethanol at pH 5‑6 (often buffered with a little acetic acid) at room temperature; NaBH₃CN is used stoichiometrically (1‑1.2 equiv) and the reaction is mild and chemoselective.
Double displacement reaction; produces silver tellurite precipitate and sodium nitrate. Typically conducted in aqueous solution with no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (carbonate–acid reaction). Formic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate, releasing CO₂ gas and forming sodium formate and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst is needed; water is the usual solvent.

Acid–base neutralization of lactic acid with calcium carbonate; purpose is formation of calcium lactate salt and release of CO₂. Two molecules of lactic acid protonate the carbonate ion, generating calcium lactate, water and carbon dioxide gas. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; excess calcium carbonate may be used to drive completion, and the evolution of CO₂ is observed.

Type: electrophilic aromatic condensation (phenol‑formaldehyde). Purpose: synthesis of the bisphenolic antiseptic hexachlorophene. Key transformation: two equivalents of 3,4,5‑trichlorophenol undergo electrophilic attack by formaldehyde (activated by sulfuric acid) to form a diaryl methylene bridge, followed by dehydration to give the bisphenol. Typical conditions: acid‑catalyzed at 50‑80 °C, often in aqueous sulfuric acid or a water‑methanol mixture; removal of water drives the reaction forward. No separate catalyst needed beyond the strong acid.

Type: acid‑base neutralization and salt formation. Purpose: preparation of calcium methacrylate, a metal salt of methacrylic acid. Key transformation: two molecules of methacrylic acid donate protons to calcium carbonate, generating calcium methacrylate, carbon dioxide and water. Typical conditions: ambient to mild heating (25‑70 °C) in aqueous suspension; solid CaCO₃ is added gradually to an acid solution with stirring. No catalyst required; the reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Type: hydrolysis of an acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: conversion of cyclopentanoyl chloride to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride and forming cyclopentanecarboxylic acid after proton transfers. Typical conditions: aqueous work‑up, often at 0 °C to room temperature; the acid chloride may be dissolved in an organic solvent (e.g., diethyl ether) and poured into ice‑cold water or a dilute NaOH solution, then the mixture is acidified to pH ≈ 2 to isolate the acid. No additional catalyst is necessary.

Type: reductive amination (nucleophilic addition of an amine to a carbonyl followed by reduction). Purpose synthesis of 3‑methoxyamphetamine from 3‑methoxyphenylacetone. Key transformation: the carbonyl of the ketone reacts with methylamine (in the presence of acetic acid as a proton source) to form an imine or iminium ion, which is then reduced by sodium borohydride to the secondary amine. Typical conditions: polar protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol, temperature 0 °C to ambient; NaBH₄ is added portionwise after imine formation, and the reaction is quenched with water. No metal catalyst is required.

Type: acid‑base (salt‑metathesis) reaction. Purpose: generation of aqueous neodymium(III) chloride and liberation of ammonia gas. Key transformation: ammonium ion protonates the hydroxide ligands of neodymium(III) hydroxide, forming water and releasing NH₃, while the chloride anion pairs with Nd³⁺ to give NdCl₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, gentle heating (≈50 °C) to promote gas evolution; the reaction is carried out under stirring in a sealed or vented vessel to capture NH₃. No catalyst needed.

Type: metal reduction of a phosphorous halide (salt metathesis). Purpose: preparation of sodium phosphide (Na₃P) and sodium chloride as by‑product. Key transformation: elemental sodium reduces phosphorus trichloride, inserting into the P–Cl bonds and forming Na₃P while chloride ions combine with sodium to give NaCl. Typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free environment (argon or nitrogen), solvent such as dry THF or liquid ammonia at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C); sodium is added in small pieces to a solution of PCl₃, and the mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases. No additional catalyst; strict exclusion of moisture is essential.

Type: Azo coupling followed by intramolecular cyclization (heterocycle formation). Purpose: synthesis of the fused nitrogen heterocycle benzo[c]cinnoline. Key transformation: the diazonium salt electrophilically attacks the ortho‑amino group of benzene‑1,2‑diamine, forming an N–N bond and then undergoes ring closure to give the cinnoline core. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (HCl, 0 °C to 5 °C) to generate the diazonium ion, then gradual warming to room temperature for coupling; often performed in water or dilute acetic acid; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces the carbonyl of benzophenone to a benzylic alcohol (diphenylmethanol). Performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, typically at room temperature to reflux.

Type: Catalytic oxidative dehydrogenation. Purpose: industrial production of styrene from ethylbenzene using oxygen as the oxidant. Key transformation: removal of two hydrogen atoms from the ethyl side chain, forming a C=C double bond and reducing O₂ to H₂O. Typical conditions: gas‑phase flow reactor, solid Fe₂O₃ (iron oxide) catalyst, temperature 450–550 °C, excess O₂ (often 10–20 % O₂ in N₂ or air); no solvent.

Fischer esterification of mandelic acid with ethanol to regenerate ethyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑phenylacetate; purpose is protection of the acid as an ester; key transformation is condensation of the carboxylic acid with ethanol, loss of water; conditions: excess ethanol, catalytic H₂SO₄ (≈5 % v/v), reflux 4‑6 h, removal of water by Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation; solvent ethanol.

Type: Lemieux–Johnson oxidative cleavage (diol formation with OsO₄ followed by periodate cleavage). Purpose: conversion of the alkene of 4‑tert‑butyl‑styrene into carbonyl fragments. Key transformation: OsO₄ adds syn‑diol across the C=C bond; NaIO₄ cleaves the vicinal diol to give aldehydes – essentially formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and a para‑tert‑butyl‑benzaldehyde (often called “cyclamen aldehyde”) from the aromatic side. Typical conditions: catalytic OsO₄ (0.5–5 mol %), stoichiometric NaIO₄, aqueous‑butanol or acetone, 0 °C to rt, reaction time 1–3 h.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming an ester. Purpose: preparation of benzyl trifluoroacetate. Key transformation: potassium trifluoroacetate attacks the benzylic carbon of benzyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the benzyl ester and potassium chloride. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, acetone, or DMSO), mild heating (40–80 °C), inert atmosphere optional; reaction proceeds in 4–12 h.

Type: Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: exchange of counter‑ions to isolate calcium sulfate. Key transformation: Ca²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to form insoluble CaSO₄, while Li⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to remain soluble as LiNO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of calcium nitrate and lithium sulfate mixed at room temperature; stirring followed by filtration of the CaSO₄ precipitate; no special catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization reaction; converts acidic sulfur dioxide gas into sulfite ion; sulfur dioxide dissolves in aqueous KOH, forming potassium sulfite and water; usually done in aqueous medium with excess KOH, often at low to moderate temperature to keep SO2 dissolved; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between calcium carbonate and lead(II) nitrate. Purpose: exchange of cations to precipitate insoluble lead(II) carbonate and form soluble calcium nitrate. Key transformation: Ca²⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻, Pb²⁺ pairs with CO₃²⁻, producing solid PbCO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring. No special solvent required; water is the reaction medium.

Acid‑catalyzed etherification; used to prepare symmetrical ether (diethyl ether). Ethanol attacks ethyl hydrogen sulfate, displacing sulfate as sulfuric acid and forming diethyl ether. Performed neat or with excess ethanol as solvent at 130–150 °C under anhydrous conditions; the reaction is driven by removal of volatile ether.

Esterification of an acyl chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); provides the mono‑methyl ester of fumaric acid (monomethyl fumarate). Methanol attacks one carbonyl of fumaryl chloride, releasing chloride as HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature, typically in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Phosgenation to give a chloroformate ester; prepares 2‑butoxyethyl chloroformate as a protected hydroxyl intermediate. One equivalent of 2‑butoxyethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of phosgene, displacing chloride and liberating HCl. Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C under inert gas, in dry dichloromethane or tetrahydrofuran, with a stoichiometric base (triethylamine, pyridine) to trap the HCl.

Hydrolysis of a tert‑butyl silyl ether; water cleaves Trimethyl‑[(2‑methylpropan‑2‑yl)oxy]silane to give 2‑methylpropan‑2‑ol and trimethylsilanol; typically performed in THF or MeCN with aqueous buffer, mild acid or base, ambient temperature.

Grignard addition to an α,β‑unsaturated ketone (1,2‑addition); purpose is to form a new C‑C bond and generate a tertiary allylic alcohol; key transformation: cyclohex‑3‑en‑1‑one + PhMgBr → 1‑phenylcyclohex‑3‑en‑1‑ol after aqueous work‑up; typical conditions: anhydrous THF or diethyl ether, –78 °C to 0 °C then rt under N₂ or Ar, then quench with NH₄Cl; reagent PhMgBr acts as nucleophile, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); converts cyclamic acid to its sodium salt, sodium cyclamate, a widely used low‑calorie sweetener. Two equivalents of cyclamic acid are deprotonated by one equivalent of sodium carbonate, producing two Na⁺ cyclamate anions, carbon dioxide and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Nitration/esterification to a nitrate ester; yields 2‑hydroxyethyl nitrate, an energetic mono‑nitrate ester. One hydroxyl of ethylene glycol reacts with concentrated nitric acid, forming the nitrate ester and water. The reaction is performed at 0–10 °C to limit over‑nitration, often in the presence of a small amount of sulfuric acid or pyridine as a catalyst/neutralizer, under anhydrous conditions.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between TiCl₄ and PBr₃; used to prepare titanium tetrabromide (TiBr₄) and phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃). Chloride ligands on TiCl₄ are swapped for bromide from PBr₃, generating volatile TiBr₄ and PCl₃. The reaction is carried out under an inert atmosphere, typically at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) in a non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or in the neat liquids, with careful removal of the gaseous PCl₃.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of Δ⁹‑tetrahydrocannabinol to cannabinol using palladium on carbon. Purpose: oxidation (loss of H₂) to convert more saturated THC to the more aromatic cannabinol. Key transformation: removal of two hydrogen atoms from the dihydropyran ring, forming an additional double bond and aromatization. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5‑10 wt %) as catalyst, heating to 80‑120 °C under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane. The reaction releases H₂ gas.

Redox (reductive) reaction: hydrogen reduces iron(II) oxide to metallic iron while being oxidized to water. Used in metallurgical reduction of iron. Key transformation FeO + H2 → Fe + H2O. Typically carried out at high temperature (≈800–1000 °C) in a flowing hydrogen or hydrogen/argon atmosphere. No solvent; solid‑gas contact; no catalyst required.

Combustion reaction; complete oxidation of anthracene to CO₂ and H₂O, releasing heat. Key transformation: aromatic hydrocarbon is broken down, carbon atoms become CO₂ and hydrogen atoms become H₂O. Typical conditions: ignition source, excess O₂, atmospheric or elevated pressure, temperature high enough for flame (≈ 800 °C). No solvent; reaction occurs in the gas phase.

Acid–base (metathesis) reaction; magnesium oxalate reacts with nitric acid to form soluble magnesium nitrate and free oxalic acid. Key transformation: exchange of anions (oxalate ↔ nitrate). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric amounts, gentle heating (≈ 60–80 °C) to ensure dissolution and complete reaction. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Aminolysis of an ester; ammonia attacks methyl tetradecanoate, yielding myristamide (the corresponding amide) and methanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic substitution at the carbonyl carbon, replacing the methoxy group with an NH₂ group. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, reflux in an anhydrous solvent such as toluene or THF, reaction time several hours. No catalyst required; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); copper(II) nitrate reacts with sodium arsenite to give copper(II) arsenite, which precipitates, and sodium nitrate remains in solution. Key transformation: exchange of cations (Cu²⁺ ↔ Na⁺). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, vigorous stirring. The insoluble copper(II) arsenite is filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of an ester; ethyl valerate is reduced with H₂ over palladium on carbon to produce two primary alcohols, ethanol and 1‑pentanol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond of the ester and addition of hydrogen to both fragments. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5–10 % loading), H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature 25–80 °C, reaction time 4–12 h. After completion, the catalyst is filtered off and the alcohols are isolated.

Alkaline ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to convert the methyl sulfonate ester into the corresponding sodium sulfonate while liberating methanol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the ester carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give methanol and the sulfonate anion; typically performed in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution at ambient temperature to reflux; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Acid–base protonation (salt formation); purpose is to convert a free amine into a water‑soluble ammonium salt. The nitrogen lone pair of isopropylamine accepts a proton from HCl, forming the isopropylammonium cation paired with chloride. Usually performed at 0–25 °C in aqueous HCl (or HCl in ethanol); no catalyst needed.

Oxidative fluorination of BiF₃ to BiF₅; raises bismuth oxidation state from +3 to +5; BiF₃ reacts with F₂ to give BiF₅; carried out with fluorine gas at 250–400 °C, commonly in liquid HF or a sealed fluorinating vessel; no separate catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (phenoxide alkylation); the phenoxide generated from 2,6‑dimethylphenol and NaOH attacks chloroacetic acid (or its sodium salt) via SN2 to give 2‑(2,6‑dimethylphenoxy)acetic acid. Reaction carried out in aqueous NaOH at 50–80 °C; the by‑products NaCl and water are formed in situ. No additional catalyst is needed.

Reductive amination using sodium triacetoxyborohydride; purpose is to form the secondary amine N‑methylcyclopamine from cyclopentanone and methylamine; key steps are condensation of the ketone with the amine to give an imine/iminium ion followed by its selective reduction by NaBH(OAc)3; usually carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote imine formation; the only by‑product is acetic acid.

Acid-base neutralization; purpose is to convert a carbonate base into its corresponding oxalate salt while releasing carbonic acid, which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Key transformation: K₂CO₃ + H₂C₂O₄ → K₂C₂O₄ + H₂CO₃ (→ CO₂ + H₂O). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, often with gentle heating to drive off CO₂. Common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Enzymatic decarboxylation of an aromatic amino acid; L‑meta‑tyrosine loses CO₂ to give meta‑tyramine; catalyzed by aromatic L‑amino‑acid decarboxylase (PLP‑dependent) under physiological pH, temperature (≈37 °C) and aqueous buffer.

Acid–base neutralization with gas evolution; purpose is to prepare iron(II) oxalate while releasing carbon dioxide; key transformation is proton transfer from oxalic acid to the carbonate anion, generating carbonic acid that decomposes to CO2 and H2O and forming the iron(II) oxalate salt; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst needed.

Acidification of sodium hypochlorite to generate chlorine gas; purpose is laboratory production of Cl₂; key transformation is oxidation of chloride ion by hypochlorite under acidic conditions, releasing Cl₂, water and sodium chloride; carried out in cold aqueous solution of NaOCl with excess concentrated HCl, often in an ice bath to control gas evolution; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Peracid‑mediated epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); purpose is conversion of Aldrin to its epoxide Dieldrin; key transformation is transfer of an electrophilic oxygen from peroxybenzoic acid to the allylic double bond of Aldrin, forming the epoxide ring and producing benzoic acid as a by‑product; usually conducted in a non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichomethane at 0 °C to room temperature; peroxybenzoic acid serves as the oxidant, no additional catalyst is required.

Diazonium formation followed by Sandmeyer chlorination (Sandmeyer reaction). Purpose: replace the aromatic amino group with chlorine to afford 4‑chloro‑3,5‑dimethyl phenol. Key transformations: (i) nitrous acid generated in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl converts the aniline to a diazonium salt (Ar‑N₂⁺ Cl⁻); (ii) CuCl (or CuCl₂) medi replacement of the diazonium group by chloride, releasing N₂ gas. Typical conditions: cold aqueous HCl (0‑5 °C) to maintain diazonium stability, NaNO₂ added portionwise, followed by CuCl catalyst addition; reaction completed within 30 min while maintaining temperature below 5 °C. Solvent: water; often a small amount of ethanol is added to improve solubility.

Hydrolysis of N,N‑dimethylcyanamide to N,N‑dimethylurea; nucleophilic addition of water to the nitrile carbon, followed by tautomerization. Typically performed in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base at 80–120 °C; can be done in water or a water‑miscible solvent such as methanol; catalyst not required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Stille cross‑coupling of 5‑bromopyrimidine with phenyltributylstannane to give 5‑phenylpyrimidine. Reaction type: carbon–carbon bond formation via Pd(0) catalysis. Common conditions: 5 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd₂(dba)₃, CuCl (optional co‑catalyst), in dry THF or toluene, 80–110 °C under nitrogen or argon, with a phosphine ligand; inert atmosphere required.

Acid‑base protonation forming quinolinium tetrafluoroborate; used to prepare a quinolinium BF₄⁻ salt for electrolytes, catalysts or protecting‑group chemistry; the nitrogen of quinoline is protonated by HBF₄ and BF₄⁻ becomes the counter‑anion; generally carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 2–25 °C under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is needed.

Base‑promoted SN2 substitution of the 2‑chloroethyl group in 1‑(2‑chloroethyl)pyrrolidine with hydroxide to afford 1‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)pyrrolidine and sodium chloride. Usually carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (≈100 °C) or at 60–80 °C for several hours; no additional catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis: SN2 alkylation of one hydroxyl of ethylene glycol with allyl chloride to form ethylene glycol mono‑allyl ether, generating HCl as by‑product. Conducted in the presence of a base (e.g., NaOH, K₂CO₃, or NaH) to neutralize HCl, typically in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF, at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed to 40–60 °C; reaction proceeds without a catalyst.

Electrophilic epoxidation (Prileschajew oxidation) – sodium hypochlorite reacts with acetic acid to generate the in‑situ peracetic acid, which transfers an oxygen atom to cyclohexene, forming cyclohexene oxide; sodium acetate and water are by‑products. Conditions: dilute NaOCl (≈5 % w/v) and glacial acetic acid, 0 °C to room temperature, often in a biphasic water/CH₂Cl₂ system.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 1,4‑dichlorobenzene with phenylboronic acid using Pd(PPh₃)₄ and potassium carbonate to form 1,4‑diphenylbenzene; a new C‑C bond is created via transmetalation and reductive elimination, producing triphenylphosphine oxide and potassium borate as by‑products. Typically run in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dioxane/water or THF/water) at 80‑100 °C under nitrogen or argon.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of acephate. Sodium hydroxide attacks the N‑acetyl group, producing O,S‑dimethyl phosphoramidothioate, sodium acetate, and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, temperature 20–50 °C; water serves as solvent, and the hydroxide ion acts as both nucleophile and base.

Redox oxidation of elemental copper by ammonium persulfate in aqueous solution, giving copper(II) sulfate and ammonium sulfate. Copper(0) is oxidized to Cu²⁺ while the persulfate anion reduced to sulfate. The reaction proceeds at room temperature or with gentle heating, simply stirring in water; no catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification of ethanol with acrylic acid to afford ethyl acrylate and water. An acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid promotes condensation; the mixture is refluxed (≈78 °C) often with azeotropic removal of water or using excess ethanol. The alcohol can serve as solvent, or an inert solvent like toluene may be employed.

Reppe‑type carbonylation of acetylene with carbon monoxide and methanol to produce methyl acrylate. Conducted under high CO pressure (10–30 atm) at 150–200 °C with a transition‑metal carbonyl catalyst (commonly Ni(CO)₄, NiCl₂/CO, or cobalt carbonyl). Liquid methanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Acid‑base neutralisation of hydrogen thiocyanate (thiocyanic acid) with lithium carbonate, yielding lithium thiocyanate, carbon dioxide and water. The carbonate deprotonates the acid, releasing CO₂ gas; the reaction is performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl bromide with sulfide ion to afford phenylmethyl sulfide (thioether); performed with sodium sulfide (Na₂S) in a polar aprotic solvent like DMF or DMSO, at moderate temperature (40–80 °C); sodium bromide is the by‑product.

Complete combustion of sucrose in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water (12 mol CO₂ and 11 mol H₂O per mole sucrose). Occurs at flame temperatures (>1500 °C) the presence of excess O₂; no solvents or catalysts are involved.

Acid–base salt formation; protonation of the basic nitrogen in alaproclate by HCl to give the alaproclate·HCl salt. Typically performed in a polar protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction mixture is often stirred and the product precipitates upon concentration or addition of a non‑solvent.

NaBH4 reduction of an aldehyde; hexanal is converted to the primary alcohol hexanol while sodium borate is generated as the waste by‑product. Conducted in a protic solvent (methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol) or in THF with a modest excess of NaBH4 at 0 °C to 25 °C; reaction is quenched with water or dilute acid after completion.

Acid–base metathesis; sulfuric acid transfers a proton to the dithionate ion, yielding potassium sulfate and dithionic acid (H2S2O6). Carried out in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature or with gentle heating to ensure complete exchange; no special catalyst is required.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen halide (Markovnikov addition). Hydrochloric acid adds across the C=C of pent‑2‑ene; the proton adds to the less substituted carbon, and chloride adds to the more substituted carbon, producing 2‑chloropentane. Conducted in aqueous or ethanolic HCl at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation; introduces a sulfonic acid group onto benzene to increase reactivity or solubility. Transformation: H on the aromatic ring replaced by –SO3H. Conditions: treat benzene with concentrated H2SO4 (≈98 %) at 80‑100 °C (higher temperature gives faster sulfonation). Solvent: sulfuric acid itself serves as reaction medium.

Acid–base dissolution (salt formation). Purpose: convert insoluble praseodymium(III) oxide into soluble praseodymium(III) chloride. Key transformation: oxide O²⁻ is protonated by HCl to form water, while Pr³⁺ coordinates chloride ions to give PrCl₃. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (conc. or 1–3 M) with heating (50–80 °C) until the solid dissolves completely; water is the solvent.

Redox/metal–acid reaction; lanthanum metal reacts with hydrogen bromide gas to produce lanthanum(III) bromide and hydrogen gas. Performed in a sealed reactor or tube furnace under a flow of dry HBr at elevated temperatures (150–300 °C) to drive the reaction; inert atmosphere may be used to avoid oxidation.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); sodium hydroxide attacks the acetate ester of chloromethyl acetate, yielding sodium acetate and chloromethanol (chloromethyl alcohol). Conducted in aqueous NaOH, often with reflux heating (80–100 °C) and sometimes a co‑solvent such as ethanol; after the reaction the mixture is cooled and acidified to isolate chloromethanol.

Halide exchange (metathesis) between a metal halide and hydrogen halide; tantalum pentachloride reacts with hydrogen bromide to form tantalum pentabromide and hydrogen chloride. Usually carried out in anhydrous, non‑coordinating solvents (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) or under gas‑phase conditions at 50–150 °C; excess HBr drives the equilibrium toward TaBr5.

Halide exchange (SN2) converting an α‑bromo ketone to the corresponding α‑fluoro ketone; KF provides F⁻ nucleophile that displaces Br⁻; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C, yielding 2‑fluoro‑1‑phenylethanone and KBr.

Oxidative coupling (disulfide formation). Thiophenol is oxidized by N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) to give diphenyl disulfide, with succinimide as the reduced by‑product and release of HCl. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; no added catalyst is required.

Oxidative fluorination of a metal carbide; UF₄ and C(F)₄ (carbon tetrafluoride) are generated from UC and F₂. Reaction carried out at 400‑600 °C with fluorine gas flow, often in a nickel or Monel reactor to resist corrosion; no solvent, and fluorine handling requires passivation and safety equipment.

Free‑radical/nucleophilic nitration of a saturated hydrocarbon; introduces a nitro group at the bridgehead carbon of adamantane to give 1‑nitroadamantane; usually carried out with concentrated (≈ 70 %) nitric acid, sometimes with added sulfuric acid to generate NO₂⁺/NO₂·; reaction is heated to reflux (≈ 100 °C) in the acid medium; water is produced as a by‑product.

Halogenolysis / methyl bromide formation. Tetramethylgermanium reacts with elemental bromine, cleaving the Ge–CH₃ bonds to generate four equivalents of bromomethane and germanium tetrabromide (GeBr₄). The reaction proceeds under reflux in an inert organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) or under neat conditions, often with gentle heating to drive complete substitution.

Redox oxidation of ferrocyanide. Ozone oxidizes potassium ferrocyanide (K₄[Fe(CN)₆]) to potassium ferricyanide (K₃[Fe(CN)₆]), concomitantly reducing ozone to molecular oxygen. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to control the vigorous oxidation; the reaction is self‑terminating once ferrocyanide is consumed.

SN2 displacement of a benzylic chloride by NaCN; typically carried out in DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to 50 °C, giving the cyanomethyl product and NaCl; the nitrile can be further transformed (e.g., hydrolysis to carboxylic acid).

Halide metathesis (chloride‑iodide exchange). Zirconium tetrachloride reacts with excess potassium iodide to exchange chloride for iodide, affording zirconium tetraiodide (ZrI₄) and potassium chloride as a solid by‑product. The reaction is carried out in anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as tetrahydrofuran or benzene under reflux, often under an inert atmosphere to avoid hydrolysis of ZrI₄.

Precipitation/neutralization of gold(III). Aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes gold(III) nitrate, precipitating gold(III) hydroxide (Au(OH)₃) and forming soluble sodium nitrate. The mixture is kept cold and stirred; the gold hydroxide precipitate is filtered and can be isolated as a brown solid, which may decompose to Au₂O₃ upon heating. No additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis/precipitation: zirconium nitrate hydrolyzes in water to form zirconium dioxide (often as a hydrated gel) and nitric acid. Purpose is to isolate ZrO2 from the nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the precipitated ZrO2 is usually filtered and washed, then calcined if needed. No catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of sodium ethoxide with hydrochloric acid; generates ethanol and sodium chloride. Proton transfer from HCl to the ethoxide ion yields ethanol while Na+ pairs with Cl‑. Performed in ethanol or mixed ethanol/water solvent, usually at 0 °C to room temperature to control exotherm; no catalyst required.

Thermal disproportionation of mercurous chloride, wherein Hg2Cl2 decomposes upon heating to give metallic mercury and mercuric chloride; carried out by heating the solid salt in a dry tube or furnace, usually 200‑300 °C; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfide to sulfone. Dimethyl sulfide is oxidized by potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous medium, yielding dimethyl sulfone (CH₃SO₂CH₃) while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to manganese dioxide (MnO₂) and water is consumed to generate potassium hydroxide. The reaction is typically performed at reflux (≈80 °C) in aqueous KOH solution; the MnO₂ precipitate is removed by filtration after completion.

Halogen exchange (halide substitution) reaction where sulfur dichloride reacts with hydrogen bromide to replace chloride ligands by bromide, forming sulfur dibromide and hydrogen chloride; generally carried out in a dry, non‑protic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) at low to moderate temperature; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: single‑displacement/redox acid‑metal reaction. Purpose: convert elemental bismuth into soluble bismuth(III) chloride and evolve hydrogen gas. Key transformation: protons from aqueous HCl reduce Bi metal, forming BiCl₃ and H₂. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HCl, aqueous medium, often heated to reflux to increase rate. Solvent: water (hydrochloric acid solution).

Reaction type: carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (condensation). Purpose: synthesize isoamyl formate from formic acid and isoamyl alcohol. Key transformation: DCC activates the carboxylic acid to an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate, which is attacked by the alcohol, yielding the ester and dicyclohexylurea by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; catalytic DMAP may be added to accelerate. No additional catalyst beyond DCC required.

Reaction type: solid‑state high‑temperature ceramic synthesis. Purpose: prepare barium niobate (BaNb₂O₆ or related phase) as an electro‑optic/ferroelectric material. Key transformation: diffusion and reaction of BaO and Nb₂O₅ powders to form the mixed‑oxide lattice. Typical conditions: intimate grinding of the oxides followed by calcination at 1200–1500 °C in air for several hours. No solvent; furnace atmosphere is air or O₂.

Reaction type: acid dissolution/complexation of a metal oxide. Purpose: generate uranyl sulfate solution for uranium processing or analytical work. Key transformation: protonation of UO₃ and coordination of sulfate anion to give uranyl sulfate (UO₂SO₄·nH₂O) with release of water. Typical conditions: sulfuric acid (concentrated or dilute) heated gently (≈50–80 °C) under stirring. Solvent: water.

Reaction type: neutralization/ionic salt formation. Purpose: produce calcium ascorbate, a calcium‑vitamin C supplement. Key transformation: deprotonation of two ascorbic acid molecules by calcium hydroxide, forming calcium ascorbate and water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature or slight warming, pH adjusted to near neutral. Solvent: water.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl‑chloride esterification). Purpose: prepare 2‑octyl benzoate ester. Key transformation: 2‑octanol attacks benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride as HCl; a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) scavenges the HCl to drive the reaction forward. Typical conditions: aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, presence of base, inert atmosphere. By‑product: hydrogen chloride (often bound to the base).

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; purpose is to introduce a methyl group at the 3‑position of cholanthrene. Aluminum chloride acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst, generating a methyl carbocation from methyl chloride which electrophilically attacks the aromatic system. Typical conditions are anhydrous, inert atmosphere, low temperature (0–5 °C) then gradual warming; common solvents are dry dichloromethane, carbon disulfide or nitrobenzene.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; trichloroacetic acid reacts with PCl₅, replacing the –OH with chlorine to give trichloroacetyl chloride, together with HCl and POCl₃ as by‑products. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, usually neat or in dry ether, starting at 0 °C and allowing the mixture to reach reflux; no additional catalyst is.

Acidic redox reaction: NaMnO4 is reduced to Mn(II) sulfate while H2O2 is oxidized to O2; Na+ combines with sulfate to give Na2SO4 and water is formed. Carried out in dilute H2SO4 aqueous solution, temperature kept below 30 °C to avoid rapid gas evolution.

Oxidative acid‑metal reaction; gadolinium metal reacts with concentrated nitric acid, yielding gadolinium(III) nitrate (Gd(NO3)3), nitrogen dioxide gas (NO2) and water; reaction is performed under reflux to control NO2 evolution, typically in a glass vessel; no additional catalyst, water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of heptyl acetate). Purpose: convert ester to corresponding alcohol and carboxylic acid. Key transformation: cleavage of the C‑O ester bond by water, yielding heptanol and acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄ or HCl) for several hours. Common solvent: a mixture of water and a polar organic co‑solvent (e.g., dioxane or THF) if needed.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation with phosgene; the reaction installs a benzoyl chloride functionality onto benzene, producing benzoyl chloride and HCl. Aluminum chloride coordinates to phosgene, forming the electrophilic acylium ion (COCl⁺) that attacks the aromatic ring. Performed anhydrously at 0–25 °C in dry dichloromethane or carbon disulfide; excess AlCl₃ is filtered off after completion.

Strecker synthesis of L‑phenylalanine: multicomponent condensation of benzaldehyde, ammonia and hydrogen cyanide to form the α‑aminonitrile (phenylglycinonitrile), followed by acidic or basic hydrolysis of the nitrile to the α‑amino acid. Typically carried out in aqueous ethanol at 0–25 °C for the addition step, then reflux with dilute H₂SO₄ or NaOH for hydrolysis. No catalyst; water/ethanol solvent.

N‑alkylation via SN2 nucleophilic substitution; propyl bromide alkylates the secondary amine of N‑isopropyl‑tryptamine in the presence of potassium carbonate, which deprotonates the amine. Typical conditions include a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, heating at 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere. The reaction yields propyl‑isopropyl‑tryptamine and potassium bromide.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous ammonium hydroxide reacts with lead arsenate, exchanging cations to form soluble ammonium arsenate and insoluble lead(II) hydroxide precipitate. Carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst is needed, and the lead hydroxide is removed by filtration.

Hydrolysis and neutralization of an acid chloride; octanoyl chloride reacts with water to give octanoic acid and HCl, the latter being neutralized by sodium carbonate to afford sodium octanoate, NaCl and CO₂. Typically performed in an ice bath to control the exotherm, then allowed to warm to room temperature, in aqueous medium with vigorous stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification. Ethanol, in the presence of a catalytic amount of a strong acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH), exchanges the methoxy group of methyl 2‑chloroacetate for an ethoxy group, yielding ethyl 2‑chloroacetate and methanol. Reaction run under reflux in ethanol, removing methanol to drive equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldose; reduces the aldehyde of D‑glucose to a primary alcohol yielding D‑sorbitol; purpose is to produce the sugar alcohol; commonly performed with Raney Ni, Pt/C or Pd/C in aqueous solution, 40–80 °C, 1–5 MPa H₂ pressure.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl chloride (nucleophilic substitution, SN1/SN2). Water acts as nucleophile, displacing chloride to give furfuryl alcohol while releasing HCl. Typically performed by stirring furfuryl chloride in aqueous medium, often at reflux; no added catalyst required, though mild acid or base can accelerate the reaction.

Base‑mediated exchange of acetate for hydroxide; phenylmercuric acetate reacts with aqueous NaOH, forming phenylmercuric hydroxide (often precipitates) and sodium acetate; conducted at room temperature in aqueous solution; no additional catalyst.

Fischer-type acylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of a primary amine with an acid chloride to form an amide; purpose is to synthesize N‑ethylacetamide. Key transformation: ethylamine attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the amide, with HCl generated as by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, anhydrous solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) under nitrogen; a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is added to neutralize the HCl.

Formation of a Grignard reagent (metal insertion); 1‑bromopentane reacts with magnesium turnings to give pentylmagnesium bromide. Carried out in anhydrous ether or THF under nitrogen or argon, the magnesium is activated (e.g., by a few drops of iodine) and the mixture is refluxed or gently heated until the magnesium is consumed, keeping the solution dry to avoid quenching.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of a secondary alkyl bromide. Hydrogen gas reduces 2‑bromobutane to butane, with concurrent formation of hydrogen bromide. Conducted under H₂ pressure (≈1–5 atm) in the presence of a metal catalyst such as palladium on carbon (Pd/C) or Raney nickel, in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate at ambient to moderate temperature.

Acid‑base gas absorption (neutralization) of sulfur dioxide with sodium carbonate. SO₂ reacts with carbonate to generate sodium sulfite and carbon dioxide gas. Carried out in aqueous solution; sodium carbonate is dissolved in water and SO₂ is bubbled through the solution at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature. No special catalyst required.

Oxidative transformation of carbamazepine to oxcarbazepine using potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone). The peroxymonosulfate oxidizes the imide nitrogen or adjacent carbonyl, inserting an oxygen to afford the 10‑keto derivative (oxcarbazepine) while being reduced to potassium bisulfate and sulfate. Typically performed in a buffered aqueous medium (pH ≈ 7–8) at 0 °C to 25 °C, with Oxone added portionwise; no organic solvent is essential, though a small amount of acetone can improve solubility.

Oxidative epoxidation/fragmentation of 1,3‑butadiene with dimethyldioxirane (DMDO). DMDO transfers an oxygen atom to one double bond of the diene, forming a vinyloxirane (epoxybutene) and concurrently decomposes to acetone. The reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to –20 °C to prevent over‑oxidation; DMDO is generated in situ from acetone and Oxone, and no additional catalyst is required.

General type: reduction of a metal oxide by hydrogen (high‑temperature redox). Purpose: production of elemental manganese. Key transformation: MnO is reduced to Mn metal while H2 is oxidized to H2O. Typical conditions: solid‑state reaction at 900‑1000 °C under a flowing H2 atmosphere, often in an inert gas furnace. No solvent; gaseous H2 serves as reductant.

Metal‑acid reduction to form a carboxylate salt and hydrogen gas. Metallic sodium reacts with hexanoic acid, deprotonating the acid to give sodium hexanoate while liberating H₂. Conducted under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in a dry, aprotic solvent such as THF or dry diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is highly exothermic and must be added slowly to control gas evolution.

Reduction; NaBH₄ reduces the nitroxyl radical TEMPO to its corresponding hydroxylamine (TEMPOH). The borohydride donates hydride to the N‑O bond, yielding TEMPOH and converting the borohydride to borate species (sodium borate). Commonly carried out in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

N‑Acylation of a tertiary amine; converts promethazine to its N‑acetyl derivative (acepromazine) by replacing a hydrogen on the nitrogen with an acetyl group, releasing HCl; typically performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature with a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to trap the generated HCl.

Reductive decomposition of a metal nitride by hydrogen; hydrogen gas reduces terbium nitride to metallic terbium while liberating ammonia (3 H₂ + 2 TbN → 2 NH₃ + 2 Tb); carried out at very high temperatures (≈800–1200 °C) under a flow of hydrogen; no solvent, often in a tube furnace or reactor made of inert material.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) between tetrabutylammonium nitrate and hydroiodic acid, yielding nitric acid and tetrabutylammonium iodide. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring until complete dissolution; no catalyst required.

Ligand exchange/complexation (formation of a β‑diketonate complex); reflux in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) often with a base such as ammonium hydroxide or triethylamine to deprotonate acetylacetone; lutetium(III) chloride reacts with acetylacetone to give lutetium(III) acetylacetonate and hydrochloric acid (or its salt); typical conditions: reflux 2–4 h under inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst needed.

Neutralization of a metal oxide by a strong acid; zinc oxide reacts with hydrofluoric acid to give zinc fluoride and water (ZnO + 2 HF → ZnF₂ + H₂O); carried out in dilute aqueous HF, typically at 0–25 °C with vigorous stirring; safety measures required due to HF toxicity; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation to give europium oxalate; europium(III) nitrate is treated with oxalic acid, producing insoluble Eu₂(C₂O₄)₃ and regenerating nitric acid in solution; conducted in aqueous medium, typically 0–25 °C, no catalyst.

Dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of a per‑fluoroalkane; 1,1,1,3,3,3‑hexafluoropropane loses HF to form hexafluoropropene (C₃F₆) and hydrogen fluoride; usually induced by high temperature (≈300–500 °C) or by a Lewis‑acid catalyst such as AlF₃ or a basic solid; reaction performed in the gas phase or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., fluorinated ether).

N‑Acetylation of a primary amine; tryptamine is converted to N‑acetyltryptamine by reaction with acetyl chloride, producing HCl as a by‑product; typical conditions involve anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to capture HCl.

Combustion oxidation of trisilane with oxygen; high‑temperature gas‑phase reaction in excess O₂ (flame or heated furnace, >500 °C) where Si–H bonds are oxidized to solid SiO₂ (silica) and H atoms form H₂O; no solvent or catalyst required.

Reduction of an acid chloride; LiAlH4 reduces 4‑methylbenzoyl chloride to 4‑methylbenzyl alcohol. Performed under anhydrous conditions in a dry ether solvent (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere. The reaction is quenched carefully with water or dilute acid after completion.

N‑alkylation of indoline with methyl iodide (MeI) to give N‑methylindoline. The reaction is an SN2 substitution on the nitrogen lone pair. Because HI is generated, a base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃, or triethylamine) is added to neutralize the acid. Typical conditions: dry DMF, acetonitrile, or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; reaction time 1–12 h depending on base and temperature.

Saponification (neutralization) of stearic acid with potassium hydroxide; carboxylic acid proton is transferred to OH⁻ forming water and potassium stearate (soap); typically carried out in aqueous ethanol or water, heated to 60–80 °C for conversion; no catalyst needed.

Eschweiler‑Clark methylation of 6‑methoxytryptamine using formaldehyde and formic acid; the primary amine is formylated then reduced, delivering two methyl groups to give 6‑methoxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine; by‑products are CO₂ and H₂O; reactions are run in methanol or aqueous medium, reflux (80–100 °C), excess formic acid; no metal catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation of silver(I) bromide from aqueous silver nitrate and potassium bromide; yields insoluble AgBr and soluble potassium nitrate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Halogen exchange (SNAr) on a heteroaromatic nucleobase KF provides nucleophilic fluoride that displaces bromide on 5‑bromouracil to give the anticancer agent 5‑fluorouracil. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often with 18‑crown‑6 to enhance fluoride solubility, and heated (80‑120 °C). The by‑product is potassium bromide.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of 2‑iodoethanol with sodium cyanide; cyanide attacks the primary carbon, displacing iodide to produce 2‑cyanoethanol while NaI precipitates; carried out in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO) at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Type: Lithium‑halogen exchange followed by nucleophilic addition (formylation). Purpose: Introduce an aldehyde function onto an aryl ring. Key transformation: n‑BuLi converts 2‑bromo‑1‑methylbenzene to the corresponding aryl lithium; the aryl lithium adds to the carbonyl carbon of DMF, and acidic work‑up yields 2methylbenzaldehyde. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF or Et₂O, −78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere, then quench with dilute acid. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Purpose: Generate insoluble manganese carbonate and soluble ammonium nitrate. Key transformation: Mn²⁺ from Mn(NO₃)₂ pairs with CO₃²⁻ from (NH₄)₂CO₃ to form MnCO₃ precipitate; NH₄⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give NH₄NO₃ in solution. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water, mix at ambient temperature, stir; filter off MnCO₃. No catalyst needed; reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Reduction of bismuth subnitrate with hydrogen gas to metallic bismuth; purpose: preparation of elemental bismuth; key transformation: Bi(III) in BiONO3 reduced to Bi(0) while nitrate is converted to nitrogen dioxide and water; typical conditions: dry H₂ flow over the solid at 300‑500 °C in an inert‑gas furnace; no solvent; catalyst not required.

Type: Halogenation/acid‑base reaction producing a volatile metal halide. Purpose: Convert boron oxide species to boron trichloride. Key transformation: B‑O bonds of boron monoxide are protonated by HCl, releasing water and forming BCl₃ gas. Typical conditions: dry, non‑aqueous environment; gaseous HCl passed over solid B₂ (or BO) at 0–100 °C, often under reduced pressure to collect BCl₃. No solvent; reaction is gas‑phase.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: Synthesize beryllium iodide. Key transformation: Two equivalents of HI protonate the hydroxide groups of Be(OH)₂, producing two molecules of water and BeI₂ salt. Typical conditions: aqueous HI (≈ 5 M), reflux or gentle heating to ensure complete reaction; reaction proceeds spontaneously. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; purpose is to synthesize potassium oxalate; key transformation: oxalic acid reacts with bicarbonate, producing potassium oxalate and releasing CO₂ and H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature, controlled addition to manage CO₂ evolution; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Type: Aqueous metathesis/precipitation (salt‑exchange). Purpose: Prepare the pharmaceutical agent bismuth subsalicylate. Key transformation: Bi³⁺ from BiCl₃ exchanges its chloride ligands for salicylate anions, forming insoluble Bi(C₇H₅O₃)₃ (often written as BiO(C₇H₅O₃)₂) while Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give NaCl. Typical conditions: dissolve sodium salicylate in water, add aqueous BiCl₃ solution dropwise under stirring, maintain temperature around 40–60 °C; a yellow precipitate of bismuth subsalicylate forms and is filtered. No catalyst needed.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of a primary alkyl halide. Purpose: Convert 2‑chloroethanol to ethylene glycol. Key transformation: Hydroxide ion attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming HO‑CH₂‑CH₂‑OH; Na⁺ balances the released Cl⁻ as NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heating to 80–100 °C for several hours, often under reflux; reaction is complete when chloride is fully consumed. No catalyst required.
Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of methyl nitrite producing methanol and nitrous acid; proceeds readily in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). Used to liberate the free base of 1,2‑dimethylhydrazine from its hydrochloride salt. The hydroxide ion deprotonates the hydrazinium cation, forming water and sodium chloride. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is both solvent and reaction medium.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Converts phenacyl acetate (an aromatic α‑acetoxy ketone) to phenacyl alcohol and acetic acid by cleavage of the ester linkage. Reaction proceeds via protonation of the carbonyl oxygen, nucleophilic attack of water, and subsequent breakdown of the tetrahedral intermediate. Performed in aqueous acidic media (e.g., 1 M HCl) under reflux; water or a water/organic co‑solvent mixture is common.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Exchanges anions between lead(II) sulfate and potassium phosphate to form insoluble lead(II) phosphate precipitate and soluble potassium sulfate. Often conducted by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at room temperature; the mixture is filtered to isolate the lead phosphate solid. No catalyst required; gentle heating can improve precipitation.

Acidic hydrolysis of N‑methylpentanamide; type: amide hydrolysis (acid‑catalyzed); purpose: revert the amide to the corresponding acid and amine; key transformation: amide carbonyl is protonated, water attacks, leading to cleavage to pentanoic acid and methylaminium chloride; typical conditions: reflux the amide in aqueous HCl (6 M or 1 M) possibly with a co‑solvent such as ethanol; reaction time several hours; after cooling, isolate pentanoic acid and methylamine·HCl.

Acid‑base metathesis producing boric acid. Hydrochloric acid protonates the metaborate anion, yielding boric acid (B(OH)₃) and potassium chloride. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperature with stirring. No special catalyst; excess acid ensures complete conversion.

Nucleophilic substitution (S_N1‑type) of a benzylic chloride. Potassium hydrosulfide provides HS⁻, which attacks the electrophilic triphenylmethyl carbon, displacing chloride to give triphenylmethanethiol and KCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often under reflux to promote substitution. No additional catalyst is required.

Electrophilic aromatic iodination mediated by copper(II) acetate. I₂ serves as the iodine source; Cu(OAc)₂ activates I₂ and is reduced to CuI while acetate ligands are protonated to give acetic acid. Four equivalents of melatonin are iodinated at the 2‑position to afford 2‑iodomelatonin. The reaction is typically run in glacial acetic acid or a mixed acetic acid/acetone solvent at reflux temperatures, with Cu(OAc)₂ acting as a stoichiometric oxidant/reagent. No external catalyst beyond the copper salt.

Mitsunobu esterification: the primary alcohol of ethylene glycol is converted to the acrylate ester (2‑hydroxyethyl acrylate) using triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate. The reaction proceeds via formation of a phosphonium intermediate and inversion of configuration (not relevant here). Typical conditions are anhydrous THF or dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, with PPh₃ (1.2 eq) and DIAD (1.2 eq); by‑products are triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazine dicarboxylate.

Metallothermic reduction of a metal halide: sodium metal reduces gallium(III) chloride to elemental gallium, generating sodium chloride as the only by‑product. This is a redox displacement reaction performed in anhydrous, oxygen‑free conditions, often in a dry ether or THF solvent at low temperature, with excess sodium (typically 3 eq) and careful exclusion of moisture.

Acid‑chloride formation with oxalyl chloride (Vilsmeier activation): a carboxylic acid (butyric acid) is converted to the corresponding acid chloride (butyryl chloride) using oxalyl chloride, with catalytic dimethylformamide to accelerate the reaction. The mixture is usually run in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt; gaseous CO, CO₂ and HCl evolve, and the product is isolated after removal of solvents and excess reagents.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of alkyl bromide (SN2 displacement): bis(2‑bromoethyl) ether reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) ether and sodium bromide. The reaction is carried out in water or aqueous ethanol, heated under reflux (often 80‑100 °C) until complete conversion, then the product is isolated by extraction or distillation.

Acylation of piperidine using acetic anhydride; a common method to install an acetyl group on an amine, yielding the same N‑acetyl product and one equivalent of acetic acid. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the amine on one carbonyl of the anhydride. Usually carried out neat or in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine to accelerate acyl transfer and neutralize the by‑product acid.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: calcium carbonate reacts with nickel(II) chloride in water to form insoluble nickel(II) carbonate precipitate and soluble calcium chloride. The mixture is stirred at ambient temperature; the solid nickel carbonate is filtered, washed, and dried, while the calcium chloride remains in the filtrate.

Hydrolysis. Purpose is conversion of ester to acrylic acid. Key transformation: water cleaves ester bond. Conditions: acidic (e.g., dilute HCl or H2SO4) or basic (e.g., aqueous NaOH); acid likely used to protonate the carbonyl. Common solvents: water-miscible systems.

Nucleophilic addition/condensation to form a biguanide (metformin). Dimethylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon of cyanoguanidine (N‑cyano‑N′‑guanidine), forming a guanidinium intermediate that subsequently undergoes intramolecular rearrangement and proton transfers to give N,N‑dimethylbiguanide (metformin). Purpose: industrial synthesis of the antidiabetic drug metformin. Typical conditions: aqueous or methanol medium, stoichiometric dimethylamine (often as the free base or 2 M solution), temperature 50‑80 °C, reaction time 3‑8 h; pH maintained mildly basic (NaOH or Na₂CO₃) to neutralize generated HCl if starting from dimethylamine·HCl.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification): 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate is hydrolyzed with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford 2‑ethoxyethanol and sodium acetate. The reaction is performed in water or aqueous ethanol, typically heated under reflux for 1–2 h; after completion the mixture is neutralized, and the alcohol is isolated by distillation or extraction.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the double bond of 2‑methylhept‑1‑ene, forming the epoxide 2‑methyl‑1,2‑epoxyheptane and acetic acid as by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0–5 °C, under stirring; reaction is usually complete within 1–2 h without additional catalyst.

Double displacement precipitation. Aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous cadmium iodide; silver iodide precipitates as a yellow solid while cadmium nitrate stays dissolved. Conducted at room temperature with stirring; water as solvent; no catalyst.

Aminolysis of a thioester (acyl substitution); dimethylamine attacks the carbonyl of S‑methyl thioacetate, displacing methanethiol and forming N,N‑dimethylacetamide. Purpose: preparation of a tertiary amide and release of a thiol. Typically carried out at room temperature to mild reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane; no catalyst required, often under inert atmosphere.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction; gaseous or liquid hydrogen fluoride reacts with tin tetrabromide to replace bromide ligands with fluoride, yielding tin tetrafluoride and hydrogen bromide. Purpose: synthesis of metal fluorides from halides. Conducted in sealed reactors using anhydrous HF as both reagent and solvent, at 100–200 °C under nitrogen or argon; no additional catalyst.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of a phosphorus halide; aqueous sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes methyl phosphonous dichloride, converting the P–Cl bonds to P–OH groups, producing water, sodium chloride and the sodium salt of methylphosphonic acid (sodium methylphosphonate). Purpose: preparation of phosphonate salts. Performed in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C (or gently warmed) with excess NaOH; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt formation; methanolic solution of mianserin (a basic amine) is treated with hydrogen chloride, protonating the amine to give mianserin hydrochloride. Purpose: generation of a pharmaceutically useful crystalline salt. Typically carried out in methanol at 0–25 , adding gaseous or aqueous HCl dropwise with stirring; no catalyst needed.

SN2 alkylation of acetate (Williamson‑type ester synthesis); sodium acetate acts as nucleophile on 1‑chloropropane, displacing chloride to form propyl acetate and sodium chloride. Purpose: preparation of an alkyl acetate ester. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often under reflux; NaCl precipitates to drive the reaction forward; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl mesylate; water attacks the cyclohexylmethyl methanesulfonate, displacing the methanesulfonate group to afford cyclohexylmethanol and methanesulfonic acid. Purpose: conversion of a good leaving‑group substrate to the corresponding alcohol. Performed in aqueous medium (or aqueous methanol) at ambient or elevated temperature; neutral or mildly basic conditions; no catalyst.

Acid–base (carbonate) reaction; zinc carbonate reacts with aqueous hydroiodic acid to release CO₂ gas and water while forming zinc iodide. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Silyl‑ester exchange between trimethylsilyl acetate and benzoic acid; forms trimethylsilyl benzoate and acetic acid. The reaction transfers the TMS group from acetate to the benzoate anion, useful for generating silyl esters of acids. It is usually performed at rt in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or THF with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) or a catalytic amount of DMAP to neutralize the liberated acetic acid and drive the equilibrium.

Oxidation reaction; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes guanidine to N‑hydxyguanidine, reducing H₂O₂ to water. Usually carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic media, often with a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) under mild temperatures (0–25 °C).

Acid–base/salt‑formation (metathesis) reaction; aluminum chloride reacts with lactic acid to generate aluminum lactate and liberate hydrochloric acid. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) with gentle heating; no external catalyst needed.

Carbonation of a metal oxide; cobalt(II) oxide reacts with carbon dioxide in an aqueous medium or under elevated CO2 pressure (often 1–5 atm) at 50–150 °C to form cobalt carbonate. No catalyst; water serves as the solvent.

Aerobic oxidation; glycolaldehyde is oxidized by molecular oxygen to glyoxylic acid with concomitant formation of water. Requires a catalyst such as copper, manganese, or cobalt salts, typically in aqueous solution under reflux or elevated temperature (50–100 °C) and aerobic atmosphere.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic cleavage); methyl 5‑aminosalicylate undergoes hydrolysis to give 5‑aminosalicylic acid and methanol. Performed in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., HCl) or dilute base, heated under reflux; water/alcohol mixture serves as solvent.

Reductive amination; 2‑tetralone reacts with ammonium acetate to form an imine intermediate, which is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to afford 2‑amino‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene. Typically carried out in methanol or ethanol at room temperature or mild heating (20–40 °C); NaCNBH₃ acts as the mild reducing agent, no additional catalyst required.

Type: Selective partial reduction of a carboxylic acid to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). Purpose: Convert 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoic acid into the corresponding aldehyde while preserving the dimethylamino group. Key transformation: R‑COOH → R‑CHO (acid to aldehyde). Typical conditions: Anhydrous reaction at –78 °C to –20 °C under nitrogen; 1 equiv DIBAL‑H in dry THF (or toluene). Work‑up with methanol or aqueous Rochelle’s salt to quench excess DIBAL‑H. No additional catalyst required.

Acyl chloride–mediated esterification (acetylation) of phenolic/alcoholic hydroxyl groups; acetyl chloride reacts with hydroxytyrosol to form the mono‑acetate and HCl; usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to rt, with pyridine (or a similar base) scavenging the generated HCl.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of a dimethyl aromatic diester. Purpose: Produce the dicarboxylic acid (isophthalic acid) from its dimethyl ester, generating methanol as a by‑product. Key transformation: –COOCH₃ groups → –COOH with release of CH₃OH. Typical conditions: Refluxing aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1–2 M H₂SO₄) for 4–8 h; often performed in a mixture of water and a co‑solvent (e.g., THF) to improve solubility. After reaction the mixture is cooled, acidified if needed, and the product is isolated by filtration. No special catalyst beyond the acid.

Type: Oxidation of a trialkylarsine to its using a peracid. Purpose: Convert trimethylarsine to the more stable oxidized form, trimethyline oxide. Key transformation: (CH₃)₃As → (CH₃)₃As=O (arsine to arsine oxide). Typical conditions: Peracetic acid (≈30 % in aqueous acetic acid) added dropwise to a solution of trimethylarsine in glacial acetic acid at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere. Reaction is usually complete within 30 min; work‑up involves extraction with an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) and removal of residual acid. No metal catalyst required.

Type: Alcoholysis (transesterification) of a carbonate. Purpose: Convert ethylene carbonate and ethanol into the valuable low‑melting carbonate ester diethyl carbonate and ethylene glycol. Key transformation: Cyclic carbonate ring by ethanol → ethylene glycol + diethyl carbonate. Typical conditions: Excess ethanol (often the solvent) heated to 150–200 °C in the presence of a basic catalyst such as K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, or a solid base (e.g., MgO) or an solid catalyst (e.g., zeolite). The reaction may be conducted under reduced pressure to remove the formed diethyl carbonate and drive equilibrium to completion. No special solvent beyond the ethanol reactant.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of methyl iodide with ammonia giving methylamine; ammonium iodide is formed as the by‑product. Highly reactive, usually performed with excess NH3 at room temperature or under mild heating; no catalyst required.

Type: Nitration (esterification) of a polyol to a nitrate ester (explosive). Purpose: Synthesize nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate) from glycerol. Key transformation: Each –OH group of glycerol is converted to an –ONO₂ group, releasing water. Typical conditions: Cold (0–5 °C) mixture of concentrated nitric acid (≈68 % w/w) and concentrated sulfuric acid (acting as a dehydrating catalyst) added slowly to glycerol while maintaining temperature below 10 °C. After addition, the mixture is stirred for 30–60 min at 0–5 °C, then the product is poured into cold water, extracted with a non‑polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane), washed, and dried. Extreme caution required due to the explosive nature of the product.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; purpose is to precipitate copper(II) carbonate; key transformation is CuCl2 + K2CO3 → CuCO3(s) + 2 KCl; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to improve precipitation; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl chloride to ester). Thiophene‑2‑carbonyl chloride is treated with methanol, producing methyl thiophene‑2‑carboxylate and HCl. Reaction is carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to rt, with pyridine or a tertiary amine base to capture HCl and prevent polymerisation of the thiophene ring.

Acid‑metal deprotonation; used to generate the sodium phenoxide (sodium resorcinolate) as a nucleophilic phenoxide salt. The phenolic O–H proton is abstracted by elemental sodium, releasing H₂ gas and forming the sodium salt. Typical conditions: dry, aprotic solvent such as anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, under inert atmosphere; reaction performed at reflux or gentle warming to promote metal activation.

Oxidative bromination (in‑situ bromination) of 5,5‑dimethylhydantoin; purpose is to prepare the brominating agent 1,3‑dibromo‑5,5‑dimethylhydantoin (DBDMH). Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes bromide (from NaBr) to hypobromous acid/Br₂, which electrophilically brominates the imide at the 1‑ and 3‑positions. Common conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium (e.g., water/acetone), temperature 0–25 °C, pH buffered (often carbonate or phosphate) to control excess acid; NaBr serves as bromide source, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑metal neutralization / salt formation with calcium; purpose is to convert benzoic acid into calcium benzoate while liberating hydrogen gas. Two equivalents of benzoic acid donate protons to metallic calcium, yielding calcium benzoate and H₂. Typical conditions: dry ether or THF, inert atmosphere, gentle heating to initiate metal dissolution; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive and performed under anhydrous conditions.

Nitrosation of a secondary urea; purpose is to synthesize N‑ethyl‑N‑nitrosourea. Sodium nitrite in acidic medium (acetic acid) generates nitrous acid, which nitrosates the nitrogen of N‑ethylurea, producing the N‑nitroso derivative and sodium acetate as by‑product; water released from the condensation step. Conditions: aqueous/acetic acid mixture, temperature 0–5 °C to avoid side reactions, pH ~3–4; the reaction proceeds without metal catalyst.

Base‑induced haloform reaction; purpose is cleavage of a trihalo‑ketone to generate chloroform and a trichloroacetate salt. Key transformation: hexachloro‑2‑propanone + NaOH → CHCl3 (chloroform) + NaOOC‑CCl3 (sodium trichloroacetate). Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), temperature 50–80 °C, stirring for 1–2 h; water as solvent; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a disulfide; purpose is to cleave the S‑S bond of allyl propyl disulfide to afford the corresponding thiols (propyl mercaptan and allyl mercaptan). Molecular hydrogen is activated on palladium on carbon (Pd/C), delivering hydrogen atoms to each sulfur and breaking the disulfide linkage. Typical conditions: hydrogen pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10% loading), solvent such as ethanol, methanol or THF, temperature ambient to 50 °C; reaction time 1–4 h until complete conversion.

Grignard addition (nucleophilic addition); purpose: convert an aldehyde to a secondary alcohol. Key transformation: octylmagnesium bromide attacks the carbonyl of ethanal, forming an alkoxide that is protonated to give 2‑decanol. Typical conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (diethyl ether or THF), temperature from 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; work‑up with aqueous NH4Cl or dilute acid.

Redox/acid‑base reaction of a metal with hydrofluoric acid; beryllium metal reacts with aqueous HF to form soluble beryllium fluoride and liberate hydrogen gas. Conducted in dilute HF solution at room temperature or slightly warmed; vigorous stirring is typical; no catalyst required, but extreme safety precautions are mandatory due to HF toxicity.

Formation of phosphotungstic acid (heteropoly acid); phosphoric acid reacts with tungsten(VI) oxide (WO₃) in aqueous solution, usually heated to 80–120 °C, to condense into phosphotungstic acid (H₃PW₁₂O₄₀) with evolution of water. No external catalyst is required; excess acid may be used to drive the condensation.

DCC‑mediated coupling (condensation); purpose: activate formic acid for nucleophilic substitution by hydrazine to give N‑formylhydrazine. Key transformation: dicyclohexylcarbodiimide reacts with formic acid to form an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate, which is displaced by hydrazine, releasing dicyclohexylurea. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or DMF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; by‑product precipitates and is filtered out.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); purpose: convert an alkene into the corresponding ep. Key transformation: peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond of trans‑β‑methylstyrene, forming 2,3‑epoxy‑1‑phenylpropane and acetic acid. Typical conditions: CH2Cl2 or acetone as solvent, 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic amount of acid or buffer to control acidity.

Acid‑catalyzed orthoester formation (orthoformylation); purpose: synthesize ethyl orthoformate from formaldehyde and ethanol. Key transformation: sulfuric acid protonates formaldehyde, promoting successive addition of two ethanol molecules loss of water yields the orthoester. Typical conditions: excess ethanol, catalytic H2SO4 (≈1–5 %); reflux (≈78 °C) with azeotropic removal of water or use of Dean‑Stark trap.

Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidation; purpose: oxidize a primary benzylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde. Key transformation: DMP transfers an oxygen to 4‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol, generating 4‑hydroxybenzaldehyde and reduced iodobenzoic acid. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric DMP (1.1 eq), inert atmosphere; reaction completes in 0.5–2 h.

Acid‑base salt formation; purpose: generate the water‑soluble dihydrochloride salt of o‑phenylenediamine. Key transformation: two equivalents of HCl protonate the two amine groups of o‑phenylenediamine, yielding 1,2‑phenylenediamine dihydrochloride. conditions: dissolve o‑phenylenediamine in aqueous HCl (≈2 M) at room temperature; precipitate or isolate the salt by evaporation or cooling.

Acid‑base neutralisation (salt metathesis). Proton transfer from HCl to the lactate anion converts potassium lactate to free lactic acid while forming KCl. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation in water. Potassium phosphate reacts with lead nitrate; lead phosphate precipitates as an insoluble solid, while potassium nitrate remains in solution. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient conditions; no catalyst.

Reaction type: halogenation of an alcohol (conversion of –OH to –Cl) using thionyl chloride. Purpose: replace the hydroxyl group of 2‑bromoethanol with chlorine to give 2‑bromoethyl chloride. Key transformation: SOCl₂ reacts with the alcohol, forming an intermediate chlorosulfite that collapses to release SO₂ and HCl gases, yielding the alkyl chloride. Typical conditions: excess thionyl chloride, reflux (40–60 °C) under inert atmosphere; optional base (pyridine) scavenges HCl. Common solvent: dry dichloromethane or neat SOCl₂; reaction is usually completed within 30 min to 2 h, then excess SOCl₂ is removed under reduced pressure.

Esterification of formic acid with diazomethane to give methyl formate. This is a carboxylic‑acid methylation (diazomethane methyl ester formation). The acidic proton is deprotonated by CH₂N₂, generating a formate anion that captures the methyl fragment as N₂ leaves, yielding the ester. Typical setup: formic acid dissolved in dry ether, cooled to 0 °C, then slow addition of 0.5–1 M diazomethane; reaction proceeds at 0 °C–rt, inert atmosphere, no catalyst.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis). Concentrated nitric acid protonates strontium oxalate, releasing oxalic acid and forming soluble strontium nitrate. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to aid dissolution; no additional catalyst needed.
double displacement reaction; praseodymium sulfate converted to praseodymium chloride; ba^2+ and so4^2- form insoluble baso4 precipitate; aqueous solution, ambient temperature; no catalyst required

Acid‑base reaction of potassium tellurite with hydrochloric acid yielding tellurous acid and potassium chloride; performed in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature; no special catalyst needed.

Combined redox and acid‑base reaction. Hydroiodic acid reacts with copper(II) carbonate; the carbonate is protonated to CO₂ and water, while Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu⁺ (as CuI) and iodide is oxidised to I₂. Performed in aqueous HI, usually under reflux; no external catalyst.

Base‑catalysed disproportionation (intramolecular Cannizzaro‑type) of glyoxal. Aqueous calcium hydroxide deprotonates glyoxal, leading to cleavage into calcium formate and calcium glycolate with formation of water. Conducted at ambient to modest temperature in water; calcium hydroxide serves both base and calcium source.

Metal‑acid single‑displacement (hydrogen evolution) reaction. Sodium metal reduces trifluoroacetic acid, liberating H₂ gas and forming sodium trifluoroacetate. Carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, often at 0 °C to control vigorous H₂ evolution; no catalyst.

Grignard carboxylation; extends a carbon chain by one carbon atom to afford a carboxylic acid. Pentylmagnesium chloride adds to CO2 (dry ice) in dry ether (THF or Et2O) at 0 °C to rt, forming the magnesium carboxylate which is then acid‑work‑up (HCl) to give pentanoic acid and MgCl2. Moisture‑free conditions are essential.

Reductive dehalogenation using zinc metal; zinc dust in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere reduces 1,1‑dichloride, removing both chlorides to afford ethane while forming ZnCl₂, typically with gentle heating.

N‑chlorination (oxidative chlorination) of an amino acid. Sodium hypochlorite reacts with glycine, effecting electrophilic chlorination of the amine nitrogen to give N‑chloroglycine while the accompanying acid‑base step generates NaOH. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at 0–5 °C and pH 7–9 to limit over‑oxidation; no additional catalyst.

Acid chloride formation using thionyl chloride. Purpose: generate 2‑methylbenzoyl chloride from the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: COOH → COCl with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: addition of SOCl₂ to the acid in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, reaction initiated at 0 °C then allowed to stir at reflux; a catalytic amount of DMF often added to activate SOCl₂; performed under inert atmosphere.

Thermal decomposition of strontium peroxide; serves to generate oxygen gas and the stable oxide SrO. The O–O bond in SrO2 breaks upon heating, producing SrO and O2.
