Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann N‑arylation; converts 2‑aminobenzoic acid (anthranilic acid) into Enfenamic acid by forming a new C–N with 2‑ethyl‑bromobenzene; potassium carbonate acts as base to deprotonate the amine and trap HBr; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or NMP at 100–130 °C under nitrogen, using CuI (often with a nitrogen‑based ligand) as the catalyst; potassium bromide is generated as a by‑product.

Acidiclysis of a metal nitride; lanthanum nitride reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce ammonia gas and soluble lanthanum chloride; the reaction proceeds at to reflux in water, with no catalyst required; the stoichiometry is 3 HCl per LaN to give LaCl₃ and NH₃.

Acid‑base (oxide‑acid) reaction; copper(II) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrogen bromide to form copper(II) bromide and water; usually heated gently in aqueous HBr to ensure complete conversion, no catalyst.

Strong oxidative cleavage; potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes 1,1‑dichloroacetone, breaking the carbon skeleton to yield dichloroacetic acid together with CO₂ and H₂O; reaction is heated under reflux, solvent water, no additional catalyst beyond KMnO₄.

Chromic‑acid oxidation (Jones oxidation); primary 1‑butanol is oxidized by the Jones reagent (CrO₃ aqueous H₂SO₄) to butyric acid; the reaction is usually run in acetone at 0 °C to room temperature, adding the alcohol solution dropwise to the reagent; the chromium(VI) reduced to chromium(III) and water is formed as a by‑product.

Peroxide oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde; vanillin is converted to vanillic acid by reaction with hydrogen peroxide, which oxidizes the aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid; the process can be performed in aqueous medium, often buffered at pH 5–7 and optionally catalyzed by a transition‑metal ion (e.g., Fe²⁺ in a Fenton‑type system) at room temperature.

Aqueous neutralization/double‑displacement; aluminum lactate reacts with three equivalents of sodium hydroxide to precipitate aluminum hydroxide and generate three equivalents of sodium lactate in solution; the reaction occurs at ambient temperature in water, with vigorous stirring; no catalyst is required.

Oxidative cleavage of the ethyl substituent on 2‑ethylpyrazine using excess potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium; strong oxidant converts the side chain to carboxylic acids, giving pyrazine‑2‑carboxylic acid and further oxidation of the terminal carbon to acetic acid; typically carried out by stirring the substrate in water with excess KMnO₄ at reflux, MnO₂ precipitates and KOH remains in solution.

Transfer‑hydrogenation (catalytic oxidation‑reduction) of isopropanol with p‑benzoquinone over palladium on carbon; Pd/C catalyzes dehydrogenation of isopropanol to acetone while the quinone is reduced to hydroquinone; performed in a polar protic solvent (e.g., or water) at 80–100 °C under atmospheric pressure.

Type: Hydrolysis (water quench) of an acyl chloride. Purpose: Convert the unstable formyl chloride back to the parent acid or to neutralize excess acyl chloride. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon, yielding formic acid and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: The acyl chloride solution (often in CH₂Cl₂) is cooled to 0 °C and aqueous buffer or ice‑cold water is added slowly with stirring; the mixture is then allowed to warm to ambient temperature. The organic layer is separated and the aqueous phase is neutralized if needed.

Direct fluorination/redox reaction: elemental fluorine oxidizes tungsten(V) fluoride to tungsten(VI) fluoride, adding a sixth fluorine atom; the gas‑phase reaction is conducted in an inert fluorinated carrier gas, often at low temperature (‑78 °C to room temperature) to control exotherm; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Generation of a Wittig ylide (methylenetriphenylphosphorane) by deprotonation of methyltriphenylphosphonium iodide with lithium diisopropylamide; LDA abstracts the phosphonium methyl proton, yielding the ylide, LiI, and diisopropylamine as by‑product; performed under anhydrous conditions in THF (or diethyl ether) at ‑78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen.

Sulfide precipitation (double‑displacement); germanium tetrachloride reacts with hydrogen sulfide gas to form germanium disulfide solid and hydrogen chloride gas. Performed in anhydrous, inert solvent (e.g., dry ether or THF) at low temperature (0 °C to room temperature) under a flow of H2S. No catalyst; the reaction proceeds by direct sulfide formation and evolves HCl.

Acid‑base double‑displacement precipitation: sulfuric acid reacts with barium carbonate to form insoluble barium sulfate and carbonic acid, which rapidly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of a trialkylborane. Purpose: decompose triethylborane to benign products and recover ethanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the boron center, successive replacement of ethyl groups by OH, producing boric acid (B(OH)3) and three equivalents of ethanol (CH3CH2OH). Typical conditions: aqueous work‑up at 0 °C to room temperature, often after the organoborane reaction is complete; solvent can be a mixture of ether (to dissolve the organoborane) and water.

Swern oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde; dimethyl sulfoxide is activated by oxalyl chloride at ‑78 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane, forming a chlorosulfonium intermediate that reacts with the alcohol; subsequent addition of a base (e.g., triethylamine) affords the aldehyde while releasing CO₂, CO, and dimethyl sulfide; low temperature and inert atmosphere are essential.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; aqueous nitric acid reacts with iron(II) sulfate, swapping anions to form soluble ferrous nitrate and sulfuric acid; performed at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Copper(I)-catalyzed halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type) on phenol; replaces bromine with iodine to give 3‑iodophenol while forming copper(I) bromide. Reaction proceeds in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, potassium carbonate deprotonates the phenol, and CuI provides iodide. Reflux temperature for several hours; no additional catalyst needed.

Ozonolysis of the alkene 4‑ethylstyrene to afford 4‑ethylbenzaldehyde; purpose is oxidative cleavage of the C=C bond to generate an aldehyde; key transformation is addition of ozone across the double bond followed by reductive work‑up that reduces the ozonide to an aldehyde; performed in a dry, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at –78 °C to 0 °C with ozone gas, then reduced with dimethyl sulfide, zinc/acetic acid, or PPh3; yields the aldehyde after aqueous work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of formic acid (generated in situ from sodium formate and H₂SO₄) with ethanol to afford ethyl formate. Conducted by mixing ethanol, sodium formate and a catalytic amount of concentrated sulfuric acid, then refluxing (≈78 °C) to drive ester formation. Water is formed as by‑product; excess ethanol may be used as solvent and to remove water by azeotropic distillation.

Esterification (acetylation) of phenol with acetic acid to give phenyl acetate; a condensation reaction forming an aryl acetate and water; generally requires a strong acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄ or HCl) and reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or acetic acid itself; purpose is preparation of phenyl acetate as a fragrance or intermediate.

This is an acyl transfer reaction. It facilitates the reversible transfer of an acetyl group between carnitine and coenzyme A, critical for fatty acid transport across mitochondrial membranes. The reaction is catalyzed by carnitine acyltransferase enzymes under physiological conditions (aqueous solution, pH ~7.4, 37°C).

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in acidic medium; phosphorous acid (H3PO3) is oxidized to phosphoric acid (H3PO4) while sodium chlorite (ClO2−) is reduced to chloride ion, forming NaCl and water; carried out in dilute mineral acid (e.g., HCl) at moderate temperature (20‑60 °C); no additional catalyst is usually needed.

E2 elimination (dehydrohalogenation). Potassium tert‑butoxide removes a β‑hydrogen from 1‑chloro‑3‑methylbutane, giving the Hofmann product 3‑methyl‑1‑butene, potassium chloride, and tert‑butanol as a by‑product. Carried out in an aprotic solvent such as THF or DMSO under reflux; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of secondary pentanol to yield 2‑pentene. Phosphoric acid (often 85 % H₃PO₄) is mixed with the alcohol and heated to 150–200 °C, either neat or on a solid support (e.g., SiO₂). The acid protonates the hydroxyl group, facilitating loss of water and formation of the alkene. No additional catalyst needed.

Redox generation of chlorine dioxide from chlorite. In acidic aqueous solution (H₂SO₄) sodium chlorite is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide, producing ClO₂ gas, O₂, Na₂SO₄ and water. Reaction is carried out at low temperature (0–10 °C) to control ClO₂ evolution, typically in dilute aqueous medium. No external catalyst; acid provides the necessary environment for the redox process.

Acid-base neutralization; reaction of solid lead(II) hydroxide with aqueous sulfuric acid to give lead(II) sulfate precipitate and water; performed in aqueous medium, often at room temperature; no catalyst needed; the product is a sparingly soluble white solid.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to exchange anions and isolate insoluble lead(II) iodide as a yellow precipitate while forming soluble potassium chlorate; key transformation is KI + Pb(ClO₃)₂ → PbI₂(s) + 2 KClO₃(aq); typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to isolate insoluble zinc phosphate while converting soluble zinc chloride and ammonium phosphate into ammonium chloride in aqueous solution; typically performed at room temperature with stirring in water; no special catalyst, aqueous medium.

Catalytic isomerization of aromatic hydrocarbons; converts meta‑xylene to ortho‑xylene to adjust product distribution for petrochemical feedstocks; key transformation is migration of a methyl group on the benzene ring; carried out over strong acidic solid catalysts such as HZSM‑5 or zeolite β at 300–400 °C under hydrogen or inert gas flow; liquid or gaseous xylene feed, no additional solvent required.

Oxidation / oxidant generation (acidic activation of persulfate); produces potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone) and water from hydrogen peroxide, sulfuric acid and potassium persulfate; carried out in cold aqueous sulfuric acid (≈ 1 M H2SO4) to keep the reaction medium acidic; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base double displacement with precipitation; HF protonates barium tungstate to give tungstic acid while Ba²⁺ precipitates as BaF₂; key transformation is BaWO₄ + 2 HF → H₂WO₄ + BaF₂(s); performed in aqueous hydrofluoric acid or neat HF, often at room temperature or with mild heating; BaF₂ precipitates, H₂WO₄ remains in solution; no catalyst required.

Acyl‑substitution esterification of an acyl chloride with an alcohol; forms methyl trichloroacetate and releases HCl; key transformation is CH₃OH + CCl₃COCl → CH₃OCOCCl₃ + HCl; typically run in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; no additional catalyst needed.

Metathesis (halide‑oxide exchange); route to Ta2O5 from TaF5 and CaO. Key transformation: fluoride ions are displaced by oxide ions, producing tantalum(V) oxide and calcium fluoride. Performed by intimate mixing of the reagents and heating to 800–950 °C in an inert atmosphere; no additional solvent or catalyst.

SNAr N‑arylation (C–N bond formation); piperazine nitrogen attacks the electron‑deficient 2‑chloropyrimidine with K2CO3 as base and tetrabutylammonium bromide as phase‑transfer catalyst, displacing chloride to give 1‑(2‑pyrimidinyl)piperazine; typical solvent DMF or DMSO, reflux temperature, inorganic base removes HCl.

Acyl substitution (acetylation) of hydrazine; acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to hydrazine forming acetylhydrazine while one acetyl moiety is hydrolyzed to acetic acid; usually performed in anhydrous pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a borate ester; aqueous NaOH cleaves triethyl borate to ethanol and sodium metaborate (NaBO2); reaction proceeds in water with gentle heating (reflux) and does not require a catalyst.

Oxidation of aldehyde to acid with KMnO₄. Potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes the aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: KMnO₄ (1.5–2 equiv) in water/acetone, pH ≈ 10 (NaOH), 0–25 °C, stir 1–3 h, then acidify with HCl to isolate 2‑cyclopentylacetic acid.

Hydrogen‑gas reduction of tin(IV) selenide; H2 reduces SnSe₂ (tin(IV) selenide) to SnSe (tin(II) selenide) while forming volatile hydrogen selenide (H₂Se); carried out at elevated temperatures (300–500 °C) under a flow of H₂ pressure, typically in a sealed tube or furnace, no additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: Amide hydrolysis (neutral or acid‑catalyzed). Purpose: Deprotect the N‑acetyl group to regenerate the free amino acid. Key transformation: Water attacks the carbonyl carbon of N‑acetylglycine, cleaving the amide bond to give glycine and acetic acid. Typical conditions: Aqueous medium heated under reflux; acid catalyst (e.g., dilute HCl) or simply prolonged heating can be used.

Metal‑acid (single‑replacement) synthesis of magnesium selenide; magnesium metal reduces hydrogen selenide. Mg metal reacts with H2Se gas, forming MgSe solid and liberating H2. Conducted in a sealed quartz tube or reactor at 200–300 °C, often under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Amide hydrolysis (acid- or base-catalyzed): converts 4‑methylpentanamide to 4‑methylpentanoic acid and ammonia; typically performed by refluxing the amide in aqueous HCl or NaOH (often 1 M) for several hours, then acidifying (if basic) to isolate the acid.

Oxidative N‑dealkylation (metabolic conversion); fenproporex undergoes hepatic CYP450‑mediated oxidation that removes the N‑ethyl group, yielding amphetamine (primary amine) and acetaldehyde; occurs in vivo under physiological conditions with NADPH and O₂ as cofactors.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction analogous to #3; KOH deprotonates NH₄⁺ to give NH₃ gas and water, iodide stays as KI; key step: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃↑ + H₂O; carried out in water, often with slight heating; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis (acid‑base reaction) of potassium cyanate; water reacts with KCNO to generate isocyanic acid (HNCO) and potassium hydroxide; performed in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; purpose: form a biaryl C–C bond; key transformation: aryl chloride (p‑chloro‑toluene) couples with phenylboronic acid to give 4‑methylbiphenyl, KCl and B(OH)₃ (boric acid) as by‑products; typical conditions: Pd(0) catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄, 5 mol %), K₂CO₃ (2 eq) as base, solvent mixture of toluene/ethanol/water, 80–110 °C under N₂; common solvents: toluene/EtOH/H₂O; catalyst: Pd(0) complex.

Redox (disproportionation) reaction used for in‑situ generation of chlorine dioxide; chloric acid (HClO3) oxidizes sulfite (SO3²⁻) to sulfate while being reduced to ClO₂; typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C with slow addition of reagents to control gas evolution; no catalyst required, dilute acid medium stabilizes ClO₂.

General type: combination (acidic oxide dimerization) equilibrium; purpose: formation of the transient N2O3 intermediate in nitrogen‑oxide chemistry; key transformation: NO adds to NO2 to give N2O3; typical conditions: low temperature (≤0 °C) to stabilize N2O3, often in an inert solvent such as chloroform or in the gas phase; common solvents/catalysts: none.

Protonolysis (hydrolysis) of an organolithium. Hexyl‑lithium reacts with water to give hexane and lithium hydroxide. The reaction is highly exothermic and is performed at 0 °C or below in an inert solvent such as diethyl ether or THF, with careful quenching of the organolithium by slow addition of cold water.

Selective N‑oxide reduction; sodium borohydride donates hydride to the N‑oxide of 2‑methylpyridine, yielding the parent 2‑methylpyridine and sodium metaborate as by‑product; commonly performed in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol (sometimes mixed with THF) at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction proceeds under neutral to mildly basic conditions, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ketal cleavage) of the enol ether 2‑methoxypropene to give acetone and methanol; performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 0.1–1 M H₂SO₄ or HCl) at ambient temperature; water acts as nucleophile; reaction is complete within minutes to an hour depending on acid strength; no special catalyst beyond the acid.

Base‑mediated disproportionation of dinitrogen trioxide; N₂O₃ reacts with aqueous NaOH to afford nitrite (NaNO₂) and nitrate (NaNO₃) ions together with water; carried out in aqueous solution, typically 0–25 °C; the reaction proceeds rapidly upon dissolution of N₂O₃ gas; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt displacement) between acetic acid and barium chromate; BaCrO₄ reacts with excess acetic acid to form soluble barium acetate and chromic acid (₂CrO₄); usually performed in aqueous medium with gentle heating (40–60 °C) to enhance solubility; the reaction proceeds without catalyst; the resulting chromic acid is often used directly in oxidations.

O‑ethylation (esterification) of benzoic acid using triethyl oxonium tetrafluoroborate as a mild ethylating agent; produces ethyl benzoate and tetrafluoroboric acid; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization and double displacement; employed to recover aluminum as a gelatinous hydroxide precipitate. Aqueous aluminum chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide, chloride is exchanged for hydroxide, yielding Al(OH)₃ solid and NaCl in solution. Conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, pH adjusted to ~7–8, slow addition of NaOH to control precipitation. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation where sodium oxalate exchanges anions with stannous sulfate to give insoluble tin(II) oxalate and soluble sodium sulfate; carried out in water at ambient temperature, often with gentle heating; product isolated by filtration; no catalyst needed.

Redox (halogen displacement); chlorine oxidizes iodide to elemental iodine while being reduced to chloride; produces BaCl2 and I2; carried out by bubbling Cl2 gas through an aqueous solution of BaI2, typically 0–25 °C; aqueous solution, no catalyst.

Fischer esterification of cyclohexanecarboxylic acid with ethanol to ethyl cyclohexanecarboxylate; acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid is employed; reaction refluxed in excess ethanol with water removal (e.g., DeanStark) to drive equilibrium; ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; 4‑fluorophenylacetonitrile is hydrolyzed to 4‑fluorophenylacetic acid while the released ammonia is captured as ammonium chloride. Conducted in concentrated HCl/H₂O, usually heated to reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours. No special catalyst required; aqueous acidic medium suffices.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening by cyanide; NaCN attacks the less hindered carbon of ethylene oxide yielding 2‑cyanoethanol. Typically performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol/H₂O) at 0 – 50 °C; phase‑transfer catalysts such as TBAB may be used to improve solubility.

Coordination complex formation of chromium(VI) oxide with pyridine yielding trioxobis(pyridine)chromium (CrO₃·2 pyridine); pyridine acts as both ligand and solvent; mixture heated under reflux; product isolated by evaporation of excess pyridine; used as a mild oxidant; no external catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation reduction of methylphosphonous dichloride to methylphosphine; hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of 5–10 % Pd/C catalyst, typically in ethanol or THF solvent; performed at room temperature to reflux; yields CH₃PH₂ with HCl as by‑product (often trapped by a base); purpose is synthesis of a primary phosphine.

O‑methylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of hexafluoro‑2‑propanol; dimethyl sulfate transfers a methyl group to the alcohol, forming hexafluoroisopropyl methyl ether while generating methyl hydrogen sulfate. Reaction requires a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or NaH) to neutralise the acid by‑product and is usually run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0–25 °C. No metal catalyst; dimethyl sulfate acts as the methylating agent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) of a carboxylic anhydride with a primary amine. Propionic anhydride reacts with ethylamine to afford N‑ethylpropanamide and a molecule of propionic acid. Key transformation: (CH₃CH₂CO)₂O + H₂NCH₂CH₃ → CH₃CH₂CONHCH₂CH₃ + CH₃CH₂COOH. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, THF, or neat, at 0 °C to room temperature; sometimes a mild base (e.g., pyridine) is added to neutralize the generated acid, but no catalyst is essential.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation between formaldehyde and methanol to give dimethoxymethane; catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid in excess methanol as solvent; reflux conditions with removal of water (e.g., molecular sieves); water is the only by‑product; used to prepare the formaldehyde acetal.

Hydrolytic deamination of cytosine to uracil. Water attacks the C4‑amino group of cytosine, releasing ammonia and forming the pyrimidine uracil. The transformation occurs under mildly acidic or basic aqueous conditions, typically at 70‑100 °C, and can be accelerated by acid (pH 2‑3) or base (pH 9‑10). It is a common metabolic or laboratory conversion of nucleobases.

Redox (hydrogen reduction) – elemental arsenic is obtained by reacting arsenic trichloride with hydrogen gas; HCl is generated as a by‑product. Typically performed in the gas phase at elevated temperatures (300‑500 °C) in a sealed tube or furnace; no solvent required and no catalyst is needed.

Copper‑catalyzed C–N coupling (Ullmann‑type or Buchwald‑Hartwig amination) to form N‑(2‑pyridyl)piperazine; a nucleophilic arylation where piperazine nitrogen replaces bromide on 2‑bromopyridine; typical conditions: CuI (5–10 mol %), ligand such as L‑proline or N‑N bidentate ligand, K2CO3 base, DMF or DMSO solvent, heat (80–120 °C) under nitrogen; no external oxidant.

Selective alkaline hydrolysis of dimethyl fumarate (partial ester saponification); purpose is to obtain the mono‑ester; key step is nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on one methyl ester, forming a carboxylate and releasing methanol; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux (50–80 °C) in a water/THF or MeOH mixture, followed by careful acidification to pH 2 to isolate monomethyl fumarate; no special catalyst beyond base.

Diazo‑cyclization – o‑phenylenediamine is nitrosated by NaNO₂ in hydrochloric acid to form a diazonium intermediate that cyclizes to 1H‑benzotriazole, releasing water and NaCl. Carried out in aqueous acidic solution, NaNO₂ added at 0‑5 °C and the mixture then warmed gently to complete cyclization. No catalyst; temperature control is essential.

Basic hydrolysis – tungsten hexafluoride is hydrolyzed by aqueous sodium hydroxide, producing sodium tungstate (Na₂WO₄), sodium fluoride and water. Reaction is carried out in excess aqueous NaOH at room temperature to reflux; vigorous stirring is used to disperse the gaseous WF₆. No additional catalyst is required.

nucleophilic substitution (SN2); hydrolytic substitution of chloride in 3-chloropropan-1-ol with hydroxide; conducted in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution; reaction conditions may involve heating; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) – methyl vinyl ether undergoes addition of HCl across its C=C bond to afford 2‑chloroethyl methyl ether. Usually performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature; may be accelerated by a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) but often proceeds without catalyst.

Acid‑chloride hydrolysis – 3,5‑dinitrobenzoyl chloride reacts with water to give 3,5‑dinitrobenzoic acid and HCl. The reaction is typically run in aqueous medium (or a water/organic mixture) at mild heating; a base can be added to neutralize the liberated HCl. No catalyst is required.

Radical reduction (organotin‑hydride dehalogenation); tributyltin hydride abstracts halogen atoms from 1,2‑diiodopropane, generating a carbon‑center radical that eliminates HI to give propene; usually initiated by AIBN or heat in anhydrous benzene/toluene under inert atmosphere; by‑product tributyltin iodide formed; no catalyst beyond the tin hydride.

Direct halogenation; synthesis of boron trichloride; B(s) + 3 Cl2(g) → BCl3(g); conducted by passing chlorine gas over heated boron (≈500‑600 °C); typically performed in a dry glass or steel reactor; no solvent, inert gas may be used to carry Cl2.

Hydroboration‑oxidation of a terminal alkyne (cyclopropylacetylene); purpose is to produce the anti‑Markovnikov aldehyde (cyclopropylacetaldehyde). Key transformation: addition of cateborane (HBcat) across the C≡C bond to give a vinylborane intermediate, then oxidative work‑up with H₂O₂/NaOH converts the C–B bond to a C–O bond, yielding the aldehyde. Typical conditions: run the hydroboration in dry THF at 0 °C to rt, then add a cold aqueous solution of NaOH and 30 % H₂O₂ while maintaining  °C → rt. No metal catalyst; catecholborane acts as the hydroborating reagent.

Oxidation of a secondary allylic alcohol to a ketone using Dess‑Martin periodinane. But‑3‑en‑2‑ol is converted to but‑3‑en‑2‑one in a mild, selective oxidation. The substrate is dissolved in dry dichloromethane, cooled to 0 °C, and Dess‑Martin periodinane (1.1–1.5 equiv) is added under nitrogen; the mixture is allowed to warm to room temperature and stirred for 0.5–2 h. The reaction is quenched with aqueous sodium bicarbonate, extracted, and the product is purified by chromatography or distillation.

Fischer esterification between formic acid and phenoxyethanol; purpose is to form phenoxyethyl formate (a formate ester). Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the protonated carbonyl of formic acid, loss of water, and regeneration of the acid catalyst. Typical conditions: reflux the reactants in a non‑reactive solvent such as toluene or benzene with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and removal of water by a Dean–Stark apparatus. The reaction proceeds under azeotropic distillation; no special catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Acid–base metathesis/precipitation reaction; purpose is to convert soluble beryllium acetate into insoluble beryllium hydroxide while generating sodium acetate in solution. Key transformation: proton transfer from acetate to hydroxide and exchange of cations, yielding Be(OH)₂ (a sparingly soluble precipitate) and NaOAc. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; the reaction is performed in water, often with slight heating to ensure dissolution of the starting salts. No additional catalysts are needed.

Enzymatic acetyl‑transfer (acyl‑CoA dependent). Purpose: acetylate the α‑amino group of L‑aspartic acid to afford N‑acetyl‑L‑aspartic acid, a common step in metabolic pathways. Key transformation: transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl‑CoA to the amine, generating CoA‑SH. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer at pH 7–8, 25–37 °C, presence of the appropriate N‑acetyltransferase enzyme; no organic solvent required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between sodium chloride and potassium hexachloroplatinate(IV); purpose is to exchange the counter‑ions, obtaining sodium hexachloroplatinate(IV) and potassium chloride. Key transformation: ion exchange in solution, maintaining the same anionic complex [PtCl₆]²⁻ but swapping Na⁺ for K⁺. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water, stir at room temperature until equilibrium is reached; the reaction may be driven to completion by crystallization or evaporation. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; purpose is to cleave the ester bond of 3‑pentyl acetate to give the corresponding carboxylic acid (acetic acid) and alcohol (3‑pentanol). Key transformation: protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by water, formation of tetrahedral intermediate, then breakdown to acids and alcohols. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (≈1 M), reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours; solvent is water or a water‑organic mixture (e.g., water/ethanol). No additional catalyst required.

Catalytic oxidation of a cycloalkane to a cyclo‑ketone using hydrogen peroxide; purpose is to install a carbonyl on cycloheptane to afford cycloheptanone. Key transformation: activation of H₂O₂ by a metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺, MnO₂, or tungsten(VI) oxide) to generate a peroxy species that abstracts a hydrogen atom from the cycloalkane and inserts an oxygen atom. Overall stoichiometry: C₇H₁₂ + 2 H₂O₂ → C₇H₁₂O + 3 H₂O. Typical conditions: 30 % H₂O₂ (1–2 equiv), catalytic amount of metal salt (0.1–5 mol %), solvent such as acetonitrile or a water‑acetone mixture, temperature 25‑80 °C, reaction time 1‑6 h.

Anion‑exchange metathesis (double displacement) between a silver salt and an imidazolium bromide; purpose is to generate the ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate and precipitate insoluble AgBr. Key transformation: Ag⁺ pairs with Br⁻ to form AgBr(s), while PF₆⁻ pairs with the imidazolium cation. Typical conditions: equimolar solutions of AgPF₆ and [Bmim]Br in dry acetonitrile or dichloromethane, stirred under inert atmosphere (N₂) at ambient temperature, protected from light; AgBr is filtered off and the filtrate dried to give the PF₆⁻ ionic liquid.

Hal exchange (fluorination) of germanium tetrachloride; purpose is to replace chloride ligands with fluoride to produce volatile GeF₄ and release Cl₂. Key transformation: reaction of F₂ with GeCl₄, where each F₂ molecule swaps two Cl atoms, forming GeF₄ and Cl₂ gas. Typical conditions: gaseous reagents mixed in a stainless‑steel or quartz reactor, temperature 0‑200 °C (often 100 °C), low to moderate pressure of F₂ (often 1‑5 atm), no solvent; reaction is usually carried out with rigorous exclusion of moisture and under remote handling due to corrosive fluorine.

Nucleophilic O‑methylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of 2,4,6‑tribromophenol using dimethyl sulfate under basic conditions; purpose is to convert the phenolic OH into a methoxy group, yielding 2,4,6‑tribromoole. Key transformation: deprotonation of the phenol by NaOH to generate the phenoxide ion, which then attacks the electrophilic methyl carbon of dimethyl sulfate in an SN2 step, displacing a methyl sulfate anion. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1 M) with a polar aprotic co‑solvent such as acetone or DMF, addition of dimethyl sulfate (1‑1.5 equiv) at 0‑50 °C, reaction time 1‑3 h; work‑up includes extraction into an organic solvent and neutralization of excess base.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; chloride ions of chromium(III) chloride are exchanged for acetate ions to give chromium(III) acetate and sodium chloride; usually carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to isolate iron(II) hydroxide as a solid. FeCl2 aqueous solution is treated with aqueous NaOH, producing insoluble Fe(OH)2 precipitate and soluble NaCl. Reaction is carried out at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Ester hydrolysis; water (often under acid or base catalysis) cleaves the methyl ester of methyl isonicotinate to afford pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid (isonicotinic acid) and methanol. Acidic conditions use dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ in refluxing water/ethanol; basic conditions employ NaOH or KOH in aqueous methanol at 60–100 °C, followed by acidification to isolate the free acid.

Acid dissolution (protonolysis) of cerium(III) sulfide with hydrochloric acid; converts the sulfide into soluble cerium(III) chloride while liberating hydrogen sulfide gas; Ce2S3 is treated with aqueous HCl, often refluxed, yielding CeCl3 in solution and H2S evolved; carried out in water or dilute HCl at 80–100 °C; no additional catalyst needed.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Purpose: deoxygenate triphenylarsine oxide to regenerate triphenylarsine. Key transformation: Ar3As=O + H2 → Ar3As + H2O. Typical conditions: hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney nickel or PtO2, in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C.

General type: oxidative oxidation using chromium(VI). Purpose: convert naphthalene to the quinone 1,4‑naphthoquinone. Key transformation: C10H8 + Na2Cr2O7 + AcOH → C10H6O2 (para‑naphthoquinone) + reduced chromium species + Na+ + water. Typical conditions: reflux of naphthalene in glacial acetic acid with sodium dichromate (often with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid) at 80–120 °C; reaction monitored until complete oxidation.

General type: peracid oxidative conversion of phenol to quinone. Purpose: oxidize thymol to thymoquinone (p‑methyl‑isopropyl‑1,4‑benzoquinone). Key transformation: phenolic C–OH group and aromatic ring undergo two‑electron oxidation forming the quinone carbonyls, with peracetic acid reduced to acetic acid. Typical conditions: excess peracetic acid (often generated in situ from acetic acid/H2O2) in acetic acid solvent 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation, reaction time 1–4 h; work‑up removes excess acid.

General type: aerobic oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid. Purpose: convert phenylpropanal to phenylpropionic acid. Key transformation: R‑CH2‑CHO + ½ O2 → R‑CH2‑COOH (water as by‑product). Typical conditions: oxygen balloon or pressurized O2 (1–5 atm) with a catalytic system such as TEMPO/CuCl/NaBr, or a metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., MnO2, Co‑acetate) in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, acetonitrile) at 40–80 °C.

General type: acid‑catalyzed cyclodehydrative condensation (Acridine synthesis). Purpose: assemble the tricyclic heteroaromatic acridine from 2‑aminobiphenyl and formaldehyde. Key transformation: condensation of the amine with formaldehyde followed by intramolecular electrophilic aromatic substitution and loss of water to give acridine. Typical conditions: reflux in concentrated HCl (6–12 M) with aqueous formaldehyde solution, temperature 80–120 °C for several hours; the reaction proceeds via a sequence of imine formation, cyclization, and dehydrogenation.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis of sec‑butyl formate; water attacks the carbonyl under acidic conditions (e.g., 5 % H2SO4) at reflux to give formic acid and sec‑butanol; common solvent: THF or MeOH/H2O mixture; reaction driven to completion by excess water.

Acid‑base neutralization / salt metathesis: aqueous 2‑aminoethanol hydrobromide is treated with excess ammonium hydroxide, liberating free 2‑aminoethanol, forming ammonium bromide and water; proceeds at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); decanoic acid reacts with aqueous potassium hydroxide to afford potassium decanoate and water. Conducted in water or an aqueous/alcohol mixture at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization (metal hydroxide with carboxylic acid). Zinc hydroxide deprotonates butanoic acid, giving zinc butyrate and water. The reaction is commonly performed in a dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol THF) at reflux, using a slight excess of acid to drive completion no catalyst is needed and the produced water is removed by evaporation or by using a Dean‑Stark apparatus.

Nitration (esterification) of glycerol to form nitroglycerin; purpose is synthesis of the energetic nitrate ester used as an explosive and vasodilator. Key transformation is conversion of the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol into nitrate esters (‑ONO2) while water is generated. Typically carried out by slowly adding glycerol to a cooled mixture (0‑5 °C) of concentrated nitric acid (≈70 %) and phosphoric acid, maintaining an ice bath to control the highly exothermic reaction; no separate solvent is required. Reaction is performed under inert atmosphere (nitrogen) to limit decomposition; phosphoric acid acts as a dehydration/acid catalyst.

SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (Williamson-type ester synthesis); purpose is to form an ethyl ester from the sodium salt; nucleophilic attack of the 3‑methylbutanoate anion on ethyl bromide gives ethyl 3‑methylbutanoate and NaBr; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at reflux or gentle heating; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation; the C=C double bond of acenaphthylene is reduced to the saturated acenaphthene using H₂; employed in synthetic upgrading of polycyclic aromatic compounds; performed under H₂ pressure (1‑5 atm) with a palladium on carbon (Pd/C) or Raney Ni catalyst in ethanol or methanol at 25‑60 °C; reaction typically completes within 1‑4 h.

Combustion (complete oxidation) of a sulfur‑containing organic compound; purpose is energy release or waste destruction; ethanethiol reacts with excess oxygen under high‑temperature flame conditions, yielding carbon dioxide, water, and sulfur dioxide as the final oxidation products; performed at flame temperatures with ample O2; no solvent or catalyst.

Acid‑base/neutralization; purpose: hydrolysis of lithium silicate to silicic acid. Dilithium dioxido(oxo)silane (Li2SiO2) reacts with aqueous HCl, protonating the silicate and forming soluble lithium chloride and silicic acid (H2SiO3) in solution. Typically done at 0–25 °C in dilute HCl to control exotherm; the mixture is stirred until dissolution is complete.

Fischer esterification of a hydroxyacid; 4‑hydroxybutanoic acid reacts with ethanol to form ethyl 4‑hydroxybutanoate and water; the carboxyl group is esterified while the pendant hydroxyl remains unchanged; performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; excess ethanol acts as solvent; removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark) drives conversion.

Acylation of a thiol to give a thioester (butyl thioacetate) using acetic anhyd; a mild esterification. The acetyl group is transferred from the anhydride to the sulfur atom of butyl mercaptan, producing butyl thioacetate and one equivalent of acetic acid. Commonly performed at room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (.g., pyridine or triethylamine) toize the generated acetic acid and accelerate the reaction. Reaction time is usually 1‑2 h, and work‑up involves aqueous wash to remove residual acid.

Metathesis/precipitation synthesis of nickel(II) selenide from hydrogen selenide and nickel(II chloride. Hydrogen selenide gas reacts with aqueous NiCl2, displacing chloride to form insoluble NiSe (nickel(II) selenide) while releasing HCl gas. Performed in a sealed, vented apparatus under an inert atmosphere (N2) at low temperature (0‑25 °C) to limit H2Se volatilization. The reaction medium is water; the solid NiSe is collected by filtration, washed, and dried under vacuum. No additional catalyst is required.

Carboxylation of sodium acetylide with carbon dioxide to give sodium propiolate (sodium propargyl carboxylate). The acetylide ion acts as a nucleophile, attacking electrophilic CO2 and forming the carbon–carbon bond, yielding the sodium salt of the α‑alkynoate. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as THF or dry diethyl ether under an inert atmosphere; CO2 is bubbled through the solution at 0‑25 °C. The reaction typically completes within 30‑60 min. The product can be isolated by solvent removal and precipitation with a non‑solvent (e.g., cold ethanol).

Double‑replacement precipitation of rhodium(III) sulfide from sodium sulfide and rhodium(III) chloride. Sulfide ions replace chloride, forming insoluble Rh2S3 (rhodium(III) sulfide) and soluble NaCl. Performed in aqueous solution with stoichiometric amounts (3 Na2S + 2 RhCl3), heated gently (50‑80 °C) to improve dissolution and mixing, then allowed to cool to promote crystallization of the metal sulfide. The solid is filtered, washed with water to remove NaCl, and dried under vacuum. No special catalyst is needed.

N‑alkylation (quaternization) of 1‑methylimidazole with 1‑bromobutane in the presence of hexafluorophosphoric acid; the bromide is displaced by the imidazole nitrogen to form 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium PF6⁻, releasing HBr; typical conditions: dry MeCN, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; PF6⁻ source provides non‑coordinating counter‑ion.

Thermal disproportionation/decomposition of sulfur dibromide, in which SBr2 converts to disulfur dibromide (S2Br2) and elemental bromine; typically induced by heating the neat liquid or gas-phase mixture, often under inert atmosphere; no additional reagents or catalysts needed.

Gas‑phase fluorination/redox reaction; fluorine reacts with ozone to give oxygen difluoride and molecular oxygen; F2 oxidizes ozone, reducing O3 to O2 while being incorporated as OF2; conducted at low temperature (typically –78 °C) in a quartz tube with dilute F2/O3 gases, often in an inert carrier (e.g., nitrogen); no solvent or catalyst.

Acid-catalyzed formylation reaction. Triethyl orthoformate serves as a formylating agent for aniline under sulfuric acid conditions, producing formanilide. Ethanol is released as a byproduct. The reaction typically requires heating in an acidic aqueous environment.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification or acidysis). Octan-3-yl acetate undergoes hydrolysis with water to yield acetic acid and 3-octanol. Conditions include aqueous environments with acid or base catalysis, though no reagents like NaOH or H2SO4 are listed; likely proceeds under neutral conditions with heat.

Hydrolytic demethylation of O6‑methylguanine. Purpose: remove the methyl group to regenerate native guanine, a model for repair processes. Key transformation: cleavage of the O‑CH₃ bond, yielding guanine and methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 50–80 °C for several hours; can also proceed under acidic (pH 2–3) or basic (pH 10) conditions, though neutral/physiological pH is common for biochemical relevance. No catalyst needed.

Double displacement/precipitation. Mixing aqueous sodium carbonate with calcium chloride precipitates calcium carbonate while forming soluble sodium chloride. Often used to prepare CaCO₃ as a solid product. Reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification of 3‑methylsalicylic acid with methanol; converts the carboxylic acid to methyl 3‑methylsalicylate while releasing water; carried out under reflux with excess MeOH and a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH); often uses a Dean–Stark trap to remove water.

Halogen exchange reaction via aromatic lithiation. n-Butyllithium facilitates deprotonation (or bromide elimination) of 1,4-dibromobenzene, followed by reaction with iodine to yield 1-bromo-4-iodobenzene. Conducted under anhydrous, inert atmosphere conditions (e.g., THF solvent) at low temperature to control regioselectivity.

Chlorination of acid anhydride. Methacrylic anhydride reacts with phosphorus pentachloride (PCl5) to form methacryloyl chloride and phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3). PCl5 acts as a chlorinating agent. Heat and inert solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) are typical reaction conditions.

Reaction type: Esterification. Purpose: To form a silyl ester from a carboxylic acid. Key transformation displaces chloride in triethylchlorosilane with the acetyl oxyanion. Conditions involve a dry environment, often at elevated temperatures. Solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) are common. A base (e.g., pyridine) may neutralize released hydrogen chloride.

Salt metathesis/halide exchange between potassium iodide and chromium(II) chloride; in aqueous or dry MeCN solution, I⁻ replaces Cl⁻ to give CrI2 and KCl; performed under inert atmosphere (N2) to prevent oxidation of Cr(II), typically at rt.

Reduction of a palladium(II) halide by hydrogen; hydrogen gas reduces PdI2 to elemental palladium metal while being oxidized to hydrogen iodide. Typically performed at elevated temperature (150–250 °C) under an inert atmosphere, often in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent required, gaseous reagents only.

Base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination) of tert‑butyl chloride with aqueous or alcoholic NaOH to afford the tertiary alkene isobutylene (2‑methyl‑1‑propene), water and sodium chloride. Reaction is carried out by heating the mixture (reflux) in water or ethanol; strong base and heat drive the elimination.

Type: Base‑catalyzed saponification (hydrolysis) of a methyl ester. Purpose: Convert the ester into its carboxylate salt while liberating methanol. Key transformation: NaOH attacks the carbonyl of methyl cyclopropanecarboxylate, yielding sodium cyclopropanecarboxylate and methanol after proton transfer. Typical conditions: Aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv), reflux 1–3 h; solvent may be water or water/ethanol mixture; after completion, the reaction mixture is cooled and the acidified to isolate the free acid if desired.

Transesterification/cyclization of propylene glycol with diphenyl carbonate to generate propylene carbonate, a five‑membered cyclic carbonate, and phenol as a by‑product. Conducted at 100–150 °C, often under reduced pressure to remove phenol, using a basic or metal‑alkoxide catalyst such as NaOMe, K₂CO₃, or Ti(OiPr)₄; solvent may be absent (neat) or highboiling solvent like toluene.

Diazomethane methylation (esterification) of eicosanoic (arachidic) acid to give methyl eicosanoate; the reaction releases nitrogen gas as the only by‑product. Performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as diethyl ether or THF, under nitrogen or argon, and the diazomethane solution is added dropwise to the acid suspension.

Reductive conversion of a nitro‑imidazole to the corresponding amino‑imidazole using sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) as the electron donor. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, typically at neutral to mildly alkaline pH, at room temperature, with stirring; sodium sulfite (Na₂SO₃) is formed as a stoichiometric by‑product.

Dehalogenation (reductive elimination) of a gem‑dihalide; zinc dust reduces 1,1‑dichlorobutane to 1‑butene while forming ZnCl₂. Typical conditions: excess zinc dust in dry ether or THF, reflux under nitrogen, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑mediated conversion of hydroxylamine sulfate to hydroxylamine‑O‑sulfonic acid; fuming H₂SO₄ protonates and sulfonates the hydroxylamine. Performed cold (0‑5 °C) with excess fuming sulfuric acid acting as solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Nitrosation of diphenylamine with nitrosyl bromide yielding N‑nitrosodiphenylamine and HBr. Conducted at low temperature (0 °C to –10 °C) in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, protected from light.

Acid‑base neutralization reaction; transforms iron(II) hydroxide into iron(II) sulfate solution and water; Fe(OH)₂ reacts with H₂SO₄, yielding FeSO₄ and H₂O; performed in aqueous medium, often at room temperature; dilute sulfuric acid is added dropwise to a stirred suspension to avoid localized overheating; no catalyst needed.

Alpha‑chlorination of dichloroacetyl chloride with chlorine gas to give trichloroacetyl chloride and HCl. Usually carried out by bubbling Cl₂ through a solution of the acid chloride in carbon tetrachloride (or chloroform) under UV light or heating (≈50 °C).

Oxidative chlorination of carbon disulfide; excess Cl₂ converts CS₂ to carbon tetrachloride and sulfur dichloride (2 SCl₂). Reaction is performed in the gas phase or in an inert, dry reactor at 200‑300 °C, with dry chlorine and no solvent; sometimes a metal chloride catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃) is used.

Protonolysis (halide exchange) of trimethylgallium with hydrogen iodide, producing gallium triiodide and methane. Conducted by bubbling HI gas through a solution of trimethylgallium in dry benzene or THF at room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Reduction; conversion a nitro group to a nitroso group. Nitrobenzene is reduced by tin(II) chloride in strongly acidic aqueous medium (excess HCl) to give nitrosobenzene, with oxidation of SnCl₂ to SnCl₄ and formation of water. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl, stoichiometric SnCl₂, inert atmosphere optional.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride to an alkene (Markovnikov addition). HCl adds across the C=C bond of 1‑methylcyclopropene, protonating the less substituted carbon and giving the more stable carbocation that captures chloride to form 1‑chloro‑1‑methylcyclopropane. Conducted in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification; formation of an ester from a carboxylic acid and a primary alcohol. Benzoic acid reacts with 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol under acid catalysis (commonly concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑tosic acid to afford 4‑bromobenzyl benzoate and water. Conditions usually involve reflux in a non‑reactive solvent such as toluene or benzene with removal of water (Dean–Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium.

Transesterification; purpose: exchange the ethoxy group for a methoxy group to obtain methyl 2‑hydroxyacetate; key transformation: the alkoxy moiety of the ester is swapped, producing methyl ester and ethanol as by‑product; typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with an acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base catalyst (e.g., NaOMe); removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium; solvent is usually the excess alcohol.

Acid dissolution of a metal oxide (metal oxide + strong acid); employed to synthesize gadolinium(III) bromide from Gd2O3; Gd2O3 reacts with hydrobromic acid to give GdBr3 and water; typical conditions are aqueous 48 % HBr, reflux or gentle heating until the solid dissolves, in water; no catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base displacement (salt metathesis) to generate nitrosyl chloride gas; purpose is preparation of NOCl for nitration or chlorination reactions; key transformation is conversion of nitrosylsulfuric acid (HNO·HSO4) and HCl into gaseous NOCl and H2SO4; typically performed in a dry, closed apparatus at 0‑25 °C, often without solvent, with excess concentrated HCl to drive off NOCl.

Acid dissolution/neutralization; metal oxide reacts with concentrated nitric acid to give the corresponding metal nitrate. Gallium(III) oxide is treated with excess conc. HNO₃, often at 80‑120 °C, producing gallium nitrate and water as by‑product. Reaction performed in aqueous medium; no catalyst required.

Addition of phenyl lithium to N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide to afford acetophenone; purpose is to generate a substituted carbonyl compound from a Weinreb amide; PhLi adds to the carbonyl, the intermediate collapses to release the amine and give acetophenone; reaction conditions parallel the methyl lithium case: dry THF, –78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere, work‑up with aqueous NH₄Cl.

Oxidation; conversion of the secondary alcohol of benzoin to a diketone (benzil). Nitric acid acts as the oxidant, typically under reflux in a mixture of nitric acid and a co‑solvent such as acetic acid or water. The reaction proceeds with loss of water and formation of benzil; temperature (often 0‑30 °C initially, then reflux) minimizes over‑oxidation.

Electrophilic halogenation of a quinone; chlorine adds to the aromatic positions of 1,4‑benzoquinone in the presence of iron(III) chloride as Lewis‑acid catalyst, yielding tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone and HCl. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride solvent, low temperature (0‑5 °C) to control chlorination, catalytic FeCl₃ (5‑10 mol %), gradual addition of Cl₂ gas.

Redox hydrolysis; chromyl chloride (CrO2Cl2) is reduced by hydrogen peroxide, which oxidizes chloride to Cl2 while being reduced to water; the chromium remains in the +6 state as CrO3 (chromium(VI) oxide); typically carried out in aqueous or acetic‑acid solution at 0–25 °C, using dilute H2O2; no additional catalyst required.

Reductive amination (hydrogenation) to produce methamphetamine hydrochloride. 1‑Phenyl‑2‑propanone is condensed with methylamine in the presence of hydrogen gas and palladium on carbon catalyst under acidic conditions (HCl present) to give the secondary amine, which is isolated as its hydrochloride salt. Common conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C (5–10 wt %), solvent methanol or ethanol, temperature ambient to 40 °C, followed by crystallization of the dl‑methamphetamine·HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed double condensation forming a heterocyclic N‑donor ligand; o‑phenylenediamine condenses with phenanthrene‑9,10‑dione in acetic acid, two molecules of water to give 1,10‑phenanthroline. Typical conditions: reflux in glacial acetic acid (≈120 °C) for several hours; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of allylic bromide; NaOH attacks the primary allylic carbon of 4‑bromo‑2‑methyl‑1‑butene to give 4‑hydroxy‑2‑methyl‑1‑butene; carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) possibly with a co‑solvent like ethanol, heated under reflux for several hours; the reaction proceeds with inversion at the carbon bearing bromine.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (etherification) of primary alcohols; two equivalents of benzyl alcohol undergo intermolecular condensation to form dibenzyl ether with loss of one molecule of water. Common practice: reflux in toluene or xylenes with a catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH; water removed by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark trap).

Alkaline hydrolysis of aluminum nitride with potassium hydroxide; yields potassium aluminate and ammonia. Used similarly to the NaOH case. Performed in aqueous KOH, heated (≈80‑100 °C); water as solvent, no catalyst.

Redox oxidation of a divalent manganese oxide; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes MnO (manganous oxide) to MnO₂ (manganese dioxide), producing water as the only by‑product. Usually performed in aqueous medium at 20–25 °C, sometimes under mild acidic conditions (e.g., HCl) to keep manganese soluble.

Catalytic hydrogenation of D‑mannose to D‑mannitol; reduction of the aldose carbonyl to a primary alcohol using H2 gas over a palladium on carbon (Pd/C) catalyst. Reaction carried out in a protic solvent such as EtOH or water under 1–5 atm H2 at ambient temperature to 50 °C. The Pd/C catalyst is filtered off after completion and the product is purified by crystallization.

Formation of a Weinreb amide; acetyl chloride reacts with N,O‑dimethylhydroxylamine·HCl in the presence of two equivalents of triethylamine, yielding N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide and two equivalents of triethylammonium chloride. Standard procedure: add acetyl chloride dropwise to a solution of the hydroxylamine salt and TEA in CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C, then stir at room temperature; the base neutralizes HCl generated.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of oxygen difluoride; water attacks the O–F bonds, producing hydrofluoric acid and molecular oxygen; proceeds rapidly in aqueous solution, often at low temperature to control exotherm, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamation); ethanol attacks dimethylcarbamoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming ethyl N,N‑dimethylcarbamate with concomitant generation of HCl; typical procedure uses pyridine or triethylamine as HCl scavenger, temperature (0 °C) to room temperature, solvent dichloromethane or THF.

Intramolecular Williamson ether cyclization to give an oxetane; potassium tert‑butoxide deprotonates 3‑chloro‑1‑propanol, the resulting alkoxide attacks the pendant chloride intramolecularly, affording oxetane, with KCl and tert‑butanol as side products. Typical conditions: dissolve reagents in dry THF or DMF, add KOtBu at 0 °C to rt under N₂; reaction proceeds rapidly, and the mixture is worked up with aqueous NH₄Cl.

Reaction type: Catalytic hydrogenation (addition of H₂ across a C=C bond). Purpose: fully saturate 1‑hexadecene to yield the corresponding alkane, hexadecane. Key transformation: syn addition of two hydrogen atoms to the double bond, converting it to a single bond. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, at 25–80 °C. Common solvent: a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) or an inert solvent (acetone, ethyl acetate).

Ligand exchange/acid dissolution of cupric glycinate with nitric acid producing copper(II) nitrate, free glycine and water; type is metathesis/acid–base reaction; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating or reflux; no special catalyst, water is the solvent.

Hydrolysis reaction; converts cyanogen fluoride (F‑CN) to hydrogen cyanide and hydrofluoric acid by nucleophilic attack of water on the carbon‑fluorine bond; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; no special catalyst required.

Oxidative desulfurization; purpose is to regenerate uracil from thiouracil by oxidizing the thio‑carbonyl back to a carbonyl; key transformation is C=S → C=O with formation of water; commonly performed by treating thiouracil with aqueous hydrogen peroxide at 0–25 °C (or mild reflux), optionally in a mixed solvent (water/acetone) and sometimes buffered to maintain pH.

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation with potassium permanganate: the benzylic methyl group of 4‑bromotoluene is oxidized to a carboxyl group to give 4‑bromobenzoic acid; reaction is carried out in aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or K₂CO₃) with excess KMnO₄, heated under reflux, and the mixture is acid‑worked‑up to isolate the acid.

Metathesis (acid‑base exchange) producing a lanthanide halide; three equivalents of hydroiodic acid replace acetate ligands of praseodymium(III) acetate, forming praseodymium triiodide and three equivalents of acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with excess HI and gentle heating (≈50 °C) to drive the equilibrium to completion; the product precipitates upon cooling.

Oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes acridine to acridone by converting a C–H bond at the 9‑position into a carbonyl (C=O); purpose is to introduce a ketone functionality on the heterocycle; typical conditions: aqueous 30 % H₂O₂, 0–25 °C, often with a mild acid catalyst (e.g., acetic acid) or in methanol; water is formed as by‑product.

Radical halogenation; photolytic chlorine adds a chlorine atom to 1,1,2‑trichloroethane, replacing a hydrogen to give 1,1,1,2‑tetrachloroethane; purpose is further chlorination of the alkane; typical conditions: chlorine gas irradiated with UV light, inert solvent such as carbonrachloride or chloroform, ambient or slightly elevated temperature.

Intramolecular SN2 cyclization (base‑induced dehydrohalogenation); 2‑chloroethylamine is treated with aqueous NaOH, the amine attacks the carbon bearing chlorine to form the three‑membered aziridine ring (ethylenimine) with loss of NaCl and water; purpose is synthesis of ethylenimine; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heat (reflux) or warmed bath, often in ethanol/water mixture.

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction; oxalic acid is oxidized by chlorine gas, producing carbon dioxide and hydrochloric acid; chlorine is reduced to chloride; purpose is decomposition of oxalic acid; typical conditions: dilute aqueous solution of oxalic acid, chlorine gas bubbled through at 0–25 °C, often in a fume hood due to HCl evolution.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2′ allylic cyanation); sodium cyanide attacks the allylic carbon of 1‑bromo‑3‑methylbut‑2‑ene, displacing bromide and forming 3‑methyl‑2‑butenenitrile; purpose is introduction of a nitrile group; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, 0 °C to room temperature, stoichiometric NaCN, inert atmosphere to avoid HCN formation.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed esterification); p‑hydroxybenzoic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid to give methylparaben and water; purpose is formation of a methyl ester protecting group; typical conditions: reflux methanol with 5–10 % p‑TsOH, removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark) to drive equilibrium forward.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction where cadmium chloride and lithium fluoride exchange anions to give cadmium fluoride and lithium chloride; typically carried out in aqueous solution, often with heating to reflux; products are isolated by evaporation or precipitation; no catalyst required.

Esterification using an acyl chloride (Schotten–Baumann type); isobutanol reacts with benzoyl chloride to produce isobutyl benzoate and HCl. Useful for preparing aromatic esters. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or ether with a stoichiometric base (pyridine, triethylamine) to trap HCl; temperature 0 °C to rt. No additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transacetalization (acetal exchange) in which ethanol reacts with acetaldehyde dimethyl acetal, replacing the methyl groups with ethoxy groups to form acetaldehyde diethyl acetal and methanol; usually performed in refluxing ethanol or another polar protic solvent with a catalytic amount of mineral acid such as p‑toluenesulfonic acid or HCl; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium; no special catalyst beyond the acid.

Salt metathesis/ion‑exchange reaction between zinc nitrate and sodium ricinolate producing zinc ricinolate (often precipitated) and sodium nitrate; conducted in aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; the insoluble zinc ricinolate is filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base/complexation reaction where copper(II) carbonate reacts with glycine; the carbonate is neutralized, releasing CO₂ and H₂O, while the copper(II) ion coordinates two glycinate ligands to give copper(II) glycinate complex; performed in water with gentle heating and pH control; no external catalyst required.

Acidic decomposition of sodium hexafluorosilicate by concentrated sulfuric acid, yielding hydrofluoric acid, sodium sulfate, and volatile silicon tetrafluoride gas; carried out under anhydrous conditions, often at low to moderate temperature in a corrosion‑resistant apparatus; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Carboxylation of a secondary amine; CO2 inserts into the N–H bond of piperidine to give piperidine‑1‑carboxylic acid (an N‑carboxylated amine); usually performed under elevated CO2 pressure (5–30 atm) in a polar aprotic solvent such as dimethyl sulfoxide or methanol, often with a base (e.g., NaH, DBU) or a catalytic amount of a metal‑complex to promote activation of CO2; temperature ranges from room temperature to 80 °C.

Oxidation (redox) of hydrogen selenide by molecular oxygen to form water and selenous acid; typically performed in aqueous solution with mild heating; a metal catalyst such as platinum or palladium can be used to accelerate the reaction, though it may also proceed uncatalyzed under controlled conditions.

Alcoholysis of phenylacetic anhydride with methanol; nucleophilic acyl substitution gives methyl phenylacetate and phenylacetic acid. Typically performed neat or in a low‑boiling aprotic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) at ambient or reflux temperature; no catalyst required.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration of 3‑amino‑2‑methyl‑2‑butanol using acetyl chloride to afford 2‑methyl‑2‑oxazoline; acetyl chloride acylates the amine, the hydroxyl attacks the acyl carbon, and HCl is eliminated. Usually carried out in an aprotic solvent (CH2Cl2) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine at 0 °C to reflux; the base scavenges the generated HCl.

Oxidation of 2‑fluorobenzyl alcohol to 2‑fluorobenzoic acid with sodium dichromate in acidic aqueous medium (Jones oxidation). Reaction is performed under reflux in a mixture of acetone and water containing dilute H2SO4; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) and water is formed as a by‑product.

Hot, aqueous potassium permanganate oxidative cleavage of 1,6‑heptadiene; the diene is fully oxidized to glutaric acid (HOOC‑(CH2)3‑COOH) and carbon dioxide, with water produced. Conducted by heating the diene in excess KMnO4 solution, followed by removal of MnO2 precipitate.

Halide exchange (metathesis/precipitation); antimony trichloride reacts with potassium iodide in solution, exchanging Cl⁻ for I⁻ to afford antimony triiodide as a solid precipitate and soluble potassium chloride. Typically carried out in water or ethanol at room temperature; the precipitation of SbI₃ drives the reaction. No catalyst needed.

Electrophilic bromination of p‑benzoquinone to give 2,6‑dibromo‑p‑benzoquinone. The bromine is added in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, often at 0 °C to ambient temperature, in the dark to avoid radical side reactions; no additional catalyst is required.

Formation of the chromium(VI) pyridine complex trioxobis(pyridine)chromium from sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid in the presence of excess pyridine; the dichromate is protonated and coordinates two pyridine ligands, yielding CrO3(pyridine)2 and sodium hydrogen sulfate. Conducted by mixing the reagents at 0–25 °C; the reaction proceeds without external reducing agents.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; sulfuric acid protonates copper(II) oxalate and exchanges cations to produce soluble copper(II) sulfate and free oxalic acid. Typically performed by stirring solid copper(II) oxalate in dilute H₂SO₄ with gentle heating. Water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of sulfide ion; Na₂S provides S²⁻ which attacks pent bromide to form di‑n‑pentyl sulfide and NaBr. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO under reflux (or in aqueous Na₂S solution). No additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (hydrogenolysis) of an amide to a primary amine; purpose is to reduce the carbonyl of the amide to a methylene, giving the corresponding benzylamine. Key transformation: Pd/C mediates addition of H₂ across the C=O bond of 1‑(4‑chloro)benzamide, cleaving the amide to produce 4‑chlorobenzylamine and water. Typical conditions: 50–100 bar H₂ pressure, 80–120 °C, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or THF; catalyst loading 5–10 wt % Pd on carbon, reaction time 4–12 h under stirring.

Thermal dehalogenation (pyrolytic decomposition) of hexachloroethane; at high temperature the compound fragments to give chlorine gas and tetrachloroethylene (C₂Cl₄). Conducted in a sealed tube or furnace at 400–600 °C, often under inert atmosphere; typically solvent‑free, occasionally with a metal chloride catalyst (e.g., CuCl) to assist Cl₂ evolution.

Acid‑catalyzed ether hydrolysis; water attacks the methyl ether of 3‑methoxy‑1,2‑propanediol, cleaving the C–O bond to yield glycerol and methanol. Performed in aqueous dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) under reflux. Water is the solvent; acid serves as catalyst.

Condensation (nucleophilic substitution) forming a P–CH₂–P bond; the P‑H of phosphorous acid attacks chloromethylphosphonic acid, displacing chloride as HCl and producing methylene diphosphonic acid. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium, heated to 50–80 °C, with pH control; no external catalyst required.

Reductive amination (Leuckart reaction); 1‑phenyl‑2‑propanone reacts with ammonium formate, which supplies ammonia and formic acid; the imine formed is reduced in situ to give amphetamine, subsequently isolated as the hydrochloride salt. Conducted by heating the mixture at 150–200 °C in a sealed tube; the formate acts as both nitrogen source and reducing agent, no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidation; SeO₂ acts as a mild oxidant converting the benzylic methylene of 1,2‑indandione into an additional carbonyl, giving indan‑1,2,3‑trione while elemental selenium is reduced; typically performed by refluxing the substrate with SeO₂ in a polar aprotic solvent such as dioxane or 1,4‑dioxane under inert atmosphere.

Reaction type: acid–base neutralization/precipitation; Purpose: synthesize calcium phosphate precipitate; Key transformation: carbonate anion is protonated to CO₂ and water while Ca²⁺ combines with phosphate to form Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (or CaHPO₄ depending on stoichiometry); Typical conditions: dilute phosphoric acid added to solid CaCO₃, gentle heating may be applied to drive off CO₂; Common solvent/catalyst: water, no catalyst.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation); CrO₃/H₂SO₄ oxidizes the primary alcohol of tetrahydrofuran‑3‑methanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid, tetrarofuran‑3‑carboxylic acid, with water as by‑product; carried out in aqueous acetone or a mixed acetone‑water solvent at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid‑base neutralization; lead carbonate reacts with acetic acid, an acid‑carbonate reaction that liberates CO₂, forms water and produces soluble lead acetate; normally conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Oxidation of a secondary benzylic alcohol to a ketone using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). Diphenylmethanol is treated with PCC in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, converting the alcohol to benzophenone while generating Cr(III) chloride, pyridine, and water as by‑products. This is a mild, non‑aqueous oxidation that stops at the ketone stage.

High‑temperature oxidative combustion; zirconium phosphide reacts with molecular oxygen, oxidizing the phosphorus to P₂O₅ (phosphorus pentoxide) and the zirconium to ZrO₂ (zirconium dioxide); requires elevated temperature (often >800 °C) in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere, no added solvent.

Hydrolysis reaction: Decomposes neodymium triacetate with water to form neodymium hydroxide and acetic acid. Used to generate metal hydroxide; key transformation involves water attacking the acetate ligand. Typically occurs under mild heating in aqueous solution without catalysts.

Oxidative halogen conversion; aqueous bromide ions are oxidized by ozone to bromate (NaBrO₃) while ozone is reduced to molecular oxygen; performed by bubbling O₃ through an aqueous NaBr solution, usually at ambient temperature and slightly basic pH to facilitate bromate formation.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); aqueous sodium carbonate hydrolyzes tert‑butyl acetate, yielding tert‑butanol (2‑methyl‑2‑propanol) and sodium acetate; carbonate generates carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ + H₂O) as the acid counterpart; typically carried out by refluxing the ester with Na₂CO₃ in water.

Oxidative demethylation (Fenton‑type oxidation). Fe2+ activates hydrogen peroxide to generate hydroxyl radicals which cleave the methoxy group of 4‑ethylguaiacol, converting it to 4‑ethylcatechol and releasing formaldehyde; water is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, acidic pH (~3), FeSO4 (0.01‑0.1 M) and H2O2 (0.1‑1 M) added dropwise at 0–25 °C. No special solvent beyond water; reaction is usually performed under ambient pressure.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; used to produce a metal silicate and remove sodium ions. In water, sodium silicate exchanges its sodium for magnesium from magnesium chloride, yielding magnesium silicate (MgSiO₃) as a precipitate and sodium chloride in solution. Conditions: aqueous solution, often warmed (30‑60 °C) to improve precipitation, stirring; no catalyst; water as solvent.

Leuckart reductive amination of indan‑1‑one with formamide; ketone is reduced to 2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑inden‑1‑ylmethanamine while formamide is oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O. Conducted at high temperature (180–200 °C) in excess neat formamide, often in a sealed tube; no external catalyst required.

Ozonolysis of an alkene (oxidative cleavage). Ozone adds across the C=C of vinyl propanoate to give an ozonide, which on reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) is cleaved to formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and propionic acid from the carbon bearing the ester group. conditions: O3 gas bubbled through a solution of the substrate in dry dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by reductive work‑up at –20 °C to 0 °C. Solvent: CH2Cl2 (or CCl4); inert atmosphere (N2).

Dehydrative conversion of a diamine to a di‑isocyanide (POCl3‑mediated isocyanide synthesis). Formic acid acts as a proton source; POCl3 activates the amine groups, promoting loss of water and formation of two –N≡C groups on the 1,5‑diamino‑naphthalene, yielding 1,5‑naphthalenediyldiisocyanide. By‑products are HCl and phosphoric acid from POCl3 hydrolysis. Typical conditions: anhydrous pyridine or triethylamine as solvent and base, POCl3 (1.2 equiv) added at 0 °C then warmed to 80‑100 °C under nitrogen for 2‑4 h. No aqueous phase.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Aqueous calcium acetate reacts with aqueous zinc sulfate; calcium ions combine with sulfate to precipitate insoluble calcium sulfate, while zinc ions pair with acetate to give soluble zinc acetate. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water at room temperature, stir until precipitation complete, then filter to isolate Ca4. Solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation. Converts a hydrazo (-N-N-) bond to an azo (-N=N-) bond. Purpose: Synthesis of azobenzene from hydrazobenzene. Key transformation: Oxidative dehydrogenation of the azane-azene system. Reaction conditions: Ferric chloride (FeCl3) acts as the oxidizing agent. Synthesis occurs in an acidic aqueous solution, typically with dilute HCl.

Single‑electron transfer reduction of ketone to a secondary alcohol using samarium(II) chloride. SmCl₂ (often generated in dry THF, sometimes with HMPA) donates an electron to cyclohexanone forming a ketyl radical anion, which after protonation (from solvent or added proton source) yields cyclohexanol. Reaction typically performed at 0 °C to –78 °C under inert atmosphere.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction where elemental fluorine oxidizes bromide ligands of niobium(V) bromide to molecular bromine while fluorine is incorporated into niobium(V) fluoride. Occurs as a gas‑phase or high‑temperature solid‑state process; no solvents or catalysts are normally used. Reaction is driven by the greater bond strength of Nb–F compared with Nb–Br.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of 1,2,3‑trichlorobenzene. Molecular chlorine adds to the vacant 4‑position of the benz ring via an arenium ion intermediate, generating 1,2,3,4‑tetrachlorobenzene and releasing hydrogen chloride. Typical conditions: Cl₂ (gas) in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or CS₂, often catalyzed by FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, at 0 °C to reflux temperature.

Oxidation of the sulfide moiety in albendazole to the corresponding sulfoxide using peracetic acid. The peracid transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfur, forming Albendazole sulfoxide and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually carried out in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0–25 °C, with the reaction quenched by aqueous sodium bicarbonate.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ring‑opening) of tetrahydropyran to give 1,5‑pentanediol. Concentrated aqueous H₂SO₄ protonates the ether oxygen, facilitating nucleophilic attack by water and cleavage of the C–O bond, producing a linear diol after work‑up. Conducted by refluxing the ether with dilute to conc. H₂SO₄ solution, followed by neutralization and extraction.

Free‑radical chlorination of 3‑methylhexane at the tertiary carbon. Initiation by UV light or heat generates chlorine radicals, which abstract a hydrogen from the tertiary carbon (C‑3), forming a carbon‑centered radical that recombines with Cl₂ to give 3‑chloro‑3‑methylhexane and HCl. Typical conditions: Cl₂ gas in a non‑reactive solvent such as CCl₄, under UV irradiation or reflux, with excess chlorine to drive substitution.

Carbodiimidemediated amidation (DCC coupling) of a carboxylic acid with dimethylamine. The reaction is performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, using dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) and a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine as nucleophilic catalyst. The by‑product dicyclohexylurea precipitates, and the desired product is N,N‑dimethylbutanamide.

Strong reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; reduces 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde to 4‑chlorobenzyl alcohol; 4‑Cl‑C6H4‑CHO + LiAlH4 → 4‑Cl‑C6H4‑CH2OH; carried out in anhydrous ether solvents such as THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen or argon, typically at 0 °C to reflux; LiAlH4 provides hydride; no external catalyst required.

Acetylation (esterification) of 2‑ethyl‑1‑butanol with acetic anhydride to afford 2‑ethyl‑1‑butyl acetate and acetic acid. Typically carried out neat or in an inert solvent (e.g., pyridine, DMAP) at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMAP acts as base and scavenges the acid.

Nitrosylation of n‑butanol with nitrosyl chloride to give n‑butyl nitrite and HCl. The reaction proceeds via electrophilic attack of the nitrosyl cation (NO⁺) on the alcohol oxygen, followed by loss of chloride as HCl. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; a base (e.g., pyridine) may be added to neutralize the liberated HCl and improve yield.

Oxidation of osmium dioxide (OsO₂) to osmium tetroxide (OsO₄) by molecular oxygen. This high‑temperature oxidation converts Os(IV) to Os(VIII). Typical conditions involve heating solid OsO₂ in a stream O₂ (or air) at 300–450 °C, often in a sealed tube or flow reactor under elevated pressure to increase O₂ concentration. No solvent is used; the process is conducted in the gas phase.

Reductive conversion of an N‑aryl‑N‑methyl imine (N[(E)‑benzylideneamino]‑N‑methylmethanamine) to the secondary amine N,N‑dimethylbenzylamine using sodium borohydride. NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the C=N bond, giving the saturated amine and forming sodium borate as waste. Performed in a protic solvent (methanol, ethanol) or a mixed THF/MeOH system at 0 °C to ambient temperature; the reaction is usually complete within 1–2 h and requires quenching with water or dilute acid.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between sodium malate and calcium hydroxide in aqueous solution. Calcium ions exchange with sodium, precipitating calcium malate (slightly less soluble) while releasing sodium hydroxide into solution. Conducted at room temperature with stirring; the mixture may be heated gently (40–60 °C) to improve precipitation. No special catalysts are needed; water acts as the reaction medium.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde (nucleophilic addition); methylmagnesium bromide adds to benzaldehyde to form a magnesium alkoxide intermediate that, after aqueous work‑up, gives 1‑phenylethanol (a secondary alcohol); performed under anhydrous conditions in dry diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; quenched with dilute NH₄Cl solution; no external catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2,4,6‑trimethyl‑1‑nitrobenzene to 2,4,6‑trimethylaniline. Three equivalents of H₂ reduce the nitro group to an amine, producing two equivalents of water.
