Transesterification (ester exchange) reaction; produces ethyl octanoate as a flavor/fragrance compound; similar to reaction 0 but with ethanol; catalyzed by acids or enzymes; solvents often ethanol or non-polar aprotic co-solvents.

Diazo oxidation (deamination) of 9‑aminophenanthrene with nitrous acid; nitrous acid generated in situ from NaNO2/HCl converts the aryl amine to a diazonium intermediate which loses N2 and undergoes hydrolysis to give 9‑phenanthrol. Conducted in cold aqueous acid (0–5 °C) then warmed; water solvent, inorganic acid catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrite; isobutyl nitrite reacts with water to cleave the O‑N bond, yielding isobutanol and nitrous acid (HONO). Typically performed at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; no special catalyst required, sometimes a trace of acid speeds the reaction.

Jones oxidation of a secondary alcohol; 2‑heptanol is oxidized by chromium(VI) oxide in the presence of sulfuric acid to afford 2‑heptanone, while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) sulfate and water is formed. Reaction is carried out in a mixture of aqueous H2SO4 and an organic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid–base/fluorination of a rare‑earth hydroxide; purpose is synthesis of SmF3 from the hydroxide precursor; key transformation: Sm(OH)3 + 3 HF → SmF3 + 3 H2O; typical conditions: aqueous HF solution at room temperature to 60 °C; water solvent, no catalyst needed.

Conversion of an epoxide to a thiirane; ethylene oxide reacts with phosphorus pentasulfide (P2S5) to replace the oxygen atom of the three‑membered ring with sulfur, forming ethylene sulfide. Typically refluxed in anhydrous, non‑protic solvents (e.g., toluene, benzene) under inert atmosphere; P2S5 acts as the sulfur donor.

SN2 displacement of a primary bromide by cyanide ion to give a straight‑chain nitrile; conducted with sodium (or potassium) cyanide in a polar protic or aprotic solvent such as aqueous ethanol, water, or DMF; reaction is typically heated to reflux; cyanide acts as nucleophile and no catalyst is required.

Oxidative hydroxylation of an aromatic amine; aniline is oxidized by carbamide peroxide (urea‑hydrogen peroxide complex) to phenylhydroxylamine, with concomitant formation of water and urea. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media at mild temperature (0–25 °C), often under neutral or slightly acidic conditions; peroxide serves as the oxidant.

Acid‑base synthesis of ammonium carbamate; ammonia reacts with ammonium bicarbonate, the latter acting as a source of CO2/HCO3−, to give ammonium carbamate and water. Performed in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid–base dissolution (salt metathesis); strong HCl protonates the phosphate anion of scandium phosphate, converting the insoluble ScPO4 into soluble scandium chloride while releasing phosphoric acid; typically carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to improve solubility; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; molecular hydrogen adds across the C=C double bond of diethylstilbestrol to give the fully saturated dihydro derivative; performed in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) using a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni); purpose is to reduce the conjugated double bond and modify biological activity.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to convert D‑gluconic acid into its sodium salt; the acidic proton of the gluconic acid is transferred to hydroxide forming water while Na⁺ replaces the proton to give sodium gluconate; usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Halogen displacement redox reaction; elemental fluorine oxidizes bromide ions to bromine while itself being reduced to fluoride, yielding lithium fluoride and bromine gas; conducted in anhydrous, inert organic solvents (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, dry perfluorinated solvents) at low temperature (0 °C to –20 °C) to control the highly exothermic nature; no catalyst, but strict exclusion of moisture and careful gas handling are required.

Acid‑base neutralization forming an ammonium phosphate salt; ammonia neutralizes phosphoric acid to give ammonium phosphate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts, stirring until dissolution; no catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral) – cleaves the acetate ester to give 2-(pyridin-2-yl)ethanol and acetic acid; used to deprotect an acetate or convert an ester to the free alcohol. Typically carried out by refluxing the ester in water or a water‑miscible solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O); no catalyst is required, though mild acid or base can accelerate the reaction.

Double/precipitation and gas‑evolving acid‑base reaction; ammonium fluoride reacts with magnesium hydroxide, precipitating insoluble magnesium fluoride while liberating ammonia gas and water; typically carried out in aqueous medium with vigorous stirring; gentle heating (up to 60 °C) helps drive off NH₃; no catalyst required.

Precipitation (metathesis) reaction; hydrogen selenide, a weak acid, protonates acetate from silver acetate, forming acetic acid and insoluble silver side solid; performed in a dilute aqueous or mixed aqueous‑ethanol solution under inert atmosphere (to avoid oxidation of H₂Se); temperature kept low (0–25 °C) to minimize H₂Se volatilization; no catalyst, but the reaction is usually conducted in a fume hood due to toxicity.
Thermal dehydration (condensation) of sodium dihydrogen phosphate; heating solid NaH₂PO₄ at 300‑500 °C yields sodium acid pyrophosphate (Na₂H₂P₂O₇) and water; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis in aqueous solution; nitric acid protonates cadmium selenite, displacing selenite as selenous acid (H₂SeO₃) while cadmium forms cadmium nitrate; carried out in water at room temperature or with gentle heating to ensure complete conversion.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; installs a bromine atom para to the phenolic OH. Key transformation: substitution of a hydrogen at C‑5 by Br, giving methyl 5‑bromo‑2‑hydroxybenzoate and HBr. Typical condition: Br₂ (1 eq) added to a solution of the substrate in glacial AcOH or CH₂Cl₂ at 0–25 °C, often with a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeBr₃ (5–10 mol %); reaction completed in 10–30 min.

Strong hydride reduction of a ketone; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl of 2‑heptanone, affording the secondary alcohol 2‑heptanol; normally conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Ring‑opening reduction of an ether; LiAlH₄ reduces tetrahydrofuran to 1,4‑butanediol by sequential hydride attacks that cleave the C–O bonds; performed in dry ether (often THF as solvent) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, with careful quenching of excess LiAlH₄.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic or basic) of ethyl tiglate to tiglic acid; purpose is to generate the free trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑butenoic acid. Key transformation: ethyl ester bond is cleaved, yielding tiglic acid and ethanol. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) for several hours; after base hydrolysis, the mixture is acidified to precipitate the acid. Common solvent: mixed water/organic (e.g., water/THF or water/acetone) to improve solubility.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Thallium(III) nitrate reacts with sodium hydroxide to give insoluble thallium(III) hydroxide, which precipitates, and soluble sodium nitrate remains in solution. Performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed phenol‑formaldehyde condensation forming a phenolic resin; ZnCl₂ catalyzes electrophilic aromatic substitution of formaldehyde onto phenol, followed by polymeric methylene bridge formation (Bakelite‑type resin); reaction carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium at 60‑100 °C for several hours.

Thermal or photochemical decomposition of XeF2; XeF2 breaks down to elemental xenon and fluorine gas; induced by heating (≈400 °C) or UV irradiation; no solvent; performed in sealed quartz tube or inert vessel.

Selective carbonyl reduction of an α‑chloro‑ketone; NaBH₄ reduces 3‑chlorobutan‑2‑one to 3‑chlorobutan‑2‑ol while leaving the chloro substituent untouched; typically performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, with sodium borate formed as a by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed O‑demethylation (hydrolysis) of 2,4,6‑trinitroanisole; the methyl ether is cleaved by aqueous H₂SO₄, yielding methanol and the phenol picric acid (2,4,6‑trinitrophenol). Typically performed by heating the substrate in concentrated sulfuric acid/water, often at 80–120 °C.

Palladium‑catalyzed St cross‑coupling of a vinyl‑tributylstannane with 2‑bromofuran to afford 2‑vinylfuran and tributylstannyl bromide as by‑product. Reaction uses Pd(0) (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄) in an inert solvent such as DMF, THF or toluene, generally at 80–120 °C under nitrogen.

Acid‑promoted condensation of hydrazine with cyanamide in the presence of HCl to form aminoguanidinium chloride (aminoguanidine·HCl) with loss of water. Conducted in aqueous HCl, often at 0–25 °C, and isolated by crystallisation from the reaction mixture.

Simple acid‑base metathesis (neutralisation) between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxymethanesulfonate, exchanging ions to give hydroxymethanesulfonic acid (the bisulfite adduct) and sodium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) cyanation; converts the bromomethyl carbonyl compound to a nitrile. Bromoacetone is mixed with an aqueous or ethanolic solution of sodium cyanide, usually at 0–5 °C to minimize elimination, then allowed to warm to ambient temperature. The cyanide ion attacks the primary carbon displacing bromide, yielding cyanoacetone and NaBr. No catalyst is needed; the reaction is performed in water, ethanol, or a water/acetone mixture.

Dehydrative cyclisation of 2‑aminothiophenol with phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) to form benzothiazole. POCl₃ acts as a dehydrating agent and chlorinating reagent, generating HCl and phosphoric acid as by‑products. Reaction is carried out by refluxing the amine‑thiol in POCl₃ (or POCl₃/pyridine) at 80–120 °C under nitrogen.

Base‑induced E2 elimination of n‑butyl p‑toluenesulfonate with sodium ethoxide, producing 1‑butene and ethanol while forming sodium p‑toluenesulfonate. Typically performed in dry ethanol as solvent, using excess NaOEt, and heating the mixture (e.g., 60–80 °C) to promote elimination over substitution.

Cyclization/condensation reaction forming a 1,2‑benzisothiazolin‑3(2H)-one. The ortho‑aminothiophenol attacks the carbonyl of ethyl chloroformate to give a carbamate intermediate, which undergoes intramolecular nucleophilic attack of the thiol on the carbamate carbonyl, expelling HCl and ethanol and closing the heterocycle. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) at 0 °C to reflux, under an inert atmosphere.

Oxidation of geraniol with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); purpose is to convert the primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde (geranial, also known as citral). Key transformation: PCC oxidizes the –CH₂OH group to –CHO, producing geranial, chromium(III) oxide (CrCl₃·H₂O) and water. Typical conditions: dichloromethane as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, under anhydrous conditions; reaction proceeds in 1–2 h. No additional oxidant required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Erbium(III) iodide reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to exchange anions, producing soluble ammonium iodide and insoluble erbium(III) hydroxide, which precipitates. Carried out in water at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required. The solid Er(OH)₃ is isolated by filtration and washing.

Acid–base reaction; HF reacts with potassium oxide to yield potassium fluoride (KF) and water; key transformation is conversion of K‑O to K‑F; generally performed in aqueous HF, sometimes with mild heating; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid–carbonate gas‑evolution reaction; calcium carbonate reacts with nitric acid to produce calcium nitrate, carbon dioxide gas, and water; key transformation is protonation of the carbonate leading to CO₂ release and formation of the nitrate salt; carried out in aqueous nitric acid at ambient or slightly elevated temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Free‑radical halogenation (multiple substitution) of acetone to give 1,1,1,3,3,3‑hexachloro‑2‑propanone. Excess chlorine gas reacts with acetone under UV irradiation or with a Lewis‑acid initiator (e.g., FeCl₃, AlCl₃) to generate chlorine radicals that substitute all three α‑hydrogens on each side of the carbonyl. Typical conditions: carbon tetrachloride or chloroform as solvent, UV light or reflux with catalyst, and excess Cl₂ pressure. Reaction is exothermic and must be controlled to avoid over‑oxidation.

Metal‑hydride reduction of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol. Lithium aluminium hydride (LAH) delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde, forming the alkoxide which upon aqueous work‑up yields 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol. Conduct under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon. Quench the reaction carefully with dilute acid or water at low temperature.

Ketoxime formation (condensation of a ketone with hydroxylamine); hexan‑2‑one reacts with hydroxylamine (often as hydroxylamine·HCl) in the presence of a base (e.g., NaOAc or pyridine) to give (E)‑N‑hexan‑2‑ylidenehydroxylamine; carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; purpose is to protect or transform the carbonyl group into an oxime.

Oxidative coupling of an aryl thiolate with iodine; purpose is to generate a disulfide (diphenyl disulfide). Two equivalents of benzenethiolate react with I₂, forming the S–S bond and producing two equivalents of NaI. Typical conditions: room temperature in a non‑protic solvent (CH₂Cl₂, THF) with stoichiometric iodine; the reaction proceeds quickly and is quenched with aqueous Na₂S₂O₃ if needed.

Pechmann‑type condensation of acetoacetic acid with resorcinol to form 3‑acetylcoumarin; involves Knoevenagel condensation followed by cyclization; performed under strong acid catalysis (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) at 80‑120 °C; solvent may be ethanol or no solvent; water eliminated as by‑product.

Diazo‑coupling (diazotization) followed by hydrolysis (Sandmeyer‑type) converting 2,5‑dichloroaniline to 2,5‑dichlorophenol. In cold aqueous 1 M HCl, NaNO₂ is added to generate the diazonium salt of the aniline at 0‑5 °C. The diaium intermediate then undergoes aqueous hydrolysis when warmed, releasing N₂ gas and producing the phenol. Standard conditions: ice‑bath during diazotization, followed by gradual warming to 25‑30 °C; water is the solvent, and no external catalyst is needed.

Redox oxidation‑reduction reaction in aqueous acidic medium; potassium metabisulfite is oxidized to sulfate while potassium permanganate is reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(II); the acid protonates intermediates and yields water; overall produces potassium sulfate, manganese(II) sulfate and water; carried out by dissolving the solids in dilute H2SO4 and gently heating; water is the solvent; no external catalyst required.

Acid–base salt formation (deprotonation) of 5,5‑diphenylhydantoin with sodium methoxide; the amide hydrogen is abstracted forming the sodium salt of phenytoin and methanol as by‑product; used to increase solubility of phenytoin for formulation or analytical work; typically performed in dry methanol at ambient temperature; methanol serves as both solvent and source of methoxide; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization forming the ammonium salt of picric acid (ammonium picrate); the phenolic proton of picric acid is displaced by NH4+, releasing water; employed to prepare the less acidic, more stable picrate for analytical or explosive applications; carried out in aqueous ammonium hydroxide solution, often kept cool (0–5 °C) to avoid decomposition; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Salt metathesis reaction in aqueous medium; cobalt(II) sulfate reacts with perchloric acid, swapping anions to give cobalt(II) perchlorate and sulfuric acid. Conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of metallic terbium in oxygen; terbium metal reacts with O2 to give the mixed‑valence oxide Tb4O7 (terbium(III,IV) oxide); used to produce the stable oxide for ceramic, phosphor, or catalyst precursors; performed in a furnace under flowing O2 at temperatures typically above 800 °C; no solvent and no catalyst; the reaction is driven by heat.

Hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) of trimethyl phosphate by water; one methoxy group is displaced, yielding methanol and dimethyl phosphate (monomethyl phosphate); useful for degrading organophosphate esters or preparing phosphate intermediates; generally carried out in aqueous media under acidic (e.g., HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions at moderate temperature (50–80 °C); water is both reactant and solvent; acid or base acts as catalyst.

Condensation/cyclization reaction between urea and ethylene oxide to form 3‑ino‑2‑oxazolidinone with water as by‑product; the epoxide ring opens, attaches to the urea nitrogen, and intramolecularly cyclizes to give the five‑membered heterocycle; employed in pharmaceutical synthesis of oxazolidinone antibiotics and as a building block; typically performed in a sealed reactor at 80–120 °C in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., methanol, THF) or under solvent‑free conditions, often with a base catalyst such as NaH or an acidic catalyst to promote ring opening; water is generated and removed to drive the reaction.

Halogenation (addition) of an alkene: chlorine adds across the C=C double bond of 1,12,3‑tetrachloropropene to give the fully saturated 1,1,1,2,3,3‑hexachloropropane. Typically carried out in an inert non‑polar solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under dark or with mild light to avoid radical side reactions.

The reaction is an acylation with thionyl chloride. It converts an N-substituted carbamic acid to a carbamoyl chloride. Thionyl chloride acts as both a reagent and a solvent, and the reaction is typically heated. Byproducts include sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride.

Acid‑base double displacement (carbonate decomposition): ammonium iodide provides acid (HI) that reacts with barium carbonate, producing soluble barium iodide, gaseous ammonia, carbon dioxide, and water. Usually performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to drive off the gases.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction: hydrofluoric acid exchanges anions with strontium chloride, forming insoluble strontium fluoride (precipitate) and soluble hydrochloric acid. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; the fluoride precipitate is filtered off.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; Na2S in aqueous solution reacts with NiSO4, precipitating NiS while Na2SO4 remains in solution; carried out at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst needed.

Chlorination of a primary alcohol using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂): the hydroxyl group of tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol is replaced by chlorine, yielding tetrahydrofurfuryl chloride with concomitant release of HCl and SO₂ gases. Typically run in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichlorometh or pyridine, at 0 °C to reflux, under anhydrous conditions.

Acid–base neutralization / salt metathesis: hydrofluoroboric acid protonates acetate to give acetic acid, while lithium cation pairs with the tetrafluoroborate anion, forming lithium tetrafluoroborate. Usually carried out in water or a mixed aqueous‑organic solvent at room temperature; the organic acid can be extracted.

Acid–base neutralization forming a basic aluminum acetate; acetic acid reacts with solid aluminum oxide to give water and a basic aluminium acetate salt. Typically carried out by heating glacial acetic acid with Al2O3 under reflux; no additional catalyst required; the reaction medium serves as both solvent and reactant.

Oxidation of phenol to a quinone using manganese dioxide as the oxidant; phenol is converted to a para‑ or ortho‑quinone while MnO2 is reduced to manganese(II) oxide and water is formed. Usually performed by stirring phenol with excess MnO2 in an aqueous or alcoholic solvent (often acetone) at reflux; no external catalyst beyond MnO2.

Alkaline hydrolysis (base‑catalyzed cleavage) of muramic acid; NaOH cleaves the amide linkage, yielding lactic acid and N‑acetyl‑D‑glucosamine. Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution, heated (50–80 °C) for several hours; after reaction the mixture is neutralized and the products are isolated by chromatography or crystallization.

Hydrolysis of methylsulfonyl fluoride to methanesulfonic acid with release of hydrogen fluoride; water attacks the sulfonyl fluoride group, producing MsOH and HF. Typically performed by adding MsF to aqueous acid or neutral water and heating gently (room temperature to 60 °C); the reaction proceeds without catalyst, though buffering may be used to control HF evolution.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling: nicotinic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which then reacts with methylamine to give N‑methyl‑nicotinamide (an amide) and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Conducted in dry dichloromethane or DMF under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to rt; catalytic DMAP may be added to accelerate the coupling.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2,3‑dihydrothiophene to tetrahydrothiophene; molecular hydrogen adds across the C=C bond of the heterocycle in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂). Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, room temperature to 50 °C, catalyst loading 5– wt %. The reaction converts the unsaturated five‑membered thiophene to the fully saturated thiane ring.

SN2 (or SN1) nucleophilic substitution (alkyl halide hydrolysis); purpose: convert secondary alkyl iodide to secondary alcohol; key transformation: replacement of iodide by hydroxide to give isopropyl alcohol and KI; typical conditions: aqueous KOH, reflux 50‑80 °C; solvent water or aqueous ethanol; no catalyst needed.

Reductive amination; the ketone 1‑indanone reacts with ammonia to form an imine which is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to afford 1‑aminoindan. Conducted in methanol or ethanol, pH buffered around 5–6, at room temperature or gentle heating; NaBH3CN is the mild reducing agent.

Oxidative homocoupling of quinoline using ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN). The reaction couples two quinoline molecules at the 2‑position to give 2,2′‑biquinoline while reducing Ce(IV) to Ce(III) and generating nitric acid. It is used to prepare biquinoline ligands. Typical conditions: aqueous acetonitrile (or MeCN:H2O 1:1), ambient temperature, CAN (1–2 equiv). No additional catalyst is required; the nitrate serves as the oxidant.

Halide metathesis converting triphenylmethyl hexafluorophosphate to triphenylmethyl chloride by treatment with sodium chloride. The reaction swaps the PF6⁻ counter‑ion for Cl⁻, precipitating NaPF₆ and liberating the reactive trityl chloride, a common protecting‑group reagent Usually in anhydrous acetonitrile or dichloromethane at room temperature with stirring, followed by filtration to remove the precipitated salt.

Reduction; conversion of isovaleric acid (3‑methylbutanoic acid) to ‑methyl‑1‑butanol using lithium aluminium hydride. Key transformation: reduction of the carboxyl group to a primary alcohol. Performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C then reflux; LiAlH4 is used in excess (4 equiv) and the reaction is quenched with aqueous NaOH or HCl, yielding LiOH as by‑product.

Disproportionation of chlorine gas by aqueous sodium bicarbonate, yielding sodium hypochlorite, sodium chloride, carbon dioxide and water. Chlorine oxidizes the bicarbonate, producing hypochlorite (ClO⁻) as the active bleach species while being reduced to chloride. Reaction is carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C; excess bicarbonate buffers the mixture and absorbs CO₂ released.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); chlorination of 2‑chlorophenol to give 2,3‑dichlorophenol. Key transformation: substitution of an ortho hydrogen by chlorine, with loss of HCl. Usually conducted in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, at 0–25 °C, often catalyzed by FeCl3 or AlCl3; the reaction liberates HCl gas.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation; acetylation ofene with acetic anhydride to afford 4‑methylacetophenone (1‑(4‑methylphenyl)ethanone). Key transformation: formation of a carbonyl‑aryl bond at the para position relative to the methyl group. Requires a Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl3, typically 1.2 equiv) in a non‑protic solvent (CH2Cl2, CS2) at0 °C then gentle warming; acetic acid is formed as a by‑product.

Acid–base salt formation; metal oxide reacts with excess acetic acid to give terbium(III) acetate and water. Typically performed by heating terbium(III) oxide in glacial acetic acid under reflux; excess acetic acid drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst needed; common solvent is the ac acid itself.

Double E2 dehydrohalogenation of 3,4-dibromobut-1-ene with potassium tert‑butoxide, a strong non‑nucleophilic base, to form the conjugated diene 1,3‑butadiene. Performed in a dry aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, using excess KOtBu, typically at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere.

Double displacement (metathesis) halide exchange; sodium iodide and thallium chloride swap anions to form sodium chloride and thallium iodide. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously as the salts dissolve. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; bromine adds to the 6‑position of the aromatic ring of tetrahydroquinoline, affording 6‑bromo‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline and HBr. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as glacial acetic acid or dichloromethane, sometimes with a Lewis acid (FeBr₃, AlCl₃) to enhance electrophilicity.

Ion‑exchange metathesis; tetraethylammonium iodide reacts with potassium bromide to give potassium iodide and tetraethylammonium bromide. Conducted in water or an alcohol (e.g., methanol) at room temperature; the products can be isolated by crystallization or solvent removal. No catalyst needed.

Single displacement redox reaction; zinc metal reduces cadmium(II) ions to cadmium metal while beingized to zinc(II); performed in aqueous cadmium sulfate solution, usually at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann C‑S coupling followed by hydrolysis; conversion of 4‑bromobenzene to 4‑bromothiophenol using potassium thioacetate. Key transformations: formation of an aryl‑thiolate bond, then cleavage of the acetate protecting group to liberate the thiol, producing acetic acid and KBr. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (DMF or DMSO) at 80–120 °C under nitrogen, with CuI (5–10 mol %) and triethylamine as base.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with ammonia to afford a primary amine andide. Performed by reacting 2‑bromoheptane with excess liquid ammonia (or aqueous NH₃) at reflux or in a sealed tube, often at 0–50 °C for gas‑phase ammonia. No catalyst required; solvent is the ammonia itself or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol) if using aqueous NH₃.

Acid‑base protonation (salt metathesis); sodium 1H‑1,2,4‑triazolate is treated with hydrochloric acid to liberate free 1H‑1,2,4‑triazole and generate sodium chloride. Conducted in water at room temperature or gentle heating; the triazole can be extracted with an organic solvent if needed. No catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ether; Pd/C under H2 pressure cleaves the 1-(2-methylpropoxy)butane ether to give the two corresponding primary alcohols, 1‑butanol and 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, Pd/C (10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or THF, 50–100 °C for several hours.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous KOH reacts with yttrium(III) chloride to exchange ions, forming soluble KCl and insoluble yttrium hydroxide precipitate, Y(OH)₃. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Metal‑acid redox reaction; elemental zinc reduces trifluoromethanesfonic acid (HOTf) producing hydrogen gas and zinc triflate, Zn(OTf)₂. Conducted in anhydrous or aqueous acidic medium, often in dichloromethane or ethanol, at room temperature under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of Zn.
Acid–base neutralization; tetramethylammonium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid to form tetramethylammonium hydrogen sulfate and water; carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C.

Oxidative chemiluminescent reaction; in basic solution (NaOH) hydrogen peroxide oxidizes luminol, a process catalyzed by Fe³⁺ (from FeCl₃). The reaction generates excited 3‑aminophthalate, which relaxes to 3‑aminophthalic acid, releasing light, nitrogen gas and water. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (pH ≈ 10–11), H₂O₂ (≈30 %), catalytic FeCl₃ (0.1–1 mol %), room temperature; used for forensic blood detection.

Phosphorylation (esterification) of 2,2,2‑trichloroethanol with dimethyl phosphorochloridate; the alcohol attacks the phosphorus center, displacing chloride to give Trichlorfon (dimethyl 2,2,2‑trichloro‑1‑hydroxyethyl phosphonate) and HCl.ed 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, with a base like pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis; water protonates the 1,1‑dimethoxy group of 2‑chloro‑1,1‑dimethoxyethane, leading to cleavage to chloroacetaldehyde and two equivalents of methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (or other mineral acid) reflux in a water‑organic mixture (e.g., THF/H₂O) for 1– h.

Acid–base neutralization (metal‐acid reaction); preparation of a sodium carboxylate. Sodium metal deprotonates octanoic acid, producing sodium octanoate and H₂ gas. Typically performed under inert atmosphere in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with careful addition of metal to avoid vigorous evolution of hydrogen.

Direct combination (synthesis) halogenation; elemental molybdenum reacts with fluorine gas to yield molybdenum tetrafluoride, MoF₄; typically carried out in a dry, inert‑gas flow reactor at elevated temperatures (≈300–500 °C) under fluorine atmosphere; no solvent, reaction vessel must be fluorine‑compatible.

Double‑displacement metathesis (halide exchange) in aqueous solution; used to convert soluble CdCl₂ into the sparingly soluble CdF₂. Mixing aqueous cadmium chloride with excess potassium fluoride precipitates cadmium fluoride while potassium chloride remains in solution. Conducted at room temperature in water; filtration isolates the CdF₂ solid.

Peracid epoxidation; oxidation of the terminal alkene of diallyl ether to give glycidyl (epoxy) allyl ether. m‑Chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen atom, forming an epoxide and m‑chlorobenzoic acid as by‑product. Usually carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to 25 °C, with the reaction mixture stirred under nitrogen; the acid is neutralized after completion.

General type: N‑alkylation of urea with an alkyl halide (SN2 substitution). Purpose: introduce a methyl group onto the nitrogen of urea. Key transformation: the nitrogen nucleophile of urea displaces iodide from methyl iodide, forming N‑methylurea and releasing HI. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, temperature 0 °C to reflux; a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃, or triethylamine) is usually added to neutralize the generated HI and drive the reaction to completion. Reaction can be performed under inert atmosphere.

Electrophilic α‑bromination of a ketone. Bromine adds to the α‑position of 2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑one, giving 2‑bromo‑2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑one and HBr. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as CCl₄ or CHCl₃, with stoichiometric Br₂ (1 equiv). Light is excluded; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of an alkene (Markovnikov addition) to afford a tertiary alcohol. 3‑Ethyl‑2‑pentene is protonated by H₂SO₄, water attacks the more substituted carbocation, yielding 3‑ethyl‑3‑pentanol after deprotonation. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid (≈ 5–10 % H₂SO₄) at 60–80 °C; the mixture is cooled and the product extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., diethyl ether).

Carbonation (acid‑base) reaction; thallium(I) hydroxide solution reacts with carbon dioxide gas (bubbled through) to give thallium(I) carbonate and water; neutralization of a strong base by carbonic acid; performed at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; no catalyst.

Metathesis / acid‑base exchange (salt displacement). Potassium methanesulfonate reacts with hydrogen chloride (gaseous or aqueous HCl); the proton converts the methanesulfonate to methanesulfonic acid and potassium chloride is formed. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no additional catalyst.

Double displacement metathesis in water; thulium nitrate reacts with potassium chloride to give thulium chloride and potassium nitrate; carried out by mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature; water as solvent; no catalyst.

Oxidative roasting of a metal sulfide; zinc sulfide is thermally oxidized by oxygen to give zinc oxide and sulfur dioxide; performed on solid powders at high temperature (≈600–900 °C) in a flow of air or O₂, no solvent.

Benzylic free‑radical chlorination of 1‑methylnaphthalene; replaces a hydrogen of the methyl group with chlorine to give 1‑(chloromethyl)naphthalene and HCl. Initiated by UV light or heat in the presence of Cl₂ gas. Performed in an inert, non‑reactive solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at ambient temperature or under gentle heating; reaction is controlled to avoid over‑chlorination.

Redox/halogen displacement reaction; iodide ion reduces Au(III) to Au(I) while being oxidized to elemental iodine; produces AuI precipitate andCl; typically carried out in aqueous solution of NaI, heated to reflux or gently heated; no external catalyst required; inert atmosphere may be used to prevent oxidation of iodine.

Synthesis/combination reaction; elemental barium metal reacts directly with chlorine gas to form barium chloride, an ionic salt; highly exothermic, often proceeds spontaneously upon contact; performed in a dry, inert environment (e.g., glove box) or in a sealed reaction vessel; no solvent; temperature controlled to manage vigor of reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); cyanide displaces bromide in 2‑bromoethanol to form 2‑cyanoethanol. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to 50 °C with NaCN; NaBr is generated as by‑product.

Thermal decomposition of an acyl azide; acetyl azide undergoes thermolysis, releasing nitrogen gas and forming ketene (CH2=C=O); useful for generating ketene in situ for polymerization or carbonylation reactions; carried out by heating acetyl azide (≈60‑100 °C) under an inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar); commonly performed in anhydrous, aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane, toluene, or in the gas phase; no catalyst required, but rapid removal of N₂ drives the reaction forward.

Acid–base/precipitation (salt metathesis) reaction; potassium titanate reacts with nitric acid to protonate the titanate framework, yielding soluble potassium nitrate and insoluble titanium dioxide solid; purpose is to isolate TiO₂ or to neutralize titanate waste; conducted in aqueous solution, typically with dilute HNO₃ at 50‑80 °C under stirring; the mixture is filtered to collect TiO₂; no special catalyst needed.

Double displacement precipitation; employed to produce silver arsenate as an insoluble pigment or analytical precipitate. Key transformation: Ag⁺ replaces Na⁺, yielding Ag3AsO4 solid and NaNO3 in solution. Conducted in water, often at ambient temperature; light exposure should be minimized. No catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement/acid‑base reaction; phosphoric acid protonates cobalt(II) chloride, producing cobalt(II) phosphate precipitate and hydrogen chloride; used for preparation of cobalt phosphate or for removal of chloride ions; performed in water with aqueous H₃PO₄ added to a CoCl₂ solution; the mixture is often heated mildly (30‑60 °C) to enhance precipitation; the solid is filtered, and the filtrate contains HCl (often retained in solution); no catalyst required.

High‑temperature redox (metallothermic reduction) reaction; carbon acts as a reducing agent for cadmium oxide, reducing Cd²⁺ to metallic cadmium while oxidizing to CO₂; employed in metal extraction or alloy preparation; carried out in a furnace at 800‑1000 °C in a sealed crucible or tube to contain gases; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst; the produced CO₂ is vented or captured.

Acid–base neutralisation; converts carbamic acid into potassium carbamate; deprotonation of the –NHCOOH group by KOH gives water and the carbamate anion; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution ambient temperature; no catalyst required; common solvent water or MeOH.

Base‑promoted intramolecular cyclisation to a β‑lactone; synthesises β‑propiolactone from 3‑iodopropionic acid; SN2 displacement of iodide by the carboxylate oxygen closes a four‑membered ring, producing β‑propiolactone and NaI; typically performed with aqueous NaOH (or NaOH in ethanol) under reflux for several hours; solvent water/ethanol; no additional catalyst.

Reductive amination of benzaldehyde with dimethylamine; forms N,N‑dimethylbenzylamine; aldehyde condenses with dimethylamine to an imine which is then reduced; common conditions use NaBH3CN or NaBH(OAc)3 in MeOH at 0 °C‑rt, or H2/Pd‑C in ethanol; solvent methanol or ethanol; catalyst Pd/C if hydrogenation is employed.

Acid–base proton transfer (neutralisation); generates tert‑butyl alcohol and sodium acetate; t‑butoxide deprotonates acetic acid, yielding tert‑butanol and acetate; usually run in an aprotic solvent such as THF or in tert‑butanol itself at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst needed.

Strong oxidative conversion of benzylic alcohol to carboxylic acid; oxidises (4‑iodophenyl)methanol to 4‑iodobenzoic acid; KMnO4 oxidises the –CH2OH group to –COOH while Mn(VII) is reduced to MnO2; typical conditions are aqueous alkaline KMn4, heated under reflux; solvent water or aqueous acetone; MnO2 precipitates as by‑product.

Condensation (hydrazone formation) of acetone with hydrazine. The carbonyl group reacts with the –NH2 of hydrazine, eliminating water to give acetone‑hydrazone (C=NNH2). Performed by refluxing the reagents in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid, and removal of water (Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation). Solvent: ethanol, methanol, or benzene as azeotrope.

Silane‑mediated deoxygenation of a phosph oxide; regenerates triphenylphosphine from its oxide; trichlorosilane reduces P=O to P, producing SiCl4, and triethylamine scavenges HCl as Et3NHCl; performed under inert atmosphere in dry THF or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C‑rt; base (Et3N) is required, no metal catalyst.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol using ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN); purpose is to convert cyclohexanol to the corresponding ketone. Key transformation is removal of two hydrogen atoms from the alcohol to form a carbonyl group while Ce(IV) is reduced to Ce(III). Typically carried out in a mixture of water and acetonitrile (or acetone) at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst and generates nitric acid and water as by‑products.

Hydrocyanation (addition) of acetylene; used to produce acrylonitrile monomer; HCN adds across the C≡C bond to give CH2=CH‑CN; performed at 150‑200 °C under 70‑100 atm HCN/acetylene, catalyzed by nickel or copper cyanide complexes (e.g., Ni(CO)4, CuCN); typically gas‑phase over catalyst or in water/organic solvent.

Fischer esterification; converts 3,5-dinitrobenzoic acid to its methyl ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carboxyl carbon with loss of water; typically performed under reflux in excess methanol with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) and removal of water to drive equilibrium.

Salt metathesis/ligand exchange to form a copper(I) acitrile complex; acetate ligands are displaced by acetonitrile and the acetate anion pairs with Ag⁺ to precipitate AgOAc, yielding [Cu(CH₃CN)₄]PF₆; carried out in dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature under inert atmosphere; silver hexafluorophosphate is used as the PF₆⁻ source and the AgOAc precipitate is filtered off.

Formation of a mesylate from 3‑pentanol using methanesulfonyl chloride and triethylamine. Triethylamine deprotonates the alcohol and traps HCl as triethylammonium chloride, yielding 3‑pentyl methanesulfonate, a good leaving group for subsequent substitution reactions. Conducted in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) using acetic anhydride to acylate tert‑butylamine, with pyridine acting as a base to scavenger the generated acetic acid; produces N‑tert‑butylacetamide; typically run in dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen, and the reaction mixture is quenched with water after completion.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation; sodium tungstate (Na2WO4) reacts with sulfuric acid to protonate the tungstate anion, yielding tungstic acid (H2WO4, often as a hydrated polymer) and sodium sulfate (Na2SO4). Performed in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C to control crystallization; no catalyst needed, water is the solvent.

Hydrolysis (or methanolysis) of dimethyl carbonate to give methanol and carbon dioxide; overall cleavage of the carbonate ester to two equivalents of methanol with release of CO₂; usually requires heating (80–120 °C) in aqueous medium, often with a base such as NaOH or K₂CO₃ to accelerate the reaction; the CO₂ evolves as gas and methanol remains in solution.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination) of m‑xylene: chlorine, activated by a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃, attacks the aromatic ring of 1,3‑dimethylbenzene preferentially at the ortho position, yielding 1‑chloro‑2,3‑dimethylbenzene and HCl. The reaction is typically carried out at 0–25 °C in a non‑polar solvent like carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane.

Oxidative chlorination (redox halogenation) of silver sulfide with chlorine gas; chlorine oxidizes sulfide to elemental sulfur while forming insoluble silver chloride precipitate; performed by passing dry Cl₂ gas over solid Ag₂S at ambient temperature, often in a sealed glass tube or under anhydrous conditions to avoid moisture interfering.

Oxidative coupling (thiol oxidation) using hydrogen peroxide. Phenyl mercaptan reacts with H₂O₂, forming diphenyl disulfide and water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions are aqueous or mixed organic–aqueous media (e.g., MeOH/H₂O) at 0–25 °C, often under mildly basic pH (Na₂CO₃ or NaHCO₃) to prevent over‑oxidation to sulfonic acid.

Strong hydride reduction of protocatechuic acid (3,4‑dihydroxybenzoic acid) to the corresponding benzyl alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; each carboxylic acid is reduced to a primary alcohol, yielding 3,4‑dihydroxybenzyl alcohol; conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, with careful quench of excess LiAlH₄; lithium aluminate is generated as the inorganic by‑product.

Type: Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: To prepare insoluble iron(II) molybdate and exchange the counter‑ions. Key transformation: Ferrous ammonium sulfate reacts with sodium molybdate in aqueous solution, exchanging Na⁺ and NH₄⁺ ions to give sodium sulfate, ammonium sulfate (both soluble) and precipitating iron(II) molybdate. Conditions: Stirring an aqueous mixture at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously. Solvent: Water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification using an acyl chloride); 1‑propanol attacks acetyl chloride to give propyl acetate and HCl; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, with pyridine acting as HCl scavenger; reaction at 0 °C to room temperature.

Metathesis precipitation (double‑displacement). Barium perchlorate reacts with ammonium oxalate in water; barium oxalate precipitates while ammonium perchlorate remains in solution. The reaction is carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; the BaC₂O₄ solid is isolated by filtration.

Type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acetylation) of an O‑methylhydroxylammonium salt. Purpose: Synthesis of N‑methoxyacetamide (a protected hydroxylamine derivative). Key transformation: The nitrogen of O‑methylhydroxylammonium chloride attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, yielding N‑methoxyacetamide, releasing one equivalent of acetic acid and chloride which pairs with the generated H⁺ to form HCl. Conditions: Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, at 0 °C to, often under a nitrogen atmosphere to avoid moisture. Solvent/Catalyst: Pyridine or a non‑nucleophilic base can be used to scavenge HCl; otherwise the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Acylation of tert‑butylamine with formic anhydride to form N‑tert‑butylformamide and one equivalent of formic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack on the anhydride carbonyl, cleavage of the anhydride bond. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; the reaction proceeds smoothly without added catalyst. The generated formic acid is usually removed by evaporation or neutralized if needed.

Oxidation; alkaline permanganate oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Ethanol is oxidized to acetic acid while Mn(VII) is reduced to MnO₂, generating cesium hydroxide and water. Usually performed in aqueous solution at reflux; water or aqueous ethanol is the solvent; no additional catalyst.

Type: Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide. Purpose: Selective preparation of di‑n‑pentyl sulfoxide from the corresponding sulfide. Key transformation: Hydrogen peroxide transfers oxygen atom to the sulfur of di‑n‑pentyl sulfide, forming the sulfoxide and water as by‑product. Conditions: Typically carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, acetonitrile, or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, often with a catalytic amount of a mild acid (e.g., acetic acid) or a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Na₂WO₄, MoO₅·H₂O) to improve selectivity and rate. Excess H₂O₂ is avoided to prevent over‑oxidation to sulfone.

Type: Double displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction. Purpose: Exchange of cations to generate ammonium hexafluorosilicate and sodium hydroxide in solution. Key transformation: Ammonium hydroxide supplies NH₄⁺ that pairs with the hexafluorosilicate anion, while Na⁺ pairs with OH⁻, yielding NH₄[SiF₆] and NaOH. Conditions: Aqueous solution at ambient temperature with thorough stirring; the reaction proceeds readily. Solvent: Water; no catalyst required.

Metathesis (silver‑mediated anion exchange) – swaps iodide for tetrafluoroborate; AgBF₄ reacts with 1,3‑dimethylimidazolium iodide to precipitate insoluble AgI, driving the exchange; carried out in dry MeCN or CH₂Cl₂ under inert atmosphere at room temperature; solid AgI is filtered off, leaving the BF₄⁻ salt.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). Purpose: Conversion of potassium phosphinate to free phosphinic acid and formation of potassium chloride. Key transformation: Protonation of the phosphinate anion by hydrochloric acid generates phosphinic acid (H₂PO₂H) and Cl⁻ combines with K⁺ to give KCl. Conditions: Performed in aqueous medium at room temperature; the reaction is rapid and complete. Solvent: Water; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative redox reaction of iodide. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes iodide ions to elemental iodine in the presence of strong acid (sulfuric acid), producing potassium sulfate and water. Performed in aqueous solution, often with dilute H₂O₂ and concentrated H₂SO₄ at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis; oxalic acid protonates stannous chloride, precipitating insoluble tin(II) oxalate while releasing hydrochloric acid. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with mild heating; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of thorium hydroxide to thorium dioxide; purpose is to obtain the oxide from the hydroxide; key transformation Th(OH)4 → ThO2 + 2 H2O; typically carried out by heating the solid to 500‑600 °C in air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of ethanol to cyanate followed by hydrolysis (urea‑type synthesis). Ethanol attacks the cyanate ion to give ethyl cyanate, which hydrolyzes to ethyl carbamate while generating potassium hydroxide. Conducted in aqueous ethanol, usually refluxed for several hours; no special catalyst is needed.

Single‑displacement redox reaction in aqueous solution. Metallic copper reduces Hg²⁺ to elemental mercury while itself being oxidized to Cu²⁺, yielding copper(II) nitrate (Cu(NO₃)₂) and liquid mercury. Conducted by adding copper metal to an aqueous solution of Hg(NO₃)₂, often with gentle heating (room‑to‑50 °C), water solvent, no catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 substitution). The phenoxide anion displaces bromide from ethyl bromoacetate to form ethyl phenoxyacetate and sodium bromide. Reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, often at 0 °C to room temperature, under anhydrous conditions.

Swern oxidation; purpose: convert 3‑nitrobenzyl alcohol to 3‑nitrobenzaldehyde under mild, low‑temperature conditions; key transformation: oxalyl chloride activates DMSO at –78 °C forming the chlorodimethylsulfonium intermediate, which reacts with the alcohol; triethylamine quenches the intermediate giving aldehyde, dimethyl sulfide, CO₂, and triethylammonium chloride; common solvent: dry CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃; reagents are added sequentially at –78 °C then warmed to –20 °C–0 °C.

Acid–base neutralization (salt‑to‑free‑acid conversion). Hydrochloric acid protonates the sodium ibuprofen salt, liberating ibuprofen (the free carboxylic acid) and forming soluble sodium chloride. Performed in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature; the ibuprofen precipitates and can be filtered. No catalyst is required.

Halogen‑lithium exchange to generate an organolithium reagent.‑Butyllithium reacts with 1‑bromonaphthalene, replacing bromine with lithium to give 1‑naphthyllithium and butyl bromide. Carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑20 °C) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); no additional catalyst is used.

Redox reaction (peroxide reducing hypobromous acid). Hydrogen peroxide reduces hypobromous acid to bromine while being oxidized to oxygen and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution, often mildly acidic; trace metal ions may catalyze the reaction, but no specific catalyst is required.

Dimerization of silylene to a disilene. Two monomeric silylene units combine to form a Si=Si bond yielding a disilene. The process occurs under matrix‑isolation or low‑temperature conditions, often in inert gas matrices or cryogenic solvents; the reaction proceeds without added reagents or catalysts.

Single‑displacement (metal‑acid) redox reaction; indium metal dissolves in dilute sulfuric acid, producing indium(III) sulfate and hydrogen gas. Key transformation: 2 In + 3 H2SO4 → In2(SO4)3 + 3 H2↑. Typically performed in aqueous solution at mild heating (≤50 °C) to control H2 evolution. No catalyst; excess acid ensures complete conversion.

Copper‑catalyzed cross‑coupling (organocuprate coupling) of a Grignard reagent with a primary alkyl halide. The methylmagnesium bromide forms a methyl‑copper species with CuI, which then undergoes an SN2‑type alkylation of 3‑iodoheptane to give 3‑methylheptane. Purpose: construct a new C–C bond in alkane synthesis. Typical conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (THF or diethyl ether), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), catalytic CuI (≈10 mol %). By‑product is magnesium bromide (often precipitates as MgBrI).

Chemoselective hydrosilylation reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) as a catalyst and 1,1,3,3‑tetramethyldisiloxane (TMDS) as the hydride source. TMDS delivers a hydride to the carbonyl of ethyl benzoate, forming a silyl hemiacetal that collapses to benzaldehyde; hexamethyldisiloxane is generated as a by‑product. Purpose: obtain aldehydes without over‑reduction to alcohols. Typical conditions: dry CH₂Cl₂ (or THF), 0 °C to rt, catalytic TFA (0.05–0.2 eq), 2–3 eq TMDS, nitrogen atmosphere, reaction time 1–4 h.

Acid–base neutralization (carbonate neutralization); purpose is to convert hydrochloric acid to a soluble cesium salt while releasing gas; key transformation: HCl protonates Cs2CO3 to form 2 CsCl, CO2 and H2O; typical conditions: aqueous solution at 0–25 °C with vigorous stirring, gentle heating may be applied to drive off CO2; common solvent: water.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of pyridin‑2‑ylmethyl acetate. Protonation of the carbonyl by HCl facilitates nucleophilic attack of water, leading to the formation of pyridin‑2‑ylmethanol and acetic acid. Purpose: convert an ester to the corresponding primary alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–6 M), reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h, often in a water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst required. The reaction mixture is then neutralized or extracted to isolate the alcohol.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) using an acid anhydride; used to prepare N‑butylpropionamide. n‑Butylamine is added dropwise to propionic anhydride in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, THF, or pyridine, usually at 0 °C to room temperature. Pyridine or a tertiary amine can be employed as an acid scavenger to neutralize the propionic acid by‑product. Reaction proceeds smoothly under inert atmosphere; work‑up involves aqueous wash to remove the liberated acid.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between potassium carbonate and strontium selenate in aqueous solution. The cations exchange, forming insoluble strontium carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium selenate remaining in solution. Purpose: separate and isolate SrCO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, stirring at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (20–60 °C), followed by filtration of the carbonate solid. No catalyst is needed.

Transesterification of ethyl hexanoate with 1‑butanol to give butyl hexanoate and ethanol. The ester alkoxy group is exchanged under catalytic conditions, converting the ethyl ester into the butyl ester. Purpose: synthesize a higher‑boiling‑point ester or modify fragrance properties. Typical conditions: excess n‑butanol, acid catalyst (e.g., 0.5 % H₂SO₄) or base catalyst (NaOEt), reflux in a solvent‑free setup or in toluene, removal of ethanol by azeotropic distillation or Dean‑Stark apparatus to drive the equilibrium. Reaction time 2–6 h.

Acid-base protonation (salt metathesis); purpose is to liberate the free tribromoacetic acid from its sodium salt; key transformation: Na⁺ of sodium 2,2,2‑tribromoacetate is replaced by H⁺ from HCl, producing 2,2,2‑tribromoacetic acid and NaCl; typical conditions: aqueous HCl, often warmed or refluxed; common solvent: water.

Alkaline oxidative side‑chain oxidation of 2‑fluorotoluene with potassium permanganate. KMnO₄ oxidizes the benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid, yielding 2‑fluorobenzoic acid while the fluorine substituent remains intact. Purpose: transform a methyl‑substituted aromatic compound into the corresponding aromatic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH or KOH solution, KMnO₄ added portionwise, reflux (80–100 °C) for 2–4 h, followed by acidification (HCl) to precipitate the acid and filtration of MnO₂ sludge. No additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization forming an ammonium salt; ammonia protonates carbamodithioic acid to give ammonium dithiocarbamate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; water acts as solvent.

Base‑catalyzed ortho‑carboxylation (Kolbe‑Schmitt type) of 3‑phenylphenol; NaOH deprotonates the phenol to a phenoxide, which reacts with CO₂ under elevated pressure (≈ 1–5 atm) and temperature (100–150 °C) to install a carboxyl group ortho to the phenoxide. Subsequent acid work‑up with HCl protonates the carboxylate, yielding 3‑phenylsalicylic acid and forming NaCl. Typical medium is aqueous NaOH/CO₂; acidification is done with aqueous HCl.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using Dess‑Martin periodinane; the reagent converts 3‑heptanol into 3‑heptanone with high selectivity. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane; inert atmosphere (N₂) is often employed. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid–carbonate reaction and salt formation; copper(II) reacts with acetic acid, the carbonate is neutralized to CO₂ and H₂O while copper(II) is converted to cupric acetate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating to CO₂; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Intramolecular esterification (lactonization) of 6‑hydroxyhexanoic acid to ε‑caprolactone; purpose is to prepare the cyclic ester monomer. Key transformation: the pendant hydroxyl attacks the carboxyl carbon, cyclizing to a seven‑membered lactone and eliminating water. Typical conditions: heating (150‑200 °C) or reflux in toluene/xylene with catalytic p‑TsOH, sometimes under reduced pressure; Dean–Stark removal of water. Common solvents: toluene, xylene, or solvent‑free.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange; aqueous Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ swap partners to give soluble NaCl and the less‑soluble calcium butyrate, which can precipitate. Performed in water at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete exchange; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; phenol attacks the carbonyl of n‑butyl acetate, displacing n‑butanol and forming phenyl acetate. Typical conditions involve refluxing the mixture in a solvent such as toluene or xylene with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or a solid acid resin; removal of the generated n‑butanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium toward products.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an allylic chloride with aqueous NaOH, converting 3‑methyl‑2‑butenyl chloride to the corresponding allylic alcohol; typically carried out in water or mixed aqueous‑alcohol solvent at reflux, producing NaCl as by‑product.

Redox (acid dissolution) reaction: Concentrated nitric acid oxidizes copper(II) arsenite, converting As(III) in the arsenite to arsenic acid (As(V)) while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas. Simultaneously copper(II) is converted to soluble copper(II) nitrate. Typically carried out in aqueous HNO₃ under reflux; the reaction evolves brown NO₂ fumes and yields an aqueous solution of Cu(NO₃)₂ and H₃AsO₄.

Oxime formation (nucleophilic addition‑elimination); purpose is conversion of acetaldehyde to an O‑methyl oxime for protection or analysis; key transformation: CH3CHO + CH3ONH2 → CH3CH=NOCH3 + H2O; conditions: typically in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to reflux, often under mildly acidic (p‑TsOH) or neutral conditions; no metal catalyst required.
Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl isobutyrate with NaOH, yielding sodium isobutyrate and methanol; performed in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol) under reflux.

Aqueous double‑replacement precipitation combined with gas evolution: ammonium bicarbonate reacts with manganese(II) nitrate to form insoluble manganese carbonate precipitate, ammonium nitrate in solution, and releases CO₂ and H₂O; conducted at ambient temperature in water.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of N‑ethylsuccinimide using selenium dioxide to give N‑ethylmaleimide and elemental selenium; usually run in refluxing dioxane or toluene with catalytic amounts of SeO₂ under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive cleavage) of the lactam N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone to the secondary amine 1‑methylpyrrolidine over Pd/C; performed under high hydrogen pressure (≈50–100 bar) in a polar solvent such as ethanol or THF at 50–100 °C, water is generated.

General reaction type: hydrolysis. Purpose: decomposition of carbon disulfide. Key transformation: CS2 reacts with water to form carbonyl sulfide and hydrogen sulfide. Conditions: typically occurs at elevated temperatures; may be catalyzed by acidic conditions or transition metal sulfides. Common catalysts: activated carbon or metal-based catalysts.

Direct fluorination (oxidative halogenation) of molybdenum dioxide with elemental fluorine, producing molybdenum hexafluoride and oxygen gas; carried out at elevated temperature (200–500 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible reactor, no solvent.

reaction type: thermite reaction (redox). purpose: thermite welding, produces molten iron. key transformations: al(0) → al(+3) oxidation, fe(+3) → fe(0) reduction. conditions: high-temperature ignition (e.g., mg ribbon). solvent: none. catalyst: none.

Oxidation; converts naphthalene to 1,4‑naphthoquinone using manganese(IV) oxide as oxidant. Key transformation is insertion of two carbonyl groups onto the aromatic ring with reduction of MnO₂ to MnO. Typically performed by heating naphthalene with excess solid MnO₂ under reflux in a high‑boiling polar solvent such as glacial acetic acid or quinoline; the reaction proceeds at 120‑150 °C for several hours. No additional catalyst required; the by‑product manganese(II) oxide is filtered off.

Transesterification of cyclohexylmethyl acetate with ethanol; acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOEt) catalyzed exchange of the ester alkoxy group; purpose is to replace the cyclohexylmethyl group with ethyl, giving ethyl acetate and cyclohexylmethanol; typically reflux in excess ethanol as solvent, removal of one product drives equilibrium.

Redox (halogen reduction); sodium hydride reduces elemental iodine to iodide while generating hydrogen gas. I2 is converted to 2 NaI and H2 evolves. Conducted in an anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or DMF) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature; NaH is the only reagent, no catalyst.

Oxime formation; condensation of 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde with hydroxylamine to give 2‑pyridinecarboxaldoxime and water. Carried out in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote imine formation, at 0 °C to room temperature for several hours.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl bromide); phosphorus tribromide activates the primary alcohol and replaces the hydroxyl group with bromide, yielding 2‑methylpropyl bromide and phosphorous acid as by‑product. Reaction is carried out in dry dichloromethane or tetrachloride, typically 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; the PBr3 itself serves as the brominating agent.

Sandmeyer‑type diazonium decomposition (aryl fluorination); phenyl diazonium tetrafluoroborate thermally loses nitrogen gas and undergoes nucleophilic fluorine transfer from BF4⁻ to give fluorobenzene. Performed by heating the solid salt (70‑100 °C) in a non‑coordinating solvent such as nitromethane or acetonitrile; no external catalyst is needed.

Ullmann-type copper-catalyzed cross‑coupling (aryl‑aryl C–C bond formation). The organocopper species (copper(I) 2‑thiophenecarboxylate) transmetallates with iodobenzene to give 2‑phenylthiophene and copper(I) iodide as by‑product. Typically carried out under inert atmosphere at 100‑150 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO; no additional ligand is required but a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) may be added to keep copper in the +1 oxidation state.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; purpose is to prepare potassium phosphate salts; key transformation: phosphoric acid protonates bicarbonate, forming phosphate anion while bicarbonate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, phosphoric acid added dropwise to a suspension of potassium bicarbonate; solvent is water, no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization; methanesulfonic acid protonates ammonia from ammonium hydroxide, forming ammonium methanesulfonate and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; mixing equimolar solutions of the acid and base gives the ammonium salt, no catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid‑base precipitation; phosphoric acid protonates acetate from barium acetate, liberating acetic acid and precipitating barium phosphate. Conducted in water, usually with gentle heating to improve dissolution and precipitation; the insoluble Ba₃(PO₄)₂ is filtered off, leaving acetic acid in solution, no catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ to give soluble NaI and sparingly soluble Ca(OH)₂ which precipitates. Performed in aqueous solution by mixing aqueous NaOH and CaI₂ at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Electrophilic addition of chlorine to prop‑1‑ene yielding 1,2‑dichloropropane; purpose is to install two vicinal chlorine atoms; reaction proceeds via a chloronium ion intermediate; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂, in the dark to avoid radical pathway; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation between aluminum triacetate and ammonium hydroxide; purpose is to obtain ammonium acetate and precipitate Al(OH)3; key transformation is Al(OAc)3 + 3 NH4OH → Al(OH)3(s) + 3 NH4OAc(aq); typical conditions are aqueous solution, mild heating may help precipitation; water is the solvent.

Staudinger reduction of an azide – Methyl 2‑azidopropanoate is treated with stoichiometric triphenylphosphine in an aprotic organic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at room temperature. The phosphine attacks the azide forming a phosphazide intermediate that is hydrolyzed by water to give methyl 2‑aminopropanoate, triphenylphosphine oxide, and nitrogen gas. No metal catalyst is needed; the reaction is typically performed under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base decomposition/preparation of chromium(VI) oxide; concentrated sulfuric acid (oleum) protonates BaCrO₄, sulfate replaces chromate, yielding insoluble BaSO₄ precipitate and volatile CrO₃ plus water. Conducted by adding BaCrO₄ to hot concentrated oleum (≥95 % H₂SO₄) under reflux; the reaction mixture is anhydrous acid, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base salt formation (hydrochloride generation); HCl protonates the amine group of 2‑fluoroethanamine to give its hydrochloride salt. Typically carried out by bubbling gaseous HCl or adding aqueous HCl to the amine in an EtOH/H₂O mixture at 0–25 °C; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal oxide; ZnO reacts with aqueous HCl to afford soluble ZnCl₂ and water. Usually performed by stirring ZnO with dilute HCl solution at room temperature; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst needed.

Pyridine‑mediated transesterification / carbonate formation. Phenyl chloroformate, pyridine (as base) and methanol produce methyl phenyl carbonate and pyridinium chloride. Typically run in dry methanol with 1‑equiv pyridine at 0 °C to rt, under anhydrous conditions. Enables synthesis of alkyl aryl carbonates for fragrances or polymer precursors.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; carbonate ion swaps between Ba²⁺ and Ca²⁺, producing insoluble CaCO₃ precipitate and soluble Ba(NO₃)₂. Conducted by mixing aqueous solutions of BaCO₃ (or a suspension and Ca(NO₃)₂ at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a conjugated diene to a saturated alkane; H₂ adds across the two C=C bonds of penta‑1,2‑diene to give pentane. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 25–50 °C. No additional reagents are needed.

Acid–base redox reaction; sodium metal reacts with hydrazoic acid to form sodium azide and release hydrogen gas. Key transformation is deprotonation of HN₃ and formation of Na⁺N₃⁻; Na⁰ is oxidized to Na⁺. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous, inert solvent such as dry ether or liquid ammonia; a controlled addition of HN₃ is essential because both reagents are hazardous and the azide product can be explosive.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; cyclohexanol attacks phosgene to give cyclohexyl chloroformate with concomitant liberation of HCl. The reaction is used to prepare chloroformate intermediates for carbamate or polymer synthesis. Conducted in a dry, non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Oxidation of bismuth by nitric acid; purpose is dissolution of Bi and preparation of Bi(NO3)3; key transformation: Bi + 6 HNO3 → Bi(NO3)3 + 3 NO2 + 3 H2O (overall stoichiometry may vary with acid concentration); conducted in aqueous nitric acid, typically at room temperature to 60 °C; water is the solvent, reaction proceeds without external catalyst.

Grignard addition to a thioester yielding a simple ketone; purpose is to produce acetone from a thioester; key transformation: methylmagnesium bromide attacks the carbonyl of S‑propyl ethanethioate, the resulting tetrahedral intermediate expels propyl thiolate, and after workup acetone is obtained while the thiolate is protonated to give propane‑1‑thiol; typical conditions: dry ether or THF, inert atmosphere, 0 °C to room temperature; quench with aqueous NH4Cl; solvent is anhydrous diethyl ether or THF; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde to 4‑methoxybenzoic acid using potassium permanganate under basic aqueous conditions. The aldehyde is converted to the corresponding carboxylic acid while Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(IV) oxide precipitate. Reaction is carried out in water with excess KMnO₄, heated under reflux; the mixture is alkaline due to formation of KOH and the solid MnO₂ is filtered off after completion.

Oxidative cyclization (intramolecular oxidation) of sulfanilic acid in the presence of sodium hydroxide and sodium dichromate to give sodium saccharin, water, and chromium(III) hydroxide precipitate. The dichromate oxidizes the sulfonamide nitrogen and facilitates ring closure to the saccharin heterocycle. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically to 120–130 °C under reflux; the reaction proceeds under strongly alkaline conditions, and the Cr(III) hydroxide is removed by filtration after cooling.

Acid–base double displacement reaction; sodium carbonate neutralizes iodic acid to produce carbonic acid (which rapidly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O) and sodium iodate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction is straightforward mixing of stoichiometric amounts of Na₂CO₃ and HIO₃ with stirring until gas evolution (CO₂) ceases.

Oxidation reaction: peroxyacetic acid acts as an electrophilic oxidant that inserts an oxygen atom onto the sulfur of thietane, converting it to the corresponding thietane S‑oxide (a sulfoxide). Typically performed in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst is required.

Carbamoyl chloride formation from triphosgene (phosgene equivalent); purpose is to obtain N,N‑diisopropylcarbamoyl chloride safely; one chlorine of the phosgene generated in situ from triphosgene is substituted by N,N‑diisopropylamine, yielding the carbamoyl chloride and HCl; typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane or THF under inert atmosphere, with a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to trap the released HCl.

Acid–base/neutralization reaction: solid barium carbonate reacts with aqueous bromic acid. The carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ gas and water, while the barium cation pairs with the bromate anion to give barium bromate (Ba(BrO₃)₂) in solution. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring is used to ensure complete dissolution and gas evolution.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base) reaction: aqueous sodium cyanide mixes with aqueous ammonium chloride. The Na⁺ exchanges with NH₄⁺, yielding soluble sodium chloride and ammonium cyanide (NH₄CN), which remains in solution at low temperature. Performed in water, usually kept below 0 °C to limit decomposition of NH₄CN; no catalyst needed.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using oxalyl chloride; cyclopentanecarboxylic acid is treated with oxalyl chloride (1.5–2 equiv) in dry CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt, often in the presence of a base (pyridine) or catalytic DMF. By‑products CO, CO₂ and HCl are released, yielding cyclopentanecarbonyl chloride. Purpose: provide an acid chloride under milder, less odorous conditions than SOCl₂.

Condensation (urea‑amine) reaction: ethylenediamine reacts with two equivalents of urea. Each –NH₂ group of the diamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of urea, forming N‑substituted urea linkages and liberating two molecules of ammonia. The product is N,N′‑(1,2‑ethanediyl)bisurea. Typical conditions involve heating a mixture of the reactants in a polar solvent (e.g., ethanol or water) at 80–120 °C while continuously removing the evolved NH₃ to drive the equilibrium forward.

Neutralization/complexation reaction: chromium trioxide (CrO₃, often present as chromic acid in aqueous solution) reacts with ammonium hydroxide. Hydroxide deprotonates the acid, and the resulting chromate (CrO₄²⁻) associates with ammonium cations to give ammonium chromate ((NH₄)₂CrO₄). The reaction proceeds in water at room temperature with gentle stirring; excess base is avoided to prevent reduction of Cr(VI).

Metathesis/precipitation reaction: aqueous sodium fluoride is mixed with aqueous lutetium sulfate. Sodium ions pair with sulfate to form soluble sodium sulfate, while lutetium(III) cations combine with fluoride to give lutetium(III) fluoride (LuF₃), which precipitates due to its low solubility. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to improve dissolution of the reactants; solid LuF₃ is filtered, washed, and dried.

Radical recombination (termination) reaction; an ethoxy radical abstracts a hydrogen atom to give ethanol; CH₃CH₂O· + H· → CH₃CH₂OH; occurs in the gas phase or low‑pressure radical systems, often during combustion or photolysis; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidation; primary alcohol is converted to a carboxylic acid using chromic acid (Jones oxidation). The CH2OH group of stearyl alcohol is oxidized to COOH, generating water as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous CrO3/H2SO4 (or Na2Cr2O72SO4) at 0–25 °C, often in acetone or a water‑acetone mixture; the reaction is acid‐catalyzed and proceeds under stirring.

TEMPO‑mediated oxidation; secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone using catalytic 2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine‑1‑oxyl (TEMPO) and stoichiometric sodium hypochlorite. Cyclohexanol is converted to cyclohexanone with water formed. Typical conditions: buffered aqueous solution (pH 8–9) at 0–25 °C, often biphasic with dichloromethane or THF; NaOCl provides the oxidant, and a small amount of NaBr is sometimes added as a co‑catalyst.

Thermal caramelization/degradation; sucrose is heated to high temperature, causing fragmentation and rearrangement to the furanone flavor compound isomaltol. No reagents are added; the reaction proceeds by dry heating (≈180–200 °C) under air or inert atmosphere. Acidic catalysts (e.g., a few drops of HCl) can accelerate the formation, but the process is generally solvent‑free.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride; benzoic acid is treated with thionyl chloride (SOCl2), typically neat or in a dry non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane, at 0 °C to reflux. Gas evolution of SO2 and HCl drives the reaction to give benzoyl chloride.

Hydrolysis (reverse amidation) – cleavage of a hydroxamic amide. Salicylhydroxamic acid is treated with aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (NaOH) and heated under reflux. The C–N bond is hydrolyzed, regenerating salicylic acid and releasing hydroxylamine. Reaction carried out in water or aqueous methanol, pH 1–2 (acidic) or pH 12 (basic).

Base‑catalyzed lactone hydrolysis (saponification); sodium hydroxide opens the 5‑membered δ‑lactone of 5‑hydroxydecanoic acid, yielding the monosodium salt of the hydroxyacid and water. Reaction is carried out in aqueous NaOH solution (1‑2 M) at room temperature to reflux (≈80 °C) for 1‑4 h, often with stirring. After completion, the mixture may be acidified to isolate the free acid, but the description ends with the sodium salt. No special solvent beyond water is required.

N‑Acetylation of a primary aromatic amine (mescaline) using acetic anhydride; yields N‑acetylmescaline and acetic acid; performed in a dry aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, pyridine, or DMF at rt or gentle heating; base (pyridine, TEA) scavenges the generated acid; used to protect the nitrogen or to prepare analytical standards.

Thermal decomposition (thermolysis) of tungsten hexacarbonyl; W(CO)₆ is heated to high temperature, causing loss of all six carbonyl ligands as CO gas and deposition of elemental tungsten metal. Typical conditions: 200–500 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) or high vacuum; no solvent is required, and the reaction may be performed in a sealed tube.

Redox halogen exchange; bromide ion is oxidized by hypochlorite to hypobromite while hypochlorite is reduced to chloride. The reaction occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often near neutral pH; it is commonly used to generate NaOBr in situ for bromination reactions. No special solvent or catalyst is needed.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic or basic saponification); cleaves the 2‑octyl acetate ester into acetic acid and 2‑octanol by attack of water on the carbonyl, breaking the CO‑O‑R bond; typically performed in aqueous acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH/KOH) under reflux, followed by neutralization; solvent is water or a water/organic mixture such as THF.

Acid–base neutralization with gas evolution; converts Te(IV) to its sodium salt. Aqueous H2TeO3 reacts with Na2CO3, yielding Na2TeO3 (sodium tellurite), CO2 gas (from decomposition of carbonic acid) and H2O. Performed in water, often with mild heating to drive off CO2; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); exchanges the carbonate anion of potassium carbonate with the sulfate anion of nickel(II) sulfate to give insoluble nickel(II) carbonate and soluble potassium sulfate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special solvent required.

Synthesis of isosorbide diglycidyl ether from isosorbide, epichlorohydrin and sodium hydroxide. General type: base‑promoted nucleophilic substitution (glycidylation) followed by intramolecular ring closure to give epoxy (glycidyl) ethers. Purpose: produce a bio‑based epoxy monomer for high‑performance thermosets.
